en: The Commentary on the Six-Thousand-Line Hevajra Tantra (*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*). Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra! [He is] free from worldly conduct, consisting of the Victorious One, eternally arisen, all-pervading, beyond duality, stainless, the bliss of the non-sensory faculties, omniscient, and thus supreme.

Having prostrated with my body before the Buddhas—their peaceful mind which is non-mind, yet non-insentient, possessing all sense faculties in every respect, and their innate, immortal nature—for the sake of awakening; || 1 ||

The eight faces of the All-pervading Lord signify the destruction of the arising of the eight qualities; the hands are the eight liberations; and these skull-bowls are the sixteen emptinesses and compassion.
The crown-garland on the shoulder is composed of the reality of fifty letters; Akṣobhya is upon the diadem, along with the crescent moon, the vajra, and the garland consisting of skull-cups.
And those who have attained liberation through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], who possess excellent conduct, stand having crushed the Māras;
they are like serpents through their union with the assembly of afflictions and the knowable, wearing the skin of the leopard as their seal.

Having bowed to him for whom the obscurations of Māra and the like are but a mere trifle, and for whom the welfare of sentient beings is an ornament, I write this commentary on his secret tantra and its medical treatises. || 3 ||
This was composed by the illustrious Vajragarbha, who desires the welfare of all sentient beings and is a lord of the ten stages, for the sake of yogis attaining the path. || 4 ||
From the great tantra consisting of five hundred thousand [verses], this small tantra of seven hundred and fifty [verses], endowed with many vajra-words, has been extracted.
This work, which is considered to consist of six thousand [verses], was composed by one impelled by Hevajra;
it follows the Root Tantra for the purpose of illuminating that tantra. (6)
Those who will become teachers of the Yogācāra in this age of five corruptions (pañcakaṣāya) shall be the promoters of the true path.
Devoid of the commentary, those of wrong conduct will teach the minor tantras, eager to go to hell out of greed for the wives and wealth of others. (8)
Some, devoid of the five supernormal knowledges and so forth, will compose commentaries out of pride in their treatises on logic, acting as mere impostors of the Yogācāra school. || 1 ||
"Having diligently gathered Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva through empowerments,
some among us who hold the Vajra will say to men: 'All monks, even those who maintain the vows of ethical discipline, are not to be venerated.'"
Clad in white garments, we are ourselves the Vajra-holders to be venerated on earth.
Servants, merchants, Śūdras, those devoted to agricultural labor, fools who sell the true Dharma, and those who consume what is unfit for consumption—[these are the ones excluded]. || 12 ||
Those belonging to Māra’s host will become teachers of disciples,
concealing their own compositions under the very pretext of the practice of yoga.
They indeed speak of the faults [of a teacher] for the purpose of abandoning those faults;
however, the virtues of the teacher are to be accepted, and his faults never at all.
There is no doubt that pupils will perceive faults [in the teacher]—
one who is merciless, wrathful, cruel, stubborn, greedy, and unrestrained.
A wise disciple should not exalt himself before the teacher;
he shall by no means teach this statement to other disciples.
He who is merciless, a cultivator of the soil, wrathful, a piercer of vital spots, cruel, a hater of mendicants, stubborn, and arrogant with false knowledge. || 17 ||

Even one who is greedy, seeking not to enjoy [the fruit], yet unrestrained by excessive intoxicants, is said here to be one who, through self-exaltation, brings harm to those possessed of virtue. || 18 ||
For the Vajrācārya who has received the supreme consecration is worshipped at the three times by the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions.
Not understanding the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) and deluded by mere names, they will reject the teachings of the Lords of Jinas and go to the Raurava hell.
He who has been consecrated at the foot of the Bodhi tree by Vajrasattva and has received the supreme consecration upon his head is a Vajrācārya by the Tathāgatas. || 21 ||
The worlds that are the bodies of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions—by means of the five aggregates residing therein, one passes away and pays homage. || 22 ||
The world-systems, which are the crowns of those [buddhas], possess boundaries of various jewels;
by the buddhas residing therein, that Vajrācārya of yogins is venerated.
The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* (Sanskrit Text): Vairocana is the urine; the semen is indeed the *samaya*.
Just as Akṣobhya and Amitābha, so too is the Master who holds the Vajra.
Just as the preceptor is the giver of the seals of feces, urine, and semen,
so too is the Vajra-holder the giver of the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind.

The consecration which [is given] in the mandala for disciples and even for yogins, both conventionally and ultimately, as well as at the foot of the Bodhi tree, is that which [occurs] before and after. || 26 ||
Just as intentional speech (saṃdhyābhāṣa) is not non-intentional, so too what is spoken is not otherwise than what is spoken;
that Tantra, characterized by the six points (ṣaṭkoṭi), has a definitive meaning (nītārtha) and is not to be led elsewhere (aneya). || 27 ||

Those qualities of the Ācārya which have been shown through conventional practice are, by that very fact, the qualities of Vajrasattva, characterized by the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth. (28)
Steadfast, disciplined, wise, patient, upright, and free from deceit, he is skilled in the application of mantras and tantras, compassionate, and proficient in the scriptures. || 29 ||
The Ācārya is one who thoroughly knows the ten principles, is skilled in the work of drawing mandalas, explains the mantras, is serene in soul, and has conquered his senses.
A monk endowed with these aforementioned qualities becomes a Vajradhara;
neither a novice nor a householder [attains this], for there is no equality between those two and a monk in this regard.
Those endowed with the ten precepts, those endowed with the five precepts, and those endowed with ten million precepts— these three are considered not equal to you.
Just as it was proclaimed in the Root Tantra regarding the state of a Vajradhara monk, something concerning disciples who propitiate their guru is now briefly stated therein. (33)
Requested by Nairātmyā, the Vajrī spoke these words for the purpose of bestowing the precepts, exactly and in proper sequence: || 34 ||
Having first bestowed the five precepts together with the poṣadha and so forth,
and having granted the renunciation of the ten unwholesome actions, one should make him an upāsaka.
Then one should make him a śrāmaṇera by giving him the ten precepts; having given the ten million precepts, one should then make him a monk who has taken the vows.
Having then understood the Prātimokṣa, and thereafter the Vaibhāṣika doctrine, and having then understood the Sūtrānta, one should [understand] the Vijñānavāda according to its own nature. || 37 ||
Then, having understood Madhyamaka, the doctrine of the Perfection of Wisdom,
and having understood all other tantras, Hevajra is subsequently known.
Having emerged from the three vehicles, he abides in the fruit of the single vehicle;
herein, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Mahāyāna as the third.
For Buddhists there is no fourth, nor is there a fifth view of the Sage; emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is the cause from the very beginning.
From the vow comes compassion, and subsequently the fruit of acting for the benefit of the world;
indeed, he who, having accomplished his own welfare, causes the welfare of others to be accomplished, is truly wise.
How can one who is himself suffering and poor bestow happiness upon others?
Only one who possesses sovereign power and wealth, and who is dedicated to compassion for the sake of sentient beings, can do so.
As long as the cause is not directly produced for those who seek cause and effect,
how could the effect exist at first without a cause?

A vehicle superior to the Mahāyāna is spoken of as "the second" only for the sake of providing rest to those who have failed in generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth; it does not exist in reality. (44)
I have taught that the emptiness of all phenomena is the escape; for that reason, it is the escape, and because of the power of my vow. (45)

There will arise a great fruit consisting of compassion that is without objective support; compassion is traditionally said to be threefold: [compassion] directed toward sentient beings, [compassion] directed toward phenomena, and [compassion] without objective support.
Among these, that which brings about benefit in a limited region has some slight objective support in sentient beings and phenomena.
Of the accomplished Bodhisattvas who have established themselves on the ten stages.

For the Sugatas, whose selves abide on all stages and for whom the twelve links [of dependent origination] have been ceased, mindfulness is known to be without objective support and to act for the benefit of the world. (48)
Whatever the nature of the cause, such is the nature of the fruit;
for indeed, rice does not arise from *kodrava* seeds. (49)
As is the seed, so is the tree; as is the tree, so is the fruit. My speech is auspicious in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end. (50)
In the beginning, from the cause which is conceptualization, emptiness becomes the result that possesses conceptualization;
and in the end, for all Buddhas, emptiness is the result arising from non-conceptuality.
First, for the sake of purifying the field, one should sow kodrava seeds;
afterwards, once the field has been purified, one should sow the śāli rice crop.
It is said that the human realm born of the land of action is not impure;
yet birth within the six states of existence is impure, arising from the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious karma. (53)
For when the seed of compassion is sown in the field of human birth—which is pure and provides no support—it becomes a wish-fulfilling tree that grants all desires. || 54 ||
From the wish-fulfilling tree of emptiness, the fruit of objectless compassion—the thought of all sentient beings—comes to pass here; of this there is no doubt. (55)
O beloved, whatever mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth have been taught by me for those whose minds are devoid of fitness for the profound and vast dharmas.
In the future, teachers belonging to the host of Māras will teach Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva by means of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth. (57)
Therefore, the monk who is the teacher in the Mahāyāna is known as the Holder of the Vajra;
he is the one who has fully understood the three vehicles and who realizes the compendium of the Dharma. || 58 ||
The distinction regarding emptiness lies between the Vedas, Siddhāntas, and Yogas composed by Īśvara and others, and the Tantras and Mantras of the Buddhists. (59)
That deluded soul who does not know will cause his disciples to fall into barrenness. || 60 ||
Action does not exist without an agent, nor is there a fruit devoid of action;
she is the Great Illusion, the Great Terrible One, who effects the destruction of all beings. 61.
He himself is the creator, he himself is the destroyer, he himself is the king, and he himself is the Lord.
In the same way, the Māyā of the Lord is also called the Lord.
Even Janārdana, who is the subduer of the unruly and the protector of the virtuous, is described by the followers of the Śaiva Siddhānta as one whose dharma is inferior.
"Whenever there is a decline of righteousness here, O Bhārata, and an emergence of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself. (64)
"For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked, and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself in age after age. (65)
Having thus fully understood all this, Hevajra urged me to compose this commentary because of his inverted teaching of the Dharma. (66)
Having prostrated to the supreme body, which is innate and stainless, accompanied by the three worlds;
to that which is called the Dharma-body, devoid of the nature of pleasure and pain; and to the Sambhogakāya, the teacher.

I shall explain the concise secret discourse of the *Laghutantra*, which includes various emanations accompanied by diverse miraculous powers, resembling a magical illusion or a conjurer’s trick, and which contains a small portion of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (67)
This concise teaching on Hevajra by the Victor is here made perfectly clear for the sake of men;
it was formerly composed by the Buddhas from among the five hundred thousand verses of the primordial collection of tantras. (68)

Whether in the work titled *Lakṣābhidhāna*, which consists of hundreds of verses multiplied by a thousand, or in any other collection of *Tantrarāja* texts, the comprehension of the meaning is achieved through commentaries (*ṭīkā*). || 69 ||
He who would point out a hidden word in a collection of minor tantras that is devoid of a commentary,
would be like one who seeks the track of a long-vanished snake in a place lacking water and eyes.
The Jinas have taught that the Tantra is of definitive meaning and not of interpretable meaning;
if that which is of interpretable meaning is revealed by a commentary, then the definitive meaning is rendered useless for awakening. (71)
The entire tantra taught by the Jinas is neither intentional speech nor non-intentional speech, and it is neither of definitive meaning nor of interpretable meaning. || 72 ||

Those aggregates which are not feces and so forth, yet are impure, are not deities; nor have the aggregates been conceived for the sake of awakening by those who partake of the faces and arms of the deities. (73)

How could that Tantra, such as the *Samāja* and others, which was sung by the Blessed One and enveloped in six points, and which crushes the pride of learned scholars, be accessible through mere logic? (74)
This non-dual gnosis, which perceives the three times, is equal to a mirror or a prognostic image; it is free from the web of conceptual constructions regarding existence and non-existence. (75)
For the Blessed One has taught that there are thirty-two channels of seminal flow in Mahāsukha, located likewise in the throat, the heart, the navel, and the secret place. (76)
Furthermore, what were the foods [prescribed] for the joints of the hands and feet, as well as for the joints of the fingers?
Even in the *Hevajra*, they were not explained by the Jina to me and Vajragarbha. (77)
Those monks who proclaim the word of the Sage speak in Māgadhī and not otherwise;
whatever is the speech of the Blessed One in the Tripiṭaka, that is according to the opinion of Sthavira. (78)

Just as one disease may have another medicine for its cure, so too this fourfold refuge is the true means for the abandonment of suffering; it is not the mere words and syllables that the Sage intended.
That which was previously taught by the gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, and others, concerning the dharmas—wonderful, marvelous, and surpassing worldly analogies. || 80 ||

This very [teaching] characterized by the marks of the conditioned was spoken even by the Blessed One, beginning with the words "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam); is this not called "language" (bhāṣā) by wise people? Is this not indeed a marvel? (81)
That body of the Blessed One which is like a supreme Indra’s net of all aspects, like an illusion, and moving through space— this is what is described as "awakening" by foolish commoners.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and secondary characteristics, he stands within the mandala together with the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and their objects. (83)
In this world, the dull-witted always desire to understand dependent origination;
however, in other tantras, it is taught through calculations such as destruction, arising, guests, and the fixed [elements]. (84)
Some, being even more childish, desire curd without milk, or [curd] without cows;
[they desire] cow's milk even when deprived of its source. What fault is there here for the ignorant? (85)
By means of Hevajra, this Cakrasaṃvara is to be known as the Four Seats;
indeed, Hevajra is thus the Four Seats through the very words of Cakrasaṃvara.
This Hevajra is to be known as the *Laghucakrasaṃvara* by means of the Four Seats.
The definitive meaning is to be known through the words of the Paramādibuddha and the Mahāsaṃvara tantras. || 87 ||
Thus, those seeking the path should always understand other tantras through other tantras, by means of summaries, detailed explanations, and commentaries. (88)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Introduction to the Tantra, titled "Praise of the Desired Deity," in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-Hevajra-ṭīkā*.
Now, the Tantra itself is being explained.

In this regard, first of all, having thoroughly considered the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*)—for the sake of those disciples who are free from constraints and act according to their own mental inclinations—the Blessed One, while abiding in the form of the syllable *Evaṃ*, surrounded by the *Ḍākinījāla*, and absorbed in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of Hevajra, was requested by Vajragarbha and questioned by Nairātmyā; thus, he taught this *Laghutantra*, measuring seven hundred and fifty verses, extracted from the five-hundred-thousand-verse *Hevajra*.
Here, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the Blessed Lord Hevajra together with Nairātmyā.

The means of expression (*abhidhāna*) is this collection of chapters, the king of tantras. The relationship between these two—the expressed and the expression—is characterized by their mutual status as the signified and the signifier.
The purpose is the conferring of initiation through entry into the mandala and so forth.
The purpose of the purpose [of this work] is the instruction through the revelation of reality.
Having considered these points for those people to be trained who are "devoid of restraint"— meaning devoid of the vows of a Śrāvaka—
and who act according to "their own mental inclinations," meaning with a mind intent on enjoying the five sensory pleasures.

"In this life" means that which bestows Buddhahood in a human birth again and again, and not among gods, asuras, and so forth. "By one abiding in the syllable *Evaṃ*" means by one abiding in the abode of all bliss through the cultivation of reality (*tattva*).

"Enveloped by the *Ḍākinījāla*" means by one characterized by the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), joined with the *Hevajra* samādhi, requested by Vajragarbha, and questioned by the wisdom of Nairātmyā—from the *Hevajra* Root Tantra of five hundred thousand [verses].

For thirty-two great aeons, the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva taught this *Laghutantra*—characterized by the *Māyājāla* of perfect enlightenment, consisting of twenty-two chapters and measuring seven hundred and fifty verses—as a condensed instruction for the sake of supramundane accomplishment through both mundane and supramundane truths. This is achieved via the generation and completion stages, through the meditation on the maṇḍala circle and through the meditation on reality (*tattva*).
In this context, "tantra" refers to the *Hevajra*.
The Tantra is the expression of Hevajra,
and it exists as the nature of both the signifier and the signified;
first, it exists as the nature of the Vajra Family chapter.
He abides as the essential nature of the chapter on consecration,
he abides as the essential nature of the chapter on reality,
and he abides as the essential nature of the chapter on conduct.
He exists as the essential nature of the chapter on the determination of the Chomāpīṭha;
he exists as the essential nature of the *Abhisambodhi-kalparāja*, the assembly of the circle of Yoginīs;
and he exists as the essential nature of the chapter on purification.

It exists as the essential nature of the chapter on the special consecration (*viśeṣābhiṣeka*), and it exists as the essential nature of the chapter on the king of rituals for perfect enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhikalparāja*);
these are the eleven sections in the first *kalpa*.
Then, in the *Māyājāla-tantra*: "Māyā" refers to the ḍākinīs; "jāla" means a collection; "saṃvara" means a gathering; and "together with Heruka" is the rule.

Right here, first of all, it abides as the nature of the chapter on the ritual procedure for the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) of the consecration-homa; it abides as the nature of the chapter on the determination of accomplishments (*siddhi*);

it abides as the nature of the chapter on the twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*) which is the introduction to all tantras; and it abides as the nature of the chapter on the essential meaning of the seals (*mudrā*) of all tantras.

He abides as the intrinsic nature of the chapter on the arising of Hevajra; he abides as the intrinsic nature of the chapter on the rules for the purification of the mudrās, the cloth, and the writing of the book;
he abides as the intrinsic nature of the chapter on the purification of food.

He abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the characteristics of the disciples to be converted by means of the Padminī; he abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the extraction of mantras for the purification of deities;
he abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the recitation of mantras.
The Blessed Lord Hevajra, abiding as the very nature of the twenty-two chapters consisting of the Sahaja-artha-yoga, Anujñā, Ādi, and Nidāna, addressed Vajragarbha.

Thereupon the Blessed One said: "The heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is gnosis, which is great bliss; that itself is the Lord, more secret than the secret, hidden even from those who delight in conceptual meditation. Oh, Vajragarbha, well done, well done!

O you of great compassion, listen to the heart of Vajrasattva, the Great Bodhisattva, the Mahāsattva, and the Mahāsamayasattva, known as Hevajra. These were the words of the Blessed One at the conclusion of the section on the places of residence.
Therefore, first the place of residence previously mentioned by the Blessed One is stated, followed by the Blessed One’s words of exhortation and Vajragarbha’s request for instruction.

Thus: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the Vajra Consorts of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas"—this is the phrase concerning his dwelling.
Now, as for the statement "Indeed, I have heard thus at one time," does this belong to the Teacher, the Omniscient One, or rather to the compiler or the requester?
In either case, there is no fault, because it is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);
for here, he speaks of exactly what was heard in the past.

In that case, there would be an absence of knowledge in the future due to a lack of thorough understanding from what is heard from others; furthermore, for the compiler [of the tantra], there would be an absence of meaning at that time because it was not spoken by Vajrasattva. Therefore, this statement is to be understood through the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) by means of intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
The definitive meaning of this is:
that divine [palace] shaped like the letter E, adorned in the center with the syllable *vaṃ*, is the abode of all blisses and the jewel-casket of the Buddhas. (1)
Mahāsukha Vajrasattva— he himself is I, the teacher; "Mahāsukha" is that which has been heard and known.

By myself, at one time, during the single-moment perfect awakening, the Blessed One Mahāsukha [taught] that all the Tathāgatas are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) according to the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*); their body, speech, and mind are the Vajra Consorts (*vajrayoṣit*),
and the activities of body, speech, and mind are the Vajra Consorts who possess the qualities of the objects— the elements such as space and so forth.

Through the distinction of the movement and return of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by way of the distinctions of the qualities (*guṇa*)— namely one, two, three, four, and five— he dwelt within the drops of awakened consciousness (*bodhicitta*) according to the divisions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, abiding in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), the forehead, the throat, the heart, the navel-lotus, the secret place, the navel, the private parts, and the jewel of the *vajra*, through the differentiation of the three qualities.

By way of unfolding—that is, by the reversal of that [delusion]—through the exhaustion of the qualities (*guṇa*) at the secret place (*vajramaṇi*), and through the exhaustion of objects (*viṣaya*) at the navel, he dwelt in these locations: the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), according to the distinctions of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth.
Thus, the culmination (*niṣpatti*) of the elements, aggregates, and so on, is said to arise from great bliss (*mahāsukha*) due to their being free from obscuration.
The syllable E is Locanā, the syllable Vaṃ is Māmakī,
the syllable Ma is Pāṇḍarā, and the syllable Yā is Tāraṇī.
The syllable ŚRŪ is Vajradhātveśvarī,
and the syllable TAṂ is Prajñāpāramitā; from these, the aggregates [arise].
And Vajrasattva is the letter Ka; Akṣobhya is Sa, and Amoghasiddhi is Ma.
The letter *sa* is Ratnasaṃbhava;
the letter *ma* is Amitābha; and the letter *ya* is Vairocana.
The syllable *bha* is Gandhavajrā;
the syllable *ga* is Rasavajrā;
the syllable *vāṃ* is Bhāṣavajrā; and the syllable *sa* is Sparśavajrā.
The syllable *rv* is Śabdavajra;
the syllable *tak* is Dharmadhātuvajra; the syllable *thā* is Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin;
and the syllable *gak* is Lokeśvara.
The letter *ta* is Kṣitigarbha; the letter *kā* is Khagarbha;
the letter *ya* is Vajrapāṇi.
The syllable VĀ is Samantabhadra;
likewise, the twelve sense bases are CI,
and the pillar is KĀ.
The letter *tta* is Māninī,
the letter *va* is Jambhī,
and the letter *jra* is Ativīryā.
The syllable *yo* is Atinīlā,
the syllable *ṣi* is Raudrākṣī, and the syllable *bha* is Śumbha.
The syllable *ge* is Uṣṇīṣa; the syllable *ṣu* is Vighnāntaka;
the syllable *vi* is Prajñāntaka.
The syllable JA is Padmāntaka; the syllable HĀ is Yamāntaka;
the syllable RA is the essence of wisdom and skillful means.
Vajrasattva, the Lord, is the thirty-seventh;
thus, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the six elements, purified according to their respective order.
The six aggregates, the six objects, the six sense faculties, and the six organs of action.
The activities of the six organs of action and great bliss arise from the exhaustion of the fourth [dhyāna];
thereafter come the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right endeavors.
The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
The noble eightfold path and the seven factors of enlightenment thus arise from the dharmakāya, which is intrinsic great bliss.
With the cessation of the fourth state, the body is in deep sleep;
with the cessation of deep sleep, dreaming ceases;
with the cessation of dreaming, waking ceases.

Through the sequential destruction of these [obscurations], the innate body (*sahajakāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arise in their respective order;
wisdom, mind, speech, and body become free from obscuration.
Consequently, hands, feet, and so forth are everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading everything.
Therefore, he is partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed, untainted, free from passion,
devoid of passion, stainless, with faults cast out, and free from disease.

Well-awakened, with a fully enlightened self, omniscient, the supreme knower of all, transcending the nature of consciousness, he bears the form of non-dual gnosis. Thus, free from all obscurations and consisting of the four bodies, the Blessed One Hevajra is the teacher and the lord of the twelve stages.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, Lord of the Ten Bhūmis, is the requester.

Thus ends the second chapter, which establishes the determination of the teacher, the requester, the title, the subject matter, their relationship, and the place of residence, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*.
Now, the request of Vajragarbha and the Blessed One’s reply are set forth in detail.
Vajragarbha said:
"By what does one become Vajrasattva? How does one become a Bodhisattva? Why does one become a Mahāsattva? And how does one become a Samayasattva? (1)

Having heard this request of Vajragarbha, the Blessed One said: "The indivisible is called 'vajra'; a being (*sattva*) who is the oneness of the three realms through this wisdom and logic is known as 'Vajrasattva.
A being established in enlightenment is called a 'Bodhisattva.'"
"Filled with the essence of great gnosis, he is called Mahāsattva;
by his constant abiding in the commitment (samaya), he is designated as Samayasattva.
Thus, the detailed exposition of this summary is revealed in the *Pañcalakṣa*.

Therefore, that very [syllable] is introduced there; the Blessed One said: "That which is revealed as the syllable *vaṃ* is called the indivisible vajra; the indivisibility of body, speech, and mind is denoted by the syllable *vaṃ*. //4//

The oneness of the three realms of existence is the essence (sattva), which is denoted by the letter *E*; the letter *E* is together with Wisdom (*prajñā*), while the syllable *Vaṃ* consists of the three families.
The Hero resides in the center of the navel, within the hidden sphere of the pericarp.
Endowed with his own appearing wisdom (*svābhā-prajñā*), he is celebrated as Vajrasattva. He is declared to be the two-armed Heruka, the very one who seizes the three worlds;
he is said to be the *svābhāvika*-kāya, the body of great bliss.
That itself is the Wisdom-Vajra (*jñāna-vajra*), and he is indeed innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
That very [state] is also called the outflow (*niṣyanda*), which is remembered as the "Single-Pointed" (*ekasūka*).
That too is the exhaustion of the fourth state (*tūryāvasthā*), the pure, supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
He who is established in awakening is also established in the heart-lotus.
The sentient being is said to be the syllable *hūṃ*, and he is indeed Akṣobhya;
he is said to be the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), and Viṣṇu himself is four-armed.
He is said to be the blazing, burning one, for he is indeed the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Vajrin, abiding in the wheel of Dharma, assumes the form of the bliss of cessation (viramānanda).
That very state is also called maturation (vipāka), which brings about the destruction of deep sleep.
Filled with the essence of great gnosis, he is called Mahāsattva. //11-12//

The Lord of the throat-enjoyment wheel is called Amitābha; he alone is declared to be Vāgvajra, the Tathāgata with the lotus in hand. He alone is called Supreme Bliss (Paramānanda) and is celebrated as Puruṣakāra;
by way of both the concealed and the revealed, he is the exhaustion of the dream state. 13–14.
He alone is the sambhogakāya, the teacher of the Dharma for the Buddhas;
he alone is Kiṭikiṭivajra, and he becomes the third Heruka.
He who abides eternally by means of the establishment of the samaya is thus described. 16
The moon, the semen, situated on the forehead as great bliss, is the being established in nectar; it is celebrated as the syllable *Oṃ*.
He is said to be Vairocana, for he is indeed the Body-Vajra.
He who holds the vajra of the body is Brahmā; he alone is thus celebrated. || 18 ||
Bliss is the form of Brahman; that is called the Form Body (rūpakāya).
He who holds the discus in his hand is said to be that very body characterized by emanation (nirmāṇa). || 19 ||
Through its unfolding, that very [state] is stainless; it is indeed the destruction of waking.
That itself is Picuvajra, known as the eight-faced Heruka. || 20 ||
The great hero has four feet and is endowed with sixteen arms;
thus, by way of the differentiation of the body, he is known as the fourth Heruka. || 21 ||

From the essential nature (svābhāvikakāya) arises the Dharma [body], from that Dharma [body] arises the Enjoyment [body], and from that the Emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) would arise; thus is the fourfold body. || 22 ||
Brahmā is the bearer of the body-vajra; Maheśvara is the bearer of the speech-vajra;
Viṣṇu is the bearer of the mind-vajra; and Vajrasattva is great bliss. || 23 ||
Thus it is taught in the *Mūlatantra* and in the introduction to the *Trikula*:
"The four families are traditionally held to be conjoined with the essential nature (*svābhāvika*);
that arrangement of the families is established by way of their fourfold activity."
It should be known by one who is engaged in yoga and who desires the path of the Buddha. || 24 ||
The syllable E-VAM is Vajrasattva;
the syllable HŪM is Cittavajra; the syllable ĀḤ is Vāgvajra.

Oṃkāra is the body-vajra; likewise, Hūṃ, Āḥ, and Oṃ. The meaning established by these individual syllabic designations is what should be grasped, for here the designation is not the syllable itself. If it were a mere entity, it would then be graspable by the mind or the eye.
But it is not so; therefore, the designation is apprehended by the ear, and the meaning established by this [designation] is what is to be grasped,
not the designation of the syllables, which is apprehended by the mind and the eye.
Furthermore, an object such as a jar or a cloth is not produced by clay, a wheel, a staff, a shuttle, a thread, bamboo, reeds, or yarn, nor is it brought into existence by a name;
for a name is merely sound and does not function as the causal basis for properties such as earth or fragrance, in the manner that clay is the cause of a jar.
Thus concludes the Blessed One’s instruction in reply.
Now, once again, Vajragarbha’s request and the Blessed One’s reply are set forth:
Vajragarbha said: "By what would Hevajra come to be, and what is the summary of his names?"
What is signified by the syllable *he*, and what is expressed by the *vajra*? || 25 ||
The Blessed One said: "By the syllable *he*, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the vajra wisdom (*prajñā*) are expressed;
that tantra which consists of wisdom and means—that I have proclaimed, listen to it. || 26 ||
The explanation of this summary is introduced from the Root Tantra itself;
therein the Blessed One said: "This compassion, which has no objective support for sentient beings or phenomena, is remembered as threefold.
The great sound 'He,' being without objective support, is denoted by the syllable *He*. (27)
Through the union of body, speech, and mind, that very syllable *vaṃ* is [the first]; by the word "vajra" is meant the syllable *e*, which is emptiness endowed with all aspects.
The meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of these two is expressed by the word "yoga."
The Yoga Tantra is proclaimed as the tantra whose essence consists of wisdom and skillful means. || 29 ||
This yoga is not [designated] by the word "means" (upāya) nor by the word "wisdom" (prajñā);
for this tantra named Hevajra is indeed without lineage (niranvaya). || 30 ||
All [tantras], such as the *Samāja* and others, consist of wisdom and means;
indeed, all Yoga Tantras are [designated] by various names for wisdom and means. (31)
The movement of the Yoginīs is where the means (upāya) is established;
thus, for the sake of the ignorant, I have described the Yoginītantra by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti). || 32 ||

Where there is the movement of skillful means (upāya) and the stabilization of wisdom (prajñā), that alone is called the "Tantra of Skillful Means" (upāyatantra); however, this is merely according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti). || 33 ||
To the extent that the meditations on mudrās and maṇḍalas are investigated, to that same extent they dissolve away as having the characteristics of arising and ceasing. || 34 ||
The meditative absorption of wisdom and means is characterized by the indivisibility of the three vajras;
it is the unity of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the non-duality of emptiness and compassion. || 35 ||
Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and furthermore, the absence of formative activity— these four are proclaimed as the liberations.
Compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are the fourth set, the divine abodes.
Because all phenomena are non-conceptual, they are imagined as non-dual by means of the unobscured dharma. || 36 ||
Likewise, the vajra-bodies are non-dual;
so too are the six aggregates, the elements, the objects, and the sense-faculties.
By means of that non-duality, the activities and the organs of action are likewise established as non-dual. (37)
The vow of all the Buddhas is established within the syllable Evaṃ. || 38 ||
"Listen as I teach the tantra consisting of wisdom and means, which is divided into three families, then into five families, further into six families, and thus into one hundred divisions. || 39 ||
This is the instruction on the Blessed One’s reply, the rule for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the Yoga Tantra. Now, the causes for the arising of the Yoginīs are explained:

in this tantra, the Yoginīs are the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the four elements (*dhātus*), and the six sense bases (*āyatanas*), [manifesting] as Nairātmā and the others through the division of the fifteen lunar digits (*kalās*).

The cause of their arising and abiding is the syllable *huṃ*, which is Heruka as the second. Therefore, one should know that the efficacy of those [goddesses] consists of gnosis and consciousness, just as the deities arise.
Thus, the wise know that the great *choma* (gesture) and the power of attraction are manifold.
"Paralysis, eradication, the immobilization of armies, and malevolent rites—
listen further, O Vajragarbha, to what shall be spoken.
Thus ends the rule concerning the cause of the arising and abiding of the deities.
Now, the cause of its arising is also stated:
first, there is "thus" (*evaṃ*);
the syllable *evaṃ* is the first cause of Heruka, and the syllable *hūṃ* is the cause of arising for the second—this is the rule.
Therefore, an entity arises through the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, as the various consciousnesses [arise] separately upon the path of objects and sense-faculties. (41)
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* (Sanskrit Text): "They are bound by the bondage of existence;
by that very bondage of existence, consciousness and the rest, as well as the eye and the other [faculties], are bound. They are liberated through the thorough knowledge of that."

Through the cessation and thorough comprehension of those objects and sense-faculties, they are not liberated in that way; rather, the six consciousnesses are liberated by means of the divine eye and so forth through the observation of past and future objects, according to the Blessed One’s statement: "That other is consciousness."
Likewise, other things such as form and so forth are also [of that nature];
therefore, it has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and ears everywhere; pervading the entire world, it stands. ||42||

Now, the ultimate cultivation of wisdom and means, as previously mentioned, is described by the words "the state to be cultivated" (*bhāvaṃ bhāvyaṃ*) and so forth. Here, the state to be cultivated is the nature of space, which is like a dream and transcends the reality of atoms;
through the thorough knowledge of that, non-existence is to be cultivated as the illumination of appearances by a mind free from conceptual construction.
Perception is defined as that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous;
it is of four kinds: sensory perception, mental perception, yogic perception, and self-reflexive perception.
This very cognition is the indicator, the motivator, the achiever, and is characterized by direct experience.
That very manifestation is established by nine similes, namely: a magical city, an echo, a dream, an illusion, a mechanical device, a mirage, a reflection in a mirror, the moon in water, and space;
thus, wisdom (prajñā) is the letter A.
For in that same way, Heruka is the non-existence to be meditated upon; Heruka is the wisdom-knowledge of great bliss.
As is wisdom, so is skillful means;
through the thorough knowledge of that [wisdom], non-existence becomes the object to be cultivated, and thus it becomes skillful means.
Likewise, in this context, as is the cause, so is the fruit.
The syllable *Evaṃ* consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*);
it resides in the body, specifically at the navel.
Thus, the great gnosis (*mahājñāna*), which is free from all conceptual constructions, is established as residing within the body.

The rule is that the wisdom of the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitājñāna), which is free from the conceptualization of the maṇḍala, the wheel, karma, and the action seal (karmamudrā), and is devoid of the web of discursive thought, is itself Vajrasattva, Heruka who seizes the three worlds, the svābhāvikakāya.

"Pervasive of all things" means that the Gnosis Body (jñānakāya) pervades these entities: the six aggregates (skandhas), the six elements (dhātus), the six sense faculties (indriyas), the six objects (viṣayas), the six action faculties (karmendriyas), and the six activities of the action faculties.
"Though residing in the body, he is not born of the body," because of the absence of arising and passing away;
here, in the second chapter on the determination of siddhis within the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, in the second kalpa, follows Vajragarbha’s request and the Blessed One’s reply.
That [pleasure of the two organs] was taught by way of the generation stage (*utpannakrama*) for the sake of awakening foolish people through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).

As Vajragarbha said: "In the yoga of the generation stage, great bliss indeed exists within the six voids; yet, if one is devoid of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), what is the purpose of the generation [stage]? (43)
"In this context, that which is called the 'arisen stage' (utpannakrama) is devoid of conceptual construction and sensory pleasure;
it alone bestows Buddhahood. Therefore, what is the purpose of the generation of the mandala through conceptualization or the generation of the consort through conceptualization?
Having heard these words, the Blessed Lord Hevajra said: "Alas! This Great Bodhisattva has been ruined by the force of his faith!"
Conventionally, when the body is absent, great bliss arises; that bliss cannot be described as [ordinary] pleasure.
The entire world is pervaded by a bliss that exists in the form of both the pervaded and the pervader.

Just as fragrance supported by a flower is not found in the absence of the flower, so too pleasure is not perceived in the absence of form and the other [sensory objects]. Thus, according to conventional truth. (45)
Furthermore, in that very context, there is a negation through explicit exposition (*vivṛti*), as follows:

"I am not existence, nor indeed am I non-existence"; "I am the Buddha because of the awakening to all aspects (*sarvākāra*) through the wisdom of non-conceptualization (*aprajñā*)," which refers to the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) as the skillful means (*upāya*).

Those fools who do not know that it is thus, and that [the mind] is "overpowered by indolence" (kausīdyāpahata) and "overpowered by the pleasure of the two organs" (dvindriyasukhenāpahata)— this should be understood according to the preceding and following context; it is of definitive meaning (nītārtha), and it shall be explained in detail in that very chapter.
Furthermore, what is stated here in the *Kulapaṭala* is as follows:

if the gnosis of the Buddha— which pervades the three realms of existence, including all that is moving and stationary, past, future, and present— were born of the body through the relationship of container and contained, like fragrance born of a flower, it would perish in its absence.

Just as there is no fragrance in the absence of a flower, it is not so in this case; because [the fragrance] pervades both the external world and the body, it is said to be "situated in the external" and "situated in the body.
Since its absence does not follow from the absence of the body, the rule that it is "born of the body" does not apply.
Thus it has been said: "Just as there is no destruction of space due to the destruction of a jar, so too there is no destruction of consciousness due to the destruction of the body. (46)
Thus ends the third chapter, the determination of the non-dual knowledge of wisdom and means, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*.
Now, the channels within the vajra-body are described;
herein Vajragarbha asks: "O Blessed One, which are the channels in the vajra-body?"
The Blessed One said: "There are thirty-two channels;
thirty-two [of them] carry the bodhicitta, flowing into the place of great bliss (mahāsukha-sthāna).
Here, "great bliss" refers to this.
Because it is the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is called "Great Bliss.
The secret wheel consists of thirty-two channels and is characterized by the thirty consonants of the six groups beginning with *ka*, which are unstruck (*anāhata*) and non-dual.
Therein, according to the nature of the elements of space, air, fire, water, earth, and consciousness, it is the nature of the syllable *Evaṃ*.

For example, *kā khā gā ghā ṅā* are the space-elements (*ākāśadhātu*). By the rule that "the letter *ka*, which is to be pronounced with the *u* and *hu* sounds, is guttural," and by the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) that "that which falls between [a group] is included by the mention of that [group]," it is established that the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) is the space-element.
And thus, by the rule that *cā-chā-jhā-ñā* and *ic-ū-ya-śa* are palatals (*tālavya*),
the letter *ya* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
Likewise, from the indication of the letter *ra* as the fire element (*tejodhātu*) in the rule "ṭā-ṭhā-ḍā-ḍhā-ṇā" and "ṛ-ṭu-ra-ṣā are retroflexes" (*mūrdhanyāḥ*),
it follows that "pā-phā-bā-bhā-mā" and "upūpadhmānīya" are labials (*oṣṭhyāḥ*).
The water element is indicated by the letter *va*;

thus, according to the rule "the letters *ta*, *tha*, *da*, and *dha* are dental," the earth element is indicated by the letter *la*. Among these, the letters *sa*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *jña*, and *jha* have the natures of earth, water, fire, wind, and space respectively; the sixth, the nature of the knowledge element (*jñānadhātu*), has its own distinct nature.
The two syllables *evaṃ* and so forth, beginning with *evaṃ*, are attractors of the bodhicitta; for that reason, they are said to bring forth the bodhicitta.
"Flowing into the place of great bliss" means flowing as urine, feces, and semen.
Among those, three channels are principal: three below and three above.
Below the navel are the channel discharging feces, the channel discharging urine, and the channel discharging semen; above the navel are the lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī.
Lalanā is established by nature as wisdom (prajñā), and rasanā as means (upāya); avadhūtī, however, is situated in the middle region, free from the grasped and the grasper. // 1 //
Thus, here the word *prajñā* denotes the moon; its nature is the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left nostril.
By that nature of the moon, the channel *lalanā*, which carries the vital breath, is situated.
By the word *upāya*, the sun is denoted.
In his right nostril is the nature of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
by that nature, the *rasanā* is situated.
Thus it is said: "The Blessed One, the Vajrī, is proclaimed as day, and Wisdom as night."
Just as the sun is declared to be Śiva, so too is the moon remembered as Śakti. // 2 //
Consciousness, mental formations, sensation, perception, and form—[these five] abide in *lalanā* according to the sequence of the creation of the five maṇḍalas;
[and] *rasanā* abides according to the sequence of the dissolution of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space.
By means of the revolution of the twelve zodiacal signs (*dvādaśalagna*) in the manner of odd and even signs, *lalanā* and *rasanā* enjoy thirty maṇḍalas each.
Here, in the Capricorn ascendant, the mandalas of earth and the other elements are [arranged] in sequence as follows: *kā khā gā ghā ṅā*;
then, in reverse order, the short vowels are [placed] in Aquarius within the left channel according to the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

For example, *ṅa gha ga kha ka* represents space and so forth, as well as consciousness and so forth; likewise on the right side, *ca cha ja jha ña* represent form and so forth, or earth and so forth, according to the distinction of speech, body, and mind, and through the relationship of the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, at the rising of the Fish [zodiac sign], *cha chā jha jā ñā* appear on the right in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Then, at the rising of Aries, [the letters] Ña, Jha, Ja, Cha, and Ca proceed in the left-hand order of emanation;
likewise, at the rising of Taurus, [the letters] Ṭā, Ṭhā, Ḍā, Ḍhā, and Ṇā.
Thus, at the rising of Gemini, there are *ṇa-ḍha-ḍa-ṭha-ṭa*;
at the rising of Cancer, *pā-phā-bā-bhā-mā*; and similarly, *ma-bha-bha-pha-pa* at the rising of Leo.
"Tāthādādhānā" occurs at the rising of Virgo;
"nadhadathata" occurs at the ascendant of Libra;
and "sāṣāśājñākṣā" occurs in Scorpio.
Then, according to the rule "kṣajñaśaṣasa," in the Sagittarius ascendant (dhanurlagna), there are sixty mandalas in one day and night;
thus, the internal channels (nāḍīs) are the carriers of the mandalas.
The indicators of those [energies], born from them at the joints of the hands and feet, are described:
in the right shoulder-arm joint is the Capricorn ascendant (*makaralagna*); for each of these, there is a mandala consisting of earth and the other elements.
In the lower joints of the thumb, index, middle, ring, and little fingers, respectively;

then, at the joint of the left shoulder and arm where the pitcher (kumbha) is situated, the mandalas of space and the other elements are placed in order starting from the little finger. At the joint of the right knee and leg where the scorpion (vṛścika) is situated, the mandalas are located in the joints of the rows of the third phalanges of the thumb and the other fingers.
In this manner, on the left leg, a bow is placed at the knee joint, and mandalas are arranged in sequence at the joints of the third line of feet beginning with the little toe;
thus, there are sixty mandalas in the *nirmāṇacakra*, and four void-places by way of the intrinsic nature of the syllable *evaṃ*.
Therefore, in the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), there are four void-places by way of the nature of the syllable *Evaṃ*.
Thus, in the emanation wheel, there is a sixty-four-petaled lotus;
by the word "petals," the channels (*nāḍī*) conveying the sixty mandalas are expressed.
"Carrying the four voids":
thus, in each lagna-nāḍī there are five locations;
in the center is the nāḍī carrying the void, in the east the one carrying air, in the right (south) the one carrying fire, in the north the one carrying water, and in the west the one carrying earth.
In the center is the Avadhūtī, which carries the circle of gnosis;
and it is said:
"The Hero resides in the middle of the navel, in the hidden sphere of the pericarp."

Thus, there are sixty *daṇḍas* that carry the sixty mandalas, and four that carry the voids for a mere moment. Just as the sixteenth digit of the moon is known to be such, they are not carriers of the complete [mandala]; thus, in the *nirmāṇacakra*, the odd conjunction (*viṣamalagna*) is the *lalanā* by the nature of the moon.
The *rasanā* and *avadhūtī* are joined together by the nature of the sun;
they are free from the even and uneven, and from the grasped and the grasper. In the central region, however, they are the indicators of the circles of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*).
Thus, in the *nirmāṇacakra*, there are sixty-four transits of the staff (*daṇḍasaṃkrānti*) and four voids (*śūnya*). Thereafter, in the *dharmacakra*, there is an eight-petalled lotus.
Therein, on the eight petals, according to the division of the watches (prahara), are the eight transits (*saṃkrānti*) consisting of half-lagnas, which are the channels (*rasanā*) of Lalanā.
Then, in the *saṃbhoga-cakra*, by the division of short vowels and consonants, there are thirty-two channels in the throat;
in the *saṃbhoga* [cakra], there is a lotus of thirty-two petals, as taught in the Tantra in reverse order according to the Guru’s instruction.
In that [forehead], there are thirty-two transits (saṃkrānti) by way of the divisions of the muhūrta;
on the sixteen-petaled lotus in the forehead,
he says, there are sixteen transits by way of the divisions of the prahara.
On the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) is a four-petalled lotus;
there, according to the divisions of the twilights, are the four transits (*saṃkrānti*).

Here, externally, upon the exit of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), at the time of that exit, the arising of the circles of the staff-nerves (*daṇḍanāḍī*) occurs in the nostrils within the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
When the space-maṇḍala flows in either of the two nostrils— whether on the left or the right— at the beginning or at the end, then it flows through the middle;
when the wind-maṇḍala flows, then it touches the upper part of the nostril.
When the fire mandala flows, it touches the right nostril;
when the water mandala flows, it touches the water [element] facing the nose, whether on the left or the right;
and when the earth mandala flows, it touches below.

Thus, the yogin should know the five locations within the two nostrils, according to the distinction between odd and even *lagnas* and so forth, whether on the left or the right. Regarding this, the detailed exposition has not been told here in the *Pañcalakṣahomavidhi* because it is too extensive; for it is the rule of the Blessed One that those of little learning fall into terror through excessive talk.
This zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*) consisting of twelve *lagnas*, beginning with Capricorn (*makara*), is to be known in the four seats (*pīṭha*).

Based on the statement that "the signs of death (ariṣṭa-lakṣaṇa) are to be understood through various tantras," it is stated in another esoteric terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*) that the channels (nāḍīs) such as Rohitā, Mohitā, and so forth, carry [the breath] during both odd and even zodiacal ascendants (*lagna*).
Through those channels, the auspicious and inauspicious, as well as misfortune and death, are described;
for this reason,
the *lalanā* carries the Akṣobhya [element] and the *rasanā* flows with blood.
Wisdom is known as the bearer of the moon; she is proclaimed as the Avadhūtī. // 3 //
Here, Akṣobhya is the water element (*toyadhātu*), and the channel carrying the water element is Lalanā in the left nostril;
Raktā is the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the channel carrying the fire element is Rasana in the right [nostril].
Thus, the lotus born of water is in the left.
On the right is the jewel born of fire;

its presiding deity is Prajñā-Avadhūtī. The moon, the bindu, and semen—these fivefold elements constitute the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*). Because it carries this, it is called the "invocation of the void" (*śūnyāvāha*); in the center, Avadhūtī is proclaimed as the presiding deity of the Vajra family.

Thus, in the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the channels of the moon, sun, and Rāhu— namely Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī— are respectively [the carriers]; while in the downward breath (*apāna*), the carriers of feces, urine, and semen are the Wheel, the Sword, the Single-Pointed [Spear], and the Vajra, located below the navel, being upward-facing and downward-facing respectively.

Regarding the phrase "the indivisible ones and so forth," here the vowels are fifteen in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), with the sixteenth being the bindu; these reside encircling the navel and the lambikā.

Namely: *a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ* are the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth [vowels] respectively; likewise, the *guṇas*—*a, e, ar, o, al*—are the sixth and so on respectively. Therein, the *yaṇ*-substitutes—*ha, ya, ra, va, la*—are to be placed in the eleventh and so on respectively; with a dot in the middle, the *lambikā* is the sixteenth.
Thus, in the forehead above the palate, nectar flows by way of the nature of the white digits;
externally it is "cool," and internally it is "the drop" (stuka)—
thus for each individual channel.
Namely: Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā, Divyā, Vāmā, and Vāminī—these are the five beginning with Pratipadā; then Kūrmmajā, Bhāvakī, Sekā, Doṣā, and Viṣṭā. || 4 ||

Thus, the sixth and so forth are Mātrikā, Śarvarī, Sītadā, and Uṣmā; the eleventh and so forth are Lalanā and the rest, in their respective order. Lalanā consists of fifteen aspects, while Avadhūtī is the sixteenth.

Then, from the first lunar day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapratipad) onwards, the fifteen lunar days (tithis) reside in the tongue (rasanā) by way of their nature as long vowels (dīrghasvara) in the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), as follows: *lā-vā-rā-yā-hā* for the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth [days] respectively;
thereafter, they appear through the divisions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
Āl, au, āra, ai, and ā are the sixth [vowels] and so forth in their respective order;
then, by means of the long vowel distinctions, lṛ, ū, ṛ, ī, and ā are the eleventh [vowels] and so forth in their respective order.
The sixteenth [vowel], the Visarga, is in the middle of these on the tip of the tongue; thus are the Rasana and the others.
For example: the Rasana is of black color, equal [in length], and the giver of causes. || 5 ||
Thus, *pratipad* and the others are established as the *viyogas* (separations) within the *preman* (love); likewise, *pāvakī*, *sumanā*,
and so forth are the *ṣaṣṭhīs* (sixths) and the rest.
Traivṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍā, and Kātyāyanī. || 6 ||
Thus, the eleven [channels] beginning with Ekādaśī—
these fifteen [channels] on the tongue, with Māradārikā in the center in the form of Kālasūtra, remain as far as the tip of the tongue; she drinks the flow from the *lambikā*.
Regarding the term *rasanā*, Vajragarbha asked again: "Lord, what are these channels like?
The Lord replied: "They are all transformations of the three realms of existence;
that is to say, they are transformations of the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense-faculties of action (*karmendriya*)."
"Free from the grasped and the grasper"—
thus one has entered the Middle Way, which is the truth.

Alternatively, by every means, those things conceived as the characteristics of entities are conceived as the characterized and the characteristic of consciousness through the means of the elements, objects, and actions;
thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of the Channels, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*. Now, the divisions of the vows (*saṃvara*) are described.
That which has been stated here in both direct and reverse order is now expanded upon by means of a commentary in its proper sequence:
"Herein, the vow of all the Buddhas is established in the *evaṃkāra* within the secret lotus of thirty-two petals."

In the four-petaled [lotus] at the *uṣṇīṣa*, there is the *saṃvara* (vow) as the gathering (*melāpaka*) of the remaining [deities] within the *nirmāṇa*, *dharma*, *saṃbhoga*, and *sahaja* wheels. At the sixty-four-petaled, eight-petaled, thirty-two-petaled, and sixteen-petaled [lotuses], located at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead respectively, *Āli* resides at the forehead and *Kāli* at the throat; *Prajñā* is at the heart and *Upāya* is at the navel.
The sahajakāya is at the navel, the dharmakāya at the heart,
and the sambhogakāya at the throat.
The nirmāṇakāya is at the forehead, the turyā at the navel,
and the suṣupta at the heart.
The dream state is at the throat; the waking state is at the forehead;
the body-vajra is at the forehead.
The speech-vajra at the throat,
the mind-vajra at the heart,
and the gnosis-vajra at the navel.

The syllable *E* is at the navel, *Vaṃ* at the heart, *Ma* at the throat, and *Yā* at the forehead. Locanā is at the navel, Māmakī at the heart, Pāṇḍarā at the throat, and Tāriṇī at the forehead. These are the four mandalas, which are the four moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Vicitra is at the forehead, Vipāka at the throat, Vimarda at the heart, and Vilakṣaṇa at the navel.
Thus, Ānanda is at the forehead, supreme bliss (paramānanda) at the throat, the bliss of cessation (viramānanda) at the heart, and innate bliss (sahajānanda) at the navel;
likewise, the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) is at the forehead and the truth of origination (samudayasatya) at the throat.
The truth of cessation is at the heart;
the truth of the path is at the navel— thus are the four realities.

The principle of the self (*ātmatattva*) is in the forehead; the principle of mantra (*mantratattva*) is in the throat; the principle of the deity (*devatātattva*) is in the heart; the principle of knowledge (*jñānatattva*) is in the navel;
egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) is in the forehead;
and the utterance of sound (*śabdoccāra*) is in the throat.
All thoughts are in the heart;
pleasant sensations are at the navel; these are the four aggregates.

The Sthāvarīyas are at the navel; the Sarvāstivādins are at the heart; the Saṃvidāyins are at the throat; the Mahāsāṃghikas are at the forehead. The Moon is at the forehead, the Sun at the throat, Rāhu at the heart, and Kālāgni at the navel.

There are sixteen transits (saṃkrāntis) at the forehead, thirty-two at the throat, eight at the heart, and sixty-four transits at the navel. These correspond to the four junctions (saṃdhyās) previously mentioned.
The morning twilight is at the forehead, the midday twilight at the throat, the afternoon twilight at the heart, and the midnight twilight at the navel.
At the forehead is enjoyment (*bhoga*), at the throat is authority (*adhikāra*), at the heart is dissolution (*laya*), and at the navel is sovereignty (*prabhutva*).
Thus, all four [twilights] are present.

The thirty-six factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) and the thirty-six elements (*dhātu*) previously mentioned are to be applied to the wheel by dividing them into four parts each, according to their respective family divisions. This is in accordance with the root tantra; as stated by one tantra through the method of another tantra, the *saṃvara* [of the deities] is established within the six wheels according to the division of the six families.

The rule is that there is the *saṃvara* (vow/union) in five wheels by way of the division of the five families, and the *saṃvara* in three wheels by way of the division of the three families; likewise, there are the tantras of the three families, the four families, the five families, and the six families, according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader, and the distinction between the support and the supported. || 1 ||
In this context, the abode (ālaya) is single-faced through the division of the support of one family (kula),
and three-faced through the division of the support of three families.
He is four-faced through the division of the support of the four families, five-faced through the division of the support of the five families,
and six-faced through the division of the support of the six families.
By means of the division of the eight families as supports, he is "eight-faced";
here, by the division of the fire of time (kālāgni), he is remembered as having one face;
and by the single division of Rāhu, consisting of wisdom and means, he is two-faced.

He has three faces through the division of body, speech, and mind as moon, sun, and Rāhu; he has four faces through the division of moon, sun, Rāhu, and the fire of time (kālāgni) as body, speech, mind, and gnosis (jñāna);
and he has five faces through the division of the five aggregates (skandhas).
By the division of the six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha*), he is Six-faced (*Ṣaḍānana*).

He is two-fold as the Moon, two-fold as the Sun, two-fold as Rāhu, and two-fold as the Fire of Time (*Kālāgni*); by these eight divisions, he is Eight-faced (*Aṣṭānana*). Here, the division of the Moon is the wheel of the uvula (*lambikācakra*) on the forehead; the division of the Sun is the wheel of the throat (*kaṇṭhacakra*) on the tongue.
The division of Rāhu is in the heart, the wheel of the Uṣṇīṣa;
the division of Kālāgni is in the navel, the secret wheel (guhyacakra).
Thus it has been said: "The sun is situated in the head of Rāhu, and the moon is above the sun."
Above the moon is Rāhu; by him the universe is set in motion.
The one who melts with the fire of time (kālāgni) is situated in two ways within his navel and secret place; he is called Vajrasūrya, wherein Caṇḍālī resides. || 3 ||
Where the nectar is situated, there the syllable *haṃ* is situated;
it rains [nectar] into the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, possessing a stainless radiance like a vajra-moon. || 4 ||
Thus concludes the rule regarding the breach of the vows;
now, the yoga of Caṇḍālī is explained,
beginning with the words "Caṇḍālī," and so forth.
The Caṇḍālī, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas; she burns Locanā and the others, and once they are burnt, the Moon (Haṃ) flows forth. || 5 ||
This is the heading;
the explanatory passage for this heading is introduced from the Root Tantra.
Therein the Blessed One said: "O Vajragarbha, I shall proclaim that which is more secret than the secret; listen."
It is the cause of all accomplishments and the bestower of liberation upon yogins.
He who is called Vajrasattva is the body of gnosis, free from causal succession; the Lord with three prongs resides between the navel and the secret place. ||7||
Emerging from him below and above, with a radiance equal to a bolt of lightning, it impels the elements of consciousness, the sense faculties, and the constituent elements residing within the body.
That Bhuvaneśvarī is established in the navel within the middle channel;
she descends like lightning into the right channel at the secret place.
One's own innate wisdom (svābhā-prajñā) is renowned as that very Caṇḍālī; here she is described as having three prongs below and likewise three above.
The Brahma-duct stands in the middle, the Viṣṇu-duct is indeed on the left,
while the Rudra-duct on the right carries feces, urine, and semen.
The needle of Rāhu is situated in the middle, the needle of Candra is on the left,
and the needle of Sūrya is on the right, carrying the elements of water, fire, and space.
Lalanā is renowned as being on the left, and Rasanā is recorded as being on the right;
indeed, Avadhūtī should be in the middle, and Dombinī is said to be the wind. (13)
Having formed a triple path from the navel to the center of the heart, they proceed again; having formed a triple path from the heart to the middle of the throat, they proceed once more. || 14 ||

Having formed a triple path between the forehead and the two necks, they proceeded again; having formed a triple path between the forehead and the crown of the head, they proceeded once more. || 15 ||
Having formed a triple path in the middle of the nose at the crown of the head, they return again;
the *lalanā* is situated in the left nostril. || 16 ||
To the right is the rasanā channel, and in the middle is the avadhūtī; from the navel upwards are the five cakras, which together constitute the triple path in five ways.

The movement and return [of the winds] occur from the center of one pericarp to another pericarp via the Avadhūtī, and also from petal to petal; this is traditionally taught for the Lalanā and Rasanā. (18)
Then Rāhu [obscures] the navel, and thereafter the Sun; having pierced the Moon and the very mark of the Moon, he goes to the uṣṇīṣa—the channel that is the Avadhūtī. 19.
When men are intoxicated with passion, and when the tongue of the woman [is likewise aroused], then by the union of those two cavities, the Caṇḍālī certainly blazes forth. (20)
Blazing in the navel-cakra, she emerges by way of the *ḍombī* path; having pierced Rāhu and the moon, she touches that syllable *haṃ*. || 21 ||
Touched by that [wisdom], that ego-sense melts into white nectar;
once the aggregates, elements, and so forth, which flow as the five maṇḍalas, have been consumed by fire. (22)
When the objects and senses have ceased and bliss and the other [states] have arisen, the drops of the moon flow forth; the *haṃkāra* is situated at the crown of the head.
From the moon on the forehead, she went to the sun; from the throat, she went to Rāhu;
at the navel, Caṇḍālikā was defiled, and from there she went to the secret wheel (guhyacakra).
In this secret wheel (guhyacakra) at the junction (saṃpāta), this "great beast" (mahāpaśu) is described;
it is where the aperture of the three channels beneath the trident is revealed. 25.
It is a "beast" for seven births and bestows the siddhi of Khecarī;
when fainted (mūrcchita), it removes disease, and when digested (jārita), it [removes] the elements of the body.
Slain by the senses of the objects of sense, he bestows the state of a universal monarch;
endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, he bestows the power of moving through the sky.
It bestows Buddhahood swiftly by following the sequence beginning with the waking state;
just as an external elixir is bound [in its effects], so too is this essence of gnosis. (28)
In this way, Brahmā, Apśu, and Viṣṇu are brought down into the secret wheel (guhyacakra);
they bestow abundant longevity until the dissolution of all things (saṃplava). || 29 ||
Above, Rāhu is declared to be a bound soul (paśu), while the Moon and Sun are great bound souls (mahāpaśu);
when they are cast down through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), they bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Blood, sinew, and likewise the *masja*—these must be diligently offered for the purpose of casting [the victim] down.
These alone are to be known as the sacrificial animals (*paśu*), and not others who possess bodies externally.
The Supreme Lord is indeed the seven-birthed one of all animals;
I shall now explain how he exists as the seven-birthed one within the body—listen to that. (32)
The food and drink consumed and drunk, being of six kinds, undergoes transformation through digestion and attains the state of rasa; this is called the first birth. (33)
Therefore, it becomes blood in the second [week]; clearly, it becomes flesh in the third; and in the fourth, it attains the state of skin. (34)
In the fifth month it attains the state of channels; in the sixth, it attains the state of bone;
in the seventh, it attains marrow; thereafter, the sevenfold [constituent] comes into being. || 35 ||
Through its connection with that which is to be placed within it, this is called the *kula* consisting of six sheaths (*ṣaṭkoṣa*).
It is said that *kula* is the body, and *koleya* is said to be the semen. (36)
His power is declared to be *rajas*, the cause of the body's production;
all-pervasive consciousness (*vijñāna*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are situated between those two. (37)
Having come together with the moon and the sun, Heruka is the essence of the three worlds;
the Hero, the leader of the *ḍākinī* wheel, is situated above and below. (38)
The crown wheel (uṣṇīṣacakra) is said to consist of four channels;
that on the forehead consists of sixteen, and that in the throat consists of thirty-two. (39)
In the heart, there is a wheel with eight [spokes], and likewise with sixty-four;
the navel-wheel is fully described, and in the secret place, there are thirty-two.
The spokes of the wheel are said to be the channels (nāḍikās), or indeed the petals of the lotus;
within them the Yoginīs are to be placed, who perform manifold activities, impelled by consciousness through the nature of the objects and the senses. || 41 ||
All the seats (pīṭhas), secondary seats (upapīṭhas), and so forth, as well as the channels (nāḍīs) and lotus petals, are contained therein;
Mahāmāyā is proclaimed to be in the uṣṇīṣa together with the four goddesses.
His rising occurs at the navel-cakra in the first circle;
on the forehead, there should be a *picūvajra* endowed with eight channels.
In the two eyes, as well as in the ears, the nose, the tongue, and the uvula, reside the deities beginning with Gaurī, the Hotṛ priests, and the stages beginning with Rūpa. || 44 ||
In this very [system], he is celebrated through the divisions of the digits of the moon of Nairātmyā;
indeed, he himself possesses three faces and six arms, with thirty-two [deities] in his throat. 45.
In the heart, this four-armed one is established with the eight goddesses;
in the mind-vajra is Mahāviṣṇu, Akṣobhya, born of the family.
He, the captor of the three worlds, is [present] at the navel by means of exactly sixty-four;
these five dākas are renowned as the five dākinīs, who are the five elements. (47)
These five reside in the five wheels, while the sixth, the Great Lord, resides in the secret place;
he is the Sovereign of the Three Realms together with thirty-two ḍākinīs. (48)
In the six cakras, there are one hundred and fifteen goddesses;
this is known as Kālacakra, unified as a single whole with the six families (ṣaṭkula). 49.
There are twenty channels on the forehead and head that carry phlegm (śleṣman);
forty in the throat and heart that carry bile (pitta);
sixteen in the navel and the private parts; eighty that carry wind (vāyu); and ten channels in the secret wheel (guhyacakra) which have the nature of the humoral combination (sannipāta). || 50–51 ||
The three channels that run above and below, which obstruct the six cakras, and the subsidiary channels from the many elements remain filling the body. (52)
There are seventy-two thousand pores on the body, and within them reside as many deities; furthermore, there are three and a half crores of living beings corresponding to the number of body hairs.
The number of hairs established as existing is the same in the external world as it is in the body.
Six breaths constitute one *pāṇīpala*, and sixty *pāṇīpalas* constitute one *ghaṭī*.
One muhūrta consists of two ghaṭīs; with three and three-quarter ghaṭīs it becomes one half-prahara, and with five ghaṭīs it becomes one lagna. (55)
A half-prahara is the *lagna*, and two praharas constitute the junction (*sandhyā*);
by those four [periods], the day and night of embodied beings are indeed declared. (56)
And that [period] is equal to twelve zodiacal signs, or twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, or the daṇḍas of the sun. (57)
By twenty-four fortnights, likewise by twelve months,
by six seasons, and as it has been declared, by four equal yugas.
Likewise, through the three times and the two solstices, a day occurs within the body;
a fortnight consists of nine hundred breaths, and a month consists of eighteen hundred.
Thirty-six [hundred] is said to be an *ṛtu*; fifty-four [hundred] is a *yuga*;
seventy-two hundred is *kāla*; and eight hundred more is an *ayana*.
Likewise, ten thousand [breaths] are said to constitute one year;
during the transit [of the sun], there are fifty-six and a quarter intermediate breaths, and in the twelve [months], there are six hundred and seventy-five additional [breaths].
And thus, through hundreds of breaths, the time that brings death to living beings occurs within three fortnights and three years via the avadhūtī.
When the wind flows in the lalanā both day and night, death occurs within three years; therefore, this shall be the fatal omen (ariṣṭa) of the moon.
When the vital breath flows through the sun for five nights in embodied beings, death occurs after three years; therefore, this is the solar omen of death (sūryāriṣṭa) in the right [nostril].

When this breath flows through the left channel for three days, there is the abandonment of the zodiacal sign from the navel; after three years, there is the loss of the solstice. If it flows thus for six days in the second [period], it will certainly flow for three months.
In this manner, by increasing the number of days by three every three months,
he gradually abandons eleven petals over the course of three years.
For thirty-three days, the left [channel] flows continuously;
then, through the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas), it enters the sun.
Then, for three days, the breath enters the pericarp in the center;
thereafter, for one night, it abandons the breaths due to death.
When the vital wind flows through the right channel for ten nights,
then death occurs after two years;
when it flows in the third zodiacal sector, death occurs after one year, corresponding to the number of lunar days (tithis).
In the fourth month, one should carry it for six months and twenty days.
70.11. Where [the breath] flows for twenty-five days in the fifth month, the lifespan there is three months;
in the sixth month, it flows for twenty-six days, and the lifespan is indeed two months.
In the seventh month, the life-force (āyuḥ) flows for twenty-seven days;
from that point, it flows continuously for thirty days.
One should discard the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh petals in sequence; these petals are abandoned on the day [of the week] by the number five multiplied by the lunar date and the directions.
73. Then, having left the right channel (savyanāḍī), the vital air (māruta) goes to the left;
after two days, it proceeds for one day through the middle path (madhyamāpada).
Then, having brought about the exhaustion of the breath, he departs from death;
the semen goes downward, while the mother's blood (rajas) moves upward.
Consciousness, bound by the latent impressions of its own karma and joined with the vital breath, undergoes rebirth after death; indeed, there is no other [rebirth] apart from that.
Just as knowledge is received from a preceptor, just as one lamp is lit from another lamp, just as one seal is impressed by another seal, and just as a face is reflected from a face in a mirror.
Just as an echo arises from sound, or fire from a sun-crystal, so too the sun does not exist without the sun; nor is there salivation from the tongue without the consumption of sour things.
78. Just as a sour sprout does not arise without the sour [seed], but arises from the seed alone, and yet it does not arise without that [sourness] because its nature is to be the cause of the fruit.
79.11 Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause,
do any entities ever exist as having arisen anywhere at all.
The white [semen] of the father and the red [blood] of the mother, as well as the pair of prāṇa and apāna joined with the mind-vajra (cittavajra), are the causes for the arising of the body. || 80 ||
Amitābha, Ratnadhṛk, Prāṇa, and Apāna follow in due order;
these are the faces of the Mind-Vajra, representing body, speech, mind, and passion.
From semen the moon is produced; from blood, the sun arises;
from the prāṇa comes the manifestation of Rāhu, and from the apāna, the fire of time (Kālāgni).
