83. From semen (śukra) the channels (nāḍī) arise; from semen the production of bone occurs. From the female reproductive essence (rajas) blood is produced; from blood the production of flesh occurs.
From the flesh comes the skin, from the marrow the bone is born;
the semen is the thunderbolt (vajra), the menstrual blood the bell (ghaṇṭā), the channel the lotus, and the great jewel (mahāmaṇi).
The red lotus is blood, the sword is bone, the flesh is known as the white lotus, and the skin and marrow belong to embodied beings. || 85 ||
These eight are the faces of one's own mind in their respective order; the eastern faces are the feet, which are the moon, the sun, darkness, and fire.
87. From blood arises the earth consisting of clay; it is proclaimed as the element of flesh.
From semen arises the solid earth, which consists of stone and bone.
From the moon, the production of water; from fire, the production of blood;
from Rāhu, the production of prāṇa; and from fire, the production of apāna is traditionally taught.
The tongue and the uvula of all embodied beings were produced from semen;
the left and right eyes were produced from passion (rajas).
90. Indeed, the two apertures for the vital breath were produced by the *prāṇa*;
likewise, the two apertures of the ears were born from the void (*śūnya*) itself.
91. Likewise, the three lower orifices were produced by Apāna, and the two breast-crevices were produced by Rāhu.
92. By means of the *apāna* [wind], the pair of testicles is formed; thus are the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).
The constituent is threefold by means of semen alone, and the constituent of the *rajas* is likewise threefold.
93 || The body is known as the "six-skin" (ṣaṭkauṣika); the body-faculty is twofold. The left [side] is produced by water, and the right is produced by fire.
94. Therefore, immortality arises through the vital breath (prāṇa) alone; thus, the three upper channels are traditionally taught.
Vāmā is produced by the wind (vāyu), while Madhyamā is below, associated with the earth (medinī).
95 || By means of inhalation and exhalation, the channel is generated; of this there is no doubt.
The body is situated in the forehead within the full moon mandala.
96 || The Speech-Vajra is in the region of the throat within a complete solar mandala;
it is the gnosis of all embodied beings, situated in the center of the Rāhu-mandala.
The jewel situated upon the earth is undoubtedly at the tail of Rāhu;
the Kālāgni-Amogha stands above the Viśvavajra.
The wheel, the lotus, the vajra, the jewel, and the sword as the fifth;
the sixth is the vajra-gem—these are remembered as being upon the heads of the Buddhas of men.
99. Thus, these six families are all the Buddhas of great power. From the earth, fragrance arises; from the cooking by fire, flavor comes into being.
100 || From water, there would be the sprout and so forth; this touch arises from wind.
The vital breath (prāṇa-vāta) becomes sound, and from the downward-voiding breath (apāna), the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) arises.
101 || Indeed, the mind-faculty of all embodied beings is to be known as being right there;
Yamāntaka is produced from bone, and Prajñāntaka is said to arise from blood.
Padmāntaka is [derived] from the channels (nāḍī); Vighnāntaka is said to be from the flesh;
Acala is declared to be from the marrow; and Ṭakkirāja is from the skin.
From the body hair comes Nīladaṇḍa; from the nails also comes Mahābala;
from the hair of the head comes Uṣṇīṣacakrin; and from the hair below [the head] comes Śumbharāja.
The joints in the hands and feet, according to the division of the three qualities (guṇas),
are known as the twelve zodiac signs (rāśis) of the four elements beginning with earth.
105 || These sixty seasonal days are the lunar nodes (parvan) formed by the teeth and the wood of the fingers;
the teeth situated above and below are the constellations (nakṣatras) here for embodied beings.
106 || Certainly, the *rajas* has gone to the head of Śukra, while Agasti has a downward course;
just as it is externally, so too within the body it is certain to be produced from the womb.
107: Heruka possesses twelve arms for the sake of the twelve [links of dependent origination];
he has four faces because he abides through the cessation of the twelve limbs.
Holding the sixteen digits of the moon in his hands, the knower of the sixteen-fold reality,
the Supreme Lord has eight faces through the cessation of the eight apertures.
109 || By whom the moon, the sun, darkness, and fire were obstructed by his steps;
and having subsequently obstructed them with twenty-four rays.
110 || Kālacakra has arisen with four faces as previously described.
Another [form] has thirty-four arms due to the cessation of the consonants from *ka* onwards; sixteen feet are taught due to the cessation of the sixteen vowels;
and Vajrabhairava has nine faces due to the cessation of the nine gates.
112 || Tantras such as these were taught by the Lord of Jinas for the sake of purifying the ignorant, through the cessation of body, speech, and mind.

113. Thus, having prostrated with my head before the Saṃbhogakāya, I shall explain here in this vehicle that very meaning which was taught through various sounds—the meaning of this [teaching] concerning the families and so forth, by means of the symbolic terminology of Mantra.
1. The wise have revealed two types of mantra-convention in the Tantra:
the convention of suchness (*tathatā-saṃketaka*) is one, and verbal expression (*pravyāhāra*) is the second.
2. That which is called the conventional designation of suchness is the speech consisting of the cries of all sentient beings;
it is the great-sounding Dharma-conch, the great drum of the Dharma with its mighty resonance.
3. Non-abiding nirvāṇa is called the all-pervading speech;
since it is the utterance that is the mantra, it indicates the meaning through convention.
4. Abiding in the neuter state, one should recite the mantra with its limbs undivided, through a beautiful recitation that follows the meaning and is devoid of intrinsic nature.
One should recite twenty-one thousand and six hundred times day and night that which has severed the vital breaths and entered the state of avadhūtī.
In five days—beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight until the three full-moon days—one reaches one hundred and eight thousand [recitations].
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should again recite [the mantra] until the three full moons; at the time of sunrise on the full moon day, he attains success.
Having paid homage to Vajrasattva, one should set the wheel of Dharma in motion with eight thousand and forty thousand recitations. 9.

Through six hundred thousand recitations of the breath (*prāṇajāpa*) performed over the course of one month, success is attained; there is no need for a rosary, nor vocal recitation, nor fire-offerings, nor ritual worship of the mantra. (10)
The libations and other rituals, both supreme and inferior, perish for those practitioners of mantra who are of childish intellect and incapable of this recitation. (11)
This recitation by means of the rosary has been revealed for those practitioners who desire external enjoyments, so that they may attain merit. (12)

When the vital breath (prāṇa) remains absorbed day and night within the middle channel (madhyamā), it removes diseases; bound by the lunar days (tithi) over the course of days, that very breath bestows the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
For one month, when [the breath] is killed while residing in the heart, it grants immortality to yogins. When burnt for six months in the navel, it bestows omniscience.
That which is fainted, bound, killed, and made to reside within the bodies of men—in the forehead, the throat-cakra, the heart, and the navel—proceeds according to this sequence. (1411, 15)
Through the cessation of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the state of being free from passion is attained; indeed, for practitioners of mantra, Buddhahood arises through both death and cremation. (16)

Through the cessation of the inhaled and exhaled breaths (prāṇa and apāna), there occurs here the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination]. By the cessation of cause and effect, who would not become a Buddha? || 17 ||
As long as there is the movement of the vital breaths in living beings, so long is there rebirth; when the movement of the vital breaths has ceased, there is death, not rebirth. (18)

Thus, the secret convention of the mantra and the recitation of the neuter [mantra] should be understood through that convention. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on mantras. It is as follows: [the mantra for the offering to all elemental spirits].
Thus.
"All derivative" means all that is derived from the elements; their mantras and his [the seed-syllable's] mantras correspond respectively as follows:
"Oṃ! The letter A is the mouth of all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the beginning."
In this context, by the word "A," the unstruck sound (anāhatadhvani) is meant:
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme syllable of great meaning; it is indeed the great vital breath, unborn, and devoid of the expansion of speech. (19)

By these and other [verses], it should be understood that in the *Māyājāla*, he is all, the omniscient one; he knows himself and knows others; he is all, the benefactor of all, for he is the foremost person (*agrapudgala*). Having transcended worldly analogies, he is to be known as the supreme Lord of Gnosis (*jñānādhipa*). (20)
By such statements as these, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that the mantra of the Omniscient One is speech consisting of all beings (*sarvasattvabhūta*).

Those who are "born of the elements" (*bhautika*) are those produced from the elements such as earth; they possess the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their characteristic. Their mantra consists of the five aggregates, which is the five-syllable [mantra].
By means of the syllable Oṃ, their aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is the body-vajra; by means of the syllable Āḥ, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) is the speech-vajra;
and by means of the syllable Hūṃ, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is the mind-vajra.
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is represented by the syllable *svā*, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) by the syllable *hā*;
[these are] the offering of the bali-oblation to them.
The dismissal is performed with three *hūṃ* syllables and two *phaṭ* syllables;
likewise, purification is by means of the syllable *oṃ*,
and awakening by means of the syllable *āḥ*.
The kindling by means of the syllable *huṃ*,
the transformation into nectar by means of the syllable *svāhā*, and the invocation by means of the syllable *hā*.
Offering with three *huṃ* syllables,
dismissal with two *phaṭ* syllables,
and purification with the left hand.
Awakening with the right hand,
igniting that which was covered by the añjali gesture,
and transforming it into nectar by means of the Garuḍa-mudrā.
The invocation is performed with the Trailokyavijaya mudrā;
the offering with the Vajra mudrā;
and the dismissal by touching [the deity] with three flicks of the hand.
Thus, the binding of the mudrās is to be understood according to another tantra;
likewise, the seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas are as follows in their respective order: by means of the syllable *vuṃ*, Vairocana is placed upon the head.
Ratnasambhava is at the navel by means of the syllable Aṃ;
Amitābha is at the throat by means of the syllable Jrīṃ; and Amoghasiddhi is at the secret place by means of the syllable Khaṃ.
With the syllable *hūṃ*, Akṣobhya is placed in the heart;
having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of Picu-vajra, this is the rule for the other Vajra-ḍākinīs as well.
Then follows the mantra of the sixteen-armed [deity].
*Oṃ deva picūvajra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Herein is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*):
by means of the syllable *oṃ*, the seat of the deity is established; likewise, by means of the first syllable of the mantra, the deity is brought to manifestation.

The placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is performed with the remaining seed-syllables for the eyes and so forth in their proper order; the summoning of the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) is performed with three *hūṃ* syllables,
its confinement with *phaṭ*,
and its gratification with *svā*.
"Equalization by means of the syllable HĀ" is the very heart of Hevajra;
likewise, for all mantra-words beginning with OṂ and ending with SVĀHĀ, the rule is that they are interspersed in the middle with the syllables HŪṂ and PHAṬ at the end.
In all cases, as before:
for the four-armed [deity], it is *oṃ jvalajvalabhyaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*; likewise for the two-armed [deity], it is *oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* and *oṃ kiṭikiṭivajra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Thus, in this chapter on the extraction of mantras, the mantra for the empowerment of the body, speech, and mind of all [deities] is to be understood through the instruction on the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ* belonging to the six-armed one.

[Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ]. By means of the syllable Oṃ, there is the empowerment of the body as Vairocana upon a moon mandala; by means of the syllable Āḥ, the empowerment of speech as Amitābha upon a sun [mandala];
and by means of the syllable Hūṃ, the empowerment of the mind as Akṣobhya at the heart upon a Rāhu mandala.
In this context, for the purpose of extracting mantras, the vowels of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth are stated according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*):
*a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ lṛ lṝ e ai o au am*.
Furthermore, according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), they are grasped through the recitation of the withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*): *ai u ṛ ṝ ka; a e ar o al; ca ha ya ra va la ṭa*.

These are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the lunar digits (*kalā*) during the bright fortnight. It is the rule in the Root Tantra that these were spoken by the Blessed One not according to the method of the literal reading for beginners (*neyārtha*), but according to the definitive meaning.
Thus is the mantra for the agitation of the city: *oṃ akacaṭatapayaśasvāhā*.
According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), this is so;
according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the letters *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the visarga are produced from the throat (*kaṇṭhya*).
The sounds *icūyaś* are palatals;
*ṛṭuraṣ* are retroflexes;
*upūpadhmānīya* are labials.
The letters *lṛ*, *tu*, and *la-sa* are dental; beginning with *a*, *ā*, *ha*, and *hā*, followed by *ṅa*,
*ña*, *ṇa*, *ma*, *na*, *ja*, *ña*, *svāhā*— this is the mantra for subduing the city.
The extraction of mantras is to be understood from the oral instruction of the guru according to the *Mūlatantra*. The teaching is given in its definitive sense (*nītārtha*):
one should recite the thirty *muhūrtas* of Āli day by day according to the divisions of the lunar digits, and the sixty consonants of Sūrya according to the divisions of the *daṇḍas*.

By the syllables *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*, the *ālikāli* (vowels and consonants) is expressed in the definitive sense (*nītārtha*). By reciting the *ālikāli* one hundred thousand times, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) shall agitate the three worlds; what need is there to mention a single city alone?
Thus the *ādi* (vowels) and *kādi* (consonants) are spoken. They are as follows:

*a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū lṛ lṛ a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā*. This is the recitation of the *āli* according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), performed with the inhalation of the breath.
With the exhalation of the breath:
*kā liḥ ka kā khakhāgagā ghaghāṅa ṅā cacācha chāja jājhajhāñañā*.
ṭa ṭhā ḍa ḍhā ṇa ṇā; pa pā pha phā ba bā bha bhā ma mā; ta tā tha thā da dā dha dhā na nā; śa śā ṣa ṣā sa sā kṣa kṣā. Thus.
At the beginning, the syllable *oṃ* is used for agitation; at the end of the attraction, *vauṣaṭ* should be given.
Thus is the mantra for the agitation of the city.
"By meditating on the single deity, by the recitation of red flowers, and by the fire-oblation"—
this is what is to be stated by means of what will be explained hereafter; thus is the mantra of Kurukullā declared.
By the syllable Oṃ, the foundation and the accomplishment of the body [are established];
by the syllable Hrīṃ, the accomplishment of speech [is established]. In the external family, Kurukullā is sealed by Amitābha.
*Oṃ* on the forehead, *hīḥ* on the tongue, *ku* at the throat, *ru* at the heart, *ku* at the navel, and *lle* at the secret place—this is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
Having filled the breath by inhaling, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
while exhaling, one must not move the rosary. This is the Kurukullā mantra.
Now, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the protection mantra is stated:
by means of the syllable *oṃ*, he describes a soft seat,
a fragrant ground location that is as delightful as the moon.
With the syllable *ra*, one first creates a sun mandala;
with the syllable *kṣa*, a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*).
Having thereby formed a ten-spoked wheel above, below, and in all directions, one then places in the center the Wrathful King Vajrahūṃkāra.
Pūri Yamāntaka is on the southern spoke, Prajñāntaka on the western spoke, and Padmāntaka on the northern spoke.
Vighnāntaka is on the northern spoke,
Acala in the southeast, and Ṭakkirāja in the southwest.
In the northwest is Nīladaṇḍa; in the northeast is Mahābala;
above is Uṣṇīṣa; and below is Śumbharāja.
Then, with the second utterance,
the solar mandala by means of the syllable *ra* and the universal vajra by means of the syllable *kṣa*.

By that one who had become greedy, the triple vajra-fence was [created] with three *huṃ* syllables; the vajra-ground, the gabled pavilion, and the vajra-lotus seat were [established] with the syllable *phaṭ*;
and the awakening of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas was [effected] with the syllable *svā*.
By the syllable *HĀ*, all worship and so forth, as well as the confession of sins and so forth, are said to be accomplished; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of this mantra.
Now, the twenty-four mantra-words for the accomplishment of rites (*karmasādhana*) as taught in the Root Tantra are stated.

Here, in this *Laghutantra*, everything is concealed in both direct and reverse order; it is to be understood through the lineage of the true oral tradition from qualified masters by wicked teachers, and not by the mere recitation of books.

Having seen another [text] that is not dependent [on the Buddha], whatever is revealed there as being consistent with many tantras—that word of the Blessed One should be accepted, and not out of dull-witted faith.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "My word is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end;
it is not the case that my word is virtuous in the beginning and middle but not at the end, nor virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end [only in a limited sense]."
Just as it has been conceptualized by foolish people—

that there is first the cultivation with conceptualization (*savikalpa-bhāvanā*), then in the middle the cultivation of the pleasure of the two organs (*dvindriya-sukha-bhāvanā*), and finally at the end the cultivation of non-conceptual emptiness (*nirvikalpaka-śūnya-bhāvanā*) which is the cultivation of great bliss (*mahāsukha-bhāvanā*)— this is a corrupt statement;
for everywhere the fruit produced is seen to correspond to its cause.
For indeed, rice grain will not arise from kodrava seeds.
From that which is produced from the seed of conceptualization, there will arise a fruit characterized by conceptualization;
from that which is produced without conceptualization, there will arise a fruit free from conceptualization.
For this reason, it is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end;
just as the seed is, so is the tree, and just as the tree is, so is the fruit— this very principle of dependent origination is seen throughout this entire world.
A mantra belonging to one class of birth cannot accomplish the ritual action of another;
nowhere in the world does the sun act as a quencher of heat.
Just as it was clearly proclaimed by Hevajra in the Root Tantra, that very same [teaching] is now being stated by me through its exposition in this Condensed Tantra.

One should perform the rites of immobilization (stambhana), as well as enchantment (mohana) and pinning (kīlana), by means of the seed-syllables of earth; likewise, one should always perform pacification (śānti), nourishment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśya), and the neutralization of poison (nirviṣa) by means of the seed-syllables of water.

By means of the fire-seeds (tejobīja), there is great attraction, subjugation, and agitation in every way; likewise, by means of the wind-seeds (vāta), there is inciting enmity, eradication, and the transmission of poison.
The cutting of poison by means of the seed-syllables of emptiness, as well as killing and reviving, and the bliss of resuscitation, are accomplished through the seed-syllables of primordial wisdom.
The mantra-practitioner shall produce muteness, deafness, and even impotence, respectively, by means of the seeds of mind, speech, and body.
Through the yoga of the mandalas of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and gnosis, the supreme practitioner should accomplish the rites of paralyzing and so forth.
Impotence, muteness, blindness, the obstruction of breath, deafness, and madness of the mind are accomplished by means of the previously mentioned seed-mantras.
One should perform [the rite] in these places: in mountain caves and groves, on the shores of the great ocean, in cremation grounds, and where the primordial Siddhas dwell.

The recitation of mantras, as well as meditation, fire-offerings, and the drawing of mandalas, grant accomplishment only when performed according to the specific ritual requirements, and not otherwise.
When a mantra-deity is accomplished by men or women in an improper place, that deity, impelled by the *tantra* and the mantra, performs the ritual action.
Therefore, the wise should recite and meditate upon both name and body;
the body constitutes the root mantra, while that called the heart possesses the nature of speech.
The upahr̥daya (near-heart) mantra is thus declared to be the citta-mantra;
it is known as the seed of gnosis (jñānabīja), and it is called the jñāna-mantra.
In the seed-syllables, as well as in the *upahṛdaya*, the *hṛdaya*, and the root-mantra,
one should meditate upon and recite knowledge, mind, speech, and body in their respective order.
The recitation and worship should be performed with diligence until they become bestowers of accomplishment;
otherwise, for one who lacks the prescribed ritual, there will be no success in mantra.
For one who has grasped this with faith, there is only physical exertion;
for the letters ya, ra, la, and va are [respectively] wind, fire, earth, and water.
One should separate [the vowels] in the east, south, west, and north;
and the long [vowels] in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, following the sequence of fire, Nairṛti, wind, and Īśvara.
One should worship Hā, Hā, and so forth above and below, and Aṃ and Aḥ in the middle;
one should cause the mandala of all Buddhas to be made before the Guru.
Indeed, for the purpose of reciting the True Dharma, there is another [mandala] consisting of the five Jinas;
it is situated upon the nature of the wind-mandala and belongs to Pūrvavideha.
By the nature of the circle of fire, Jambudvīpa is triangular;
Aparagodānīya is square, characterized by the mandala of earth.
By the nature of the water-maṇḍala, Uttarakuru is a half-moon;
the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) has the characteristic of the moon-maṇḍala in the form of emptiness.
Below, in the form of knowledge, is the solar orb of the fire of time;
in the center is the bindu and visarga, and below that is the mountain of the gods.
Having thus prepared the mandala, one should then worship the mantra and so forth.
One should fashion another mandala on the ground using colored powders;
one should always worship the thirty-six [deities] consisting of the six aggregates, the six elements, and form and so forth.
Earth, water, fire, air, semen, and likewise passion—
these six elements are known here as the aggregate of form belonging to embodied beings.
The throat, palate, roof of the mouth, lips, teeth, and nose—
these are declared to be the sixfold designation that indicates the existence or non-existence of objects.
The aggregate of consciousness is declared to be sixfold, according to the eye and the other [senses]: by means of the sense-faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In this way, from the consciousness of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu), feelings are said to arise.
Thus, the sixfold formative force (saṃskāra) is said to be that which sets the consciousnesses in motion through the doors of the six sense faculties, impelling them toward their respective objects.
The carrier of the prāṇa and apāna winds constantly flows through the lotus channels;
the aggregate of knowledge (jñānaskandha) is also sixfold, existing within the three upper and lower paths.
The yogi should worship the great mind with thirty-six [elements] and the supreme thirty-seventh, surrounded by the elements, beginning with the letter Ā and so forth.
These seventy-two elements exist by way of the nature of the vowels beginning with *ā* and the consonants beginning with *ka*;
they consist of the letters of the six groups, distinguished by short and long [vowels].
The seventy-two vowels are indeed thirty-six;
joined with the letters beginning with 'A' and 'Ka', they are proclaimed as the rosary (akṣasūtra).
For the recitation of mantras by yogins, [it consists] of one hundred and eight syllables,
joined with thirty-six short consonants and eighteen vowels.
That rosary is proclaimed to have one hundred and eight purposes;
it is proclaimed as the third [type] by means of the division of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
The fourth [application] is indeed performed in the same manner by means of half-constellations;
the fifth is proclaimed through the differentiation of the thirty-six vowels.
The sixth is proclaimed by means of the division of the enjoyment of the lunar mansions;
the seventh is proclaimed by means of the division of the eighteen vowels.
Furthermore, by means of the distinction of syllables, the eighth [type] consists of thirty-six;
thus, the rosary of ascetics is said to be of eight kinds.
The practitioner should have one rosary made of eighteen crystal beads for rites of pacification (śāntika);
for men, one made of thirty-six pearl beads should be used for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
Killing is prescribed with twenty-seven constellations that have human-like teeth;
twice that number, those with donkey-like teeth, are for causing hatred and expulsion as well.
Pure with thirty-six consonants, beginning with the rites for subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth, using *putrajīvaka* seeds;
combined with vowels and consonants, these are called "lotuses" (*padma*), each consisting of four syllables.
With fifty [syllables] for a great attraction, or else with seeds of sandalwood;
elsewhere, it is taught that for enchantment, one should use *riṣṭaka* wood with half-padas of the lunar mansions.
A rudrākṣa that is pure in its vowels, consonants, and words is prescribed for the rite of immobilization (stambhana). Thus, the eightfold [rudrākṣas] have been declared for pure and purifying rites.
For this purpose, using sixty-five kinds of various seeds or gems,
fashion them according to the colors of the metals, distinguishing each according to what is available.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the mantras of the yogis,
by which a mantra arising from the Kula becomes quickly effective in bringing about accomplishment.
And those gutturals beginning with *ha*, characterized as vowels and consonants,
are born from the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) by means of the indicator *ha*.
The letters *i*, *cu*, and *yaś* are palatals, characterized by both vowels and consonants;
they are produced from the wind element, as indicated by the letter *ya*.
The retroflex consonants, characterized by vowels and consonants, arise from the fire element; they are made known by the letter *ra*.
And those labial sounds, characterized as vowels and consonants, such as the upadhmānīya,
are produced from the water element, as indicated by the letter *va*.
The dentals— lṛ, t, u, la, and sa— which possess the characteristics of vowels and consonants,
have originated from the earth element, as indicated by the letter *la*.
The anusvāra and the visarga, devoid of vowels and consonants, are born from the element of gnosis; thus is the family of the six elements.
Earth, water, fire, air, semen, and the menstrual blood—
these elements constitute what is known here as the great person, the individual composed of the six constituents.
The progenitor of all mantras, the Lord whose nature consists of the first vowels and consonants,
Śaṅkara, is the essence of the mantras of the aggregates and elements through the practice of pratyāhāra.
One who has attained mastery of the mantra should teach that very [mantra] for the sake of all accomplishments;
likewise, even an omniscient one does not [teach] mantras through the methods of recitation used by children.

Those which are mixed—produced in the throat and palate, the gutturals, labials, consonants, and vowels—as well as those produced in two places and others, are not pure; they are born of their own nature [only when unmixed].
The pure vowels born of nature reside in a single location, such as the throat;
when uttered, they constitute the Great Mantra, which is not produced by utterance from two locations.
That which is conjoined with the vowel *a*, does not abandon its own place,
and is pure by nature— that is the consonant (*vyañjana*), including the *visarga* and the *bindu*.
That which is joined with vowels such as *i* and so forth, and occurs in two places, is not born of the original nature (*prakṛti*); it is a pure consonant that becomes doubled.
The Maheśvara-maṇḍala is yellow, arising from the syllable *la*;
the Vāruṇa-maṇḍala is white, arising from the syllable *va*.
The fiery mandala is red, arising from the syllable *ra*;
the aerial mandala is black, arising from the syllable *ya*.
The mandala of space is dark blue, arising from the syllable *ha*;
it is produced from the visarga and the bindu, known as gnosis, and born from all phonemes.
Thus, that which is born from the *tavarga* is yellow and arises from the vowel *ḷ*;
that which is born from the *pavarga* is said to be white and arises from the vowel *u*.
The red [element] arises from the *ṭa*-group and is born from the vowel *ṛ*;
the black [element] is said to be born from the *ca*-group and is produced from the vowel *i*.
The letter *ka* is declared to be dark green and born from the vowel *a*; likewise, that which is born from the letter *sa* is yellow and born from the vowel *a*.
The white [syllable] is produced from the letter *ya* and arises from the quality of the syllable *oṃ*;
the red [syllable] is produced from the letter *ṣa* and arises from the quality of the syllable *e*. || 87 ||
Kṛṣṇa is born from the letter Śa and arises from the quality of E; Śyāma is born from the letter Kṣa and arises from the quality of A. || 88 ||
Ai, au, and al—these are the pure vowels produced from the *prakṛtis*.
A, e, ar, o, and al—these are of two kinds: those produced from the *prakṛtis* and the *guṇas*. (89)

Hayaravalati—these are the two types [of mantras] resulting from the substitution of *yaṇ*; likewise, between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the leaders of the circle (*maṇḍalanāyaka*) are the foremost. || 10 ||
Furthermore, the nature of each individual class is said to be fivefold:
*ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *ma*, and *na*—these arise from the element of space (*śūnyadhātu*). (91)
Gha, jha, ḍha, dha, and dhya arise from the wind element (vāyudhātu);
ga, ja, ḍa, ba, and da arise from the fire element (tejodhātu). || 92 ||
kha, cha, ha, ṭha, pha, tha, and tya—these arise from the water element (toyadhātu); ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ti, and tya—these arise from the earth element (pṛthivīdhātu). || 13 ||
The six families (ṣaṭkula) arise through the division of groups according to the primary distinctions of primordial nature (prakṛti);
by means of the distinction of each individual syllable, the family becomes fivefold.
Just as yellow is the earth-tail, so is form the body-faculty;
just as white is water and the moon, so is perception the tongue-faculty. || 95 ||
Just as the sun is red in its brilliance, so is sensation (vedanā) the eye;
just as Rāhu is black like the wind, so is mental formation (saṃskāra) the nose. || 96 ||
Just as space is eternal and dark blue, so too is consciousness and hearing;
just as the Agasti flower is blue, so is knowledge said to be the mind.
In this way, odor, color, taste, and likewise touch, as well as sound and the dharma-element—these six elements constitute the family in sequence. (98)
In this way, the anus, as well as the feet, the hands, the organ of speech, the generative organ,
and the divine organ, arise from the families beginning with Earth.
Thus, conversation, grasping, movement, excretion, and the emission of semen—these actions arise from the families of earth and the other elements. || 100 ||
Thus the six elements have been declared, as well as the six aggregates, the sense faculties, the six objects, the organs of action,
and the activity of the sixth organ of action.
Through the division of the six aggregates, there are thirty-six elements;
wisdom is thirty-sevenfold, as all phenomena are the single emptiness. (102)
The elements exist in the external body as they do within the [inner] body;
from pure earth comes immobilization, and from pure water comes pacification. (103)

Through pure *tejas* one effects subjugation (*vaśya*); through pure air, incitement to hatred (*vidveṣa*); through the pure *jīvana* [element], [one effects] pacification; and through the pure void and pure knowledge, killing (*māraṇa*).
The six rites are pure, as well as others which are mixed;
nourishment for all embodied beings is performed with earth mixed with water. (105)
Through the mixture of wind and fire, trembling occurs for embodied beings;
through the mixture of wind and water, attraction occurs for embodied beings. (106)
By the conjunction of Earth and Void, the falling of embodied beings occurs;
by the conjunction of Earth and Knowledge, there is the raising up again of one who has fallen. (107)
The liquefying of women and men is said to occur through [the mantra] mixed with water and fire;
through that mixed with earth and air, there shall be enchantment and pinning. (108)
Through the mixture of emptiness and water, there shall be nourishment for a sentient being;
through the mixture of emptiness and gnosis, there shall be restoration to life. || 109 ||
When mixed with the element of fire (tejas), it causes distress to all embodied beings;
when mixed with that which is devoid of fire, it becomes fever for embodied beings. (110)
Through the mixture of fire and wisdom, the paralysis of embodied beings occurs;
through the mixture of wind and space, one certainly effects the eradication of the universe.
By means of the wind mixed with gnosis, one may bind the three worlds in an instant;
by means of the void mixed with gnosis, there is the arising of all embodied beings. 112.
For those who proclaim knowledge, knowledge alone performs all actions;
there is no recitation, no rosaries, no fire-offerings, and no worship with mantras.
By mere meditation, all the activities of yogins are accomplished.
In this way, the mantras of the three families and those of the four and five families perform infinite activities through the ritual procedure according to the nature of the elements. (114)
Thus, these six family mantras are pure when combined with one another;
O Great Being, they are innumerable for the accomplishment of the siddhi of the deities.
I shall describe the characteristics of mantras according to the nature of the five elements; they are declared as enemy, friend, or neutral for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. (116)
And those gutturals which are characterized as vowels and consonants, he always remains for the sake of friendship with the mantras of Śūnya, Vāyu, and the others. || 117 ||
The letters *i*, *cu*, and *yaś* are palatals (*tālavya*), characterized by both vowels and consonants;
they arise from the wind element and are the enemies of those born from the water element. 118.

The retroflex consonants (ṛ, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḷ), along with their corresponding vowels, characterized by both vowels and consonants, are born from the fire element; they are the enemies of those born from the earth. 119.
Furthermore, those vowels and consonants characterized by the labial position (u-pu-va-śa-au-ṣṭha-yāḥ), which originate from the element of water, are the enemies of those born from fire. 120.
The letters *l*, *ṛ*, *t*, *l*, *s*, and *ś*, which possess the characteristics of vowels and consonants, are born from the earth element and are enemies to those born from the air element. (121)
Space is always the friend of air, remaining neutral by virtue of the power of water;
air is always the friend of fire, remaining neutral by virtue of the power of earth. || 122 ||
Water and the friend of water (fire) are set aside by earth, as is wind;
for water, the earth is the friend, while fire is set aside by its own power.
Excluding the *praṇava*, the first syllable of the mantra is its *kula*;
that alone is the mind of mantras, the cause for the manifestation of their form. (124)
Others hold that the first syllable of the mantra may be joined with a consonant;
in that case, the preceding vowel must be taken, because it is the cause for the initial utterance. (125)
Through the distinction between vowels and consonants, that very [system] becomes twofold;
it is declared to be both the enemy and the friend of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as well as of the body. (126)

The vowels are traditionally known as the enemies of the *prāṇa* (vowel) and the friends of the *udātta* (acute accent); the consonants are traditionally known as the enemies of the body (*kāya*) and the friends of the *udātta*. || 127 ||
A vowel that is an enemy [of another] takes away the life-force of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.

That which possesses the characteristics of a consonant that is an enemy brings about disease and other ailments in the body. (128) Even within a single group (*varga*), those five letters beginning with *ka* possess the nature of consonants.
Their families, such as Earth and the others, must be known in the practice of mantra (*mantrasādhana*). (129)
Ṅa, ña, ma, na, and na—these are situated in friendship, while others are not;

gha, jha, ḍha, bha, dha, and dhā—these are the enemies of those born from water (the vowels). Ga, ja, ḍa, ba, da, and da—these are the enemies of those born from earth (the consonants *ka* through *ta*). Kha, cha, ṭha, pha, tha, and tha—these are the enemies of those born from wind (the consonants *ca* through *ta*). 130–131.

In this way, as before, the friendship or neutrality of the letters situated in the mantra and so forth toward one another should be understood; [this applies] whether they are within their own groups or among others. (132)
For practitioners, letters are of two kinds: those born of birth and those born of name. Each of these is further to be known as twofold, characterized by consonants and vowels. || 133 ||
Even at the time of birth, whatever five-danda period constitutes the ascendant (lagna), one should purify it using the consonant of the man or woman beginning with the letter 'ma'. || 134 ||

In Makara, one should purify the letters beginning with *ka* according to the fivefold division of the staffs (*daṇḍa*); likewise, in Kumbha, the letters beginning with *ṅa* are purified according to the sequence of the five voids (*śūnya*) and so forth. || 135 ||

In Pisces as well, the letters beginning with 'ca' [are assigned]; likewise, in Taurus, the letters beginning with 'da'; and in the five signs beginning with Gemini, the letters beginning with 'ṇa' are placed in order. (136)
In Cancer-lagna, [the syllables] beginning with *pā* are used; in Leo-lagna, those beginning with *mā*;
in Virgo, those beginning with *tā*; and in Libra, likewise those beginning with *nā*. (137)

In Vṛścika, the letters beginning with *sā* are [assigned], and in Dhanus, those beginning with *kā* are traditionally taught; thus, through the distinction of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the sixty letters [cycle] day and night.
In the movement from right to left, there are the carriers of the five maṇḍalas;
according to the divisions of seasons and fortnights, as it is externally, so it is within the body.

One should purify the vowels within the four *kalās* by means of thirty divisions; starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) and ending with the new moon (*amā*), there are thirty deities. || 140 ||
These—*a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ, g*—are proclaimed as the first group, corresponding to the *pratipad* and so forth in their respective order;
these—*a, e, ar, o, al, v*—are proclaimed as the second group, corresponding to the *ṣaṣṭhī* and so forth. || 141 ||
Haya, Rava, and Laha—these are remembered as the eleventh days and so forth; while La and the others, in reverse order, are remembered as the first days of the dark fortnight and so forth. || 142 ||

The five vowels beginning with Ā—namely Ā, Āl, Ār, Ālṛ, and Āu—correspond to the sixth lunar day and so forth of the dark fortnight; likewise, the five vowels beginning with LṚ—namely LṚ, LṜ, E, Ai, and O—are the eleventh lunar day and so forth. (143)

At the end of the full moon is said to be the *bindu*, and at the end of the new moon is the *visarjanī*; these are known as the individual digits (*kalās*) of the moon during its appearance for a single *muhūrta*. || 144 ||
Whichever tone rises in its respective art during the first muhūrta shall be the tone of this person's birth. (145)
Then, by means of the second [day] itself, the second [note]; thus, all [notes] are said to be the sounds of birth according to their sequence through the division of thirty muhūrtas. || 146 ||
There is no doubt that for practitioners, the loss of vital breath is a great disease, occurring through sound preceded by mantra, whether by vowel or indeed by consonant. || 147 ||

Due to the lack of knowledge regarding the vowel of birth and because the consonant is not awakened, the vowel of the name and so forth should be grasped; for the consonant is indeed other than the preceding one. || 148 ||

Furthermore, for one performing service and recitation (sevājāpa) for the sake of accomplishing the sixfold ritual purpose, [the practice] for the realization of the consonants of the mantras and so forth, as well as the vowels, has been proclaimed. || 149 ||
First, the practitioner should perform the striking (tāḍana), then the entry (āveśa) and the burning (dāhana); then the nourishing (āpyāyana), and after that, the feeding (poṣaṇa). || 150 ||
Overcome by the void accompanied by the visarga and struck by the king of mantras preceded by the mantra, it enters a state of swoon. || 151 ||
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, that deity becomes unconscious;
having abandoned her ego, she comes under the control of the practitioner. || 152 ||
Thus, when assailed by the wind, she moves forth from the beginning;
when assailed by fire, she is burned; and thereafter, she is nourished by water. (153)
When Puṣṭi, who resides upon the crown of the earth, is recited, she goes to the head of the deity;
once gratified and crowned by the digit of the moon, she becomes the bestower of boons. || 154 ||

Thus, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is declared in all the root tantras by the Sugata to be performed with six hundred thousand recitations for the sake of attaining the desired accomplishment. (155)
The practitioner of the vow should employ the six syllables— phaṭ, hūṃ, vauṣaṭ, namaḥ, svāhā, and vaṣaṭ— at the end of the mantra, corresponding respectively to the six ritual acts.
Having first placed Vairocana, one should begin the recitation again;
having performed ten million recitations, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that amount.
Then, by means of the procedure taught in the Tantra, everything is accomplished; that deity, having been mastered, grants the boon requested by the practitioners. (158)

If the caste is one thing and the ritual action another, or if the time, the mantra-lineage, the family, the location, the direction, or the foundation are different, it is fruitless for all ritual actions. || 159 ||
Those men on earth who perform spiritual practice with mantras read from books, devoid of the oral tradition, only undergo suffering. (160)
What indeed is that tradition, if it is obtained from books and the like, as revealed through a literal reading according to the provisional meaning (neyārtha)? || 161 ||
Deprived of the true essence of mantra, practitioners who seek to propitiate deities and others by means of mantras recited from books desire to consume space itself. (162)
Through firm vigor of one's own mind or by the recitation of mantras, the desired worldly accomplishment shall arise for practitioners who seek the welfare of others. || 163 ||

"Through the recitation of mantras, as well as through fire-offerings (homa), and through the sequential performance of ablutions and worship, those who are devoid of ritual action do not attain success; this statement is exactly as it is. (164)
Since this is currently the instruction of the divine beings regarding the Teachers, the Bodhisattvas, therefore it is accepted with every effort by the wise. || 165 ||
Oṃ khaṃ svāhā. For "expulsion" (*uccāṭana*), the wind element is to be accomplished by means of the syllable *khaṃ*; thus, expulsion is to be performed. Oṃ jūṃ svāhā. For "enmity" (*vidveṣa*).
The element mixed with wind and fire is to be accomplished; through those two, one should perform the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*).

With the mantra *oṃ buṃ svāhā*, it is called *abhicāruka*; by means of the syllable *buṃ*, fire and water are to be accomplished, and through those two, one should perform the rite of sorcery (*abhicāruka*).
Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā: "Attraction" means that by means of the syllable *hrīṃ*, the elements of wind, fire, and space are to be mastered; through them, attraction is to be performed.
Oṃ ghūḥ svāhā: "Slaying."
By the sound "ghūḥ," wind and water are to be accomplished; by those two, killing is to be performed.
This, which is the direct perception of the senses yet is mentally constructed, I shall declare according to the language of the twilight (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
In the stage of generation, that knowledge which produces a Buddha does not exist. || 166 ||
That which is the direct perception of the yogin and that which is self-cognized is the supreme knowledge in the stage of the arisen [mandala], which brings about Buddhahood. (167)
That very [reality], divided fivefold according to its beginning, middle, and end, is described as the five eyes of the Tāyins in the *Dharmasaṃgraha*. || 168 ||
From that, the fleshly eye arises; from that, the divine eye;
from that, the wisdom-eye (prajñācakṣus) should arise; and the knowledge-eye (jñānacakṣus) is the fifth. || 169 ||
First, there is the fleshly eye for the yogins who are beginners;
thereafter, they possess the divine eye, just as the gods do. (170)
Therefore, the eye of the Śrāvakas is as it is, whereas the eye that reaches knowledge of the Sugatas is as it is. || 171 ||
Therefore, the eye of wisdom belongs to the Bodhisattvas; for in whatever way there are four kinds of eyes, he possesses that knowledge, and thus he is so called. || 172 ||
Through the distinction between knowledge and the knower, he is shown to be twofold; that which is the eye of knowledge for the Tāyins is called the "knower. (173)
The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, devoid of causal succession;
he is the unique gnosis, stainless, the embodiment of gnosis, the Tathāgata. || 174 ||

Thus, according to the principle of dependent origination in worldly convention (*laukika-saṃvṛti*), it should be understood by yogins that all means for accomplishing ritual actions (*karma-sādhana*) arise once this has been obtained—just as redness arises from the contact of turmeric powder—rather than through the egoism of thinking "I am performing the Buddha's work. This is the rule for the accomplishment of ritual action.
The sixth chapter, the section on the accomplishment of the expansion of ritual action, is concluded.
Having paid homage to Hevajra with *hūṃ*, the various means of accomplishment are now declared.
For the sake of providing shelter for the earth and out of compassion for all sentient beings. || 1 ||
Having fashioned an image of Ananta, with the two syllables "Āḥ" and "Phūḥ," one should here create an image of Ananta made of fragrant sandalwood,
having the form of a human being from the navel upward and the form of a serpent's tail below.
She has four arms; in her left hand she holds a skull-cup of nectar, and in her right hand she holds a jewel and an amṛta-fruit.
Above her head are seven hoods. Likewise, to her left is the Naga Queen, [generated] by the syllable Aṃ.
One should bathe it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)—
one should bathe it with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, which constitute the five nectars—
and thereafter worship it with blue lotuses.
One should smear the body with the juice of *nāgadamanaka* and smear the head with the ichor of an elephant.

Having joined two shallow bowls together as a hollow vessel and filled them with the milk of a black cow, one should place them [over the head], measuring twelve and a half finger-breadths from the forehead to the end of the nose and chin, reaching four finger-breadths [downward].
One should wrap the eight directions with thread spun by a black maiden and dyed blue.
Then, having drawn a mandala on the bank of a lotus pond in the north-western direction, one should place that Ananta, the king of serpents, in the middle of the pond.
Subsequently, one should again draw Hevajra, trampled upon by Ananta, within the mandala.
In this mandala, the application of colored powders is described: black with charcoal from a cremation ground,
and white with powdered human bone.
Yellow with yellow orpiment, red with a brick from a cremation ground,
and green with a leaf from a thorn-apple tree.
Having prepared some human bone powder and having drawn the maṇḍala with these five powders, first one should mark it out using a cemetery cord— that is,
a cord made from the sinews of a corpse— measuring three cubits plus three finger-breadths, by means of back-and-forth movements according to the measurements from the center to the edge.

With half of the mandala, one draws an eight-petalled lotus; there, the pericarp occupies one-third [of the space]. Within the pericarp is the seat of the sun, and upon that are Ananta and Anantarājñī.
At the base of the left and right feet, one should draw Jayā and Vijayā;
[and] Hevajra, who has eight faces, four legs, and is adorned with sixteen arms.
With his neck embraced by Nairātmyā,
possessing the twenty-four eyes to be described hereafter, and then the eight lords of the nāgas.
On the lotus petals, [the deities] should be depicted joined with five fruits;
the remaining ones are to be drawn in the likeness of Ananta,
with Ananta himself on the left petal.
Vāsuki is in the south,
Takṣaka in the west, and Karkoṭaka in the east.
In the southeast is Padma,
in the northwest is Mahāpadma,
and in the southwest is Saṃkhapāla.
In the northeast is Kulika;
with these seed-syllables, there is Ā PHUḤ in the center, and PHUḤ on the right and left petals.

(4) Having fully manifested the eight nāgas by means of these eight *phuḥ*-syllables: Kṛṣṇa in the eastern fire [direction], Rakta in the south and the southwest, and Pīta in the west and the northwest.

In the north and the northeast, the two white [deities] are to be drawn with their faces distinguished as mind, speech, and gnosis-body; all of them are to be drawn lying supine, trampled by the feet and toes of the Lord.
Likewise, the ground in the east is black, in the south red, in the west yellow, and in the north white, up to the five lines.
The door-jamb and the *niryūha* (projecting arch) shall each be one-eighth of the mandala;

the pedestal (*vedikā*) and the *hārabhūmi* (garland-ground) shall be half the size of the door, and the five-lined frieze (*pañcarekhā-paṭṭikā*) and the *bakuli* shall be half the size of the pedestal. The archway (*toraṇa*) shall be three times the width of the door, with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) at the corner and vajras with flames on the exterior. Having thus drawn the mandala, one should then perform the fire-offering (*homa*) in a circular hearth (*kuṇḍa*).
Then, for the sake of pacification,

having performed the consecration of the mandala and offered the *bali* as will be described, the preceptor should subsequently recite the mantra with a mind focused on cruelty, using the mantra beginning with "Inda-yama-jala-ukha... and so forth.

Regarding "the state of a mind possessed of majesty": with a somewhat exalted mind, one should then station doorkeepers in a secluded place, arrange ten water jars, and place bowls filled with milk upon them. Having hoisted blue banners toward the ten directions outside, one should recite this mantra:
Oṃ ghuru (2) ghuṭa maśa (2) ghuṭa (2) ghoṭaya (2) anantakṣobhakarāya nāgādhipataye heherurukaṃ saptapātālagatān nāgān ākarṣaya varṣaya garjaya tarjaya hūṃ (8) phaṭ svāhā.
If it rains in this manner and yet does not rain, then one should recite the mantra in reverse:
HĀSVĀ PHAṬ (3) HŪṂ (3) HŪṂ (8) YARJATA YARJAGA YARṢAKA YARṢAKA NĀGĀNĀTAṂGALATĀPĀPTASAKARURUHEHE YETA-PADHIGĀNĀYARĀKABHAKṢONANTĀNAAYAṬAGHO (2) ṬAGHA (2) ŚAMA (2) ṬAGHŪ (2) ṬAGHA (2) OṂ.

When this has been recited in this manner, if the nāgas do not send rain, then their heads will burst open like the cluster of an *arjaka* flower. The *arjaka* is a white-stemmed plant resembling the black *mallikā*;
just as its cluster bursts open under the heat of the sun, such is the rule.
Thus ends the procedure for the rain-summoning rite (*varṣāpaṇavidhi*).
One hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for this mantra;
through ten million recitations (*koṭijapa*), the mantra is perfected (*mantrasiddhi*).
When it occurs through one million homas, then by means of the mantra for the offering of the bali, the practitioner causes the nāgas to rain;
in that case, there is no requirement for the mandala ritual.

Regarding the mandala ritual, the preliminary service consisting of one hundred thousand recitations and ten thousand homas must be performed; then the nāgas will rain, and not otherwise—such is the rule of the Root Tantra.
Now, the dispersal of clouds is described:
when excessive rain occurs here, the practitioner, having filled a shallow bowl with the ashes of a cremation ground and having bathed that Ananta [serpent],
should sit upon a cloth from a cremation ground and recite this mantra.
"Oṃ ārya smaśānapriyāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—with this, one should shatter [the clouds].
For this as well, the service is performed as before through fire-offerings (homa) and recitations (japa); such is the procedure for shattering the clouds.
Now the practice for the Vajra-Sickle is described:
here, for the sake of training beings who are difficult to subdue,
one should accomplish it by reciting the mantra of the Vajra-Sickle ten million times.
Then, after performing one million oblations (*daśalakṣahoma*), one should perform the ritual preparation (*sādhana*) of chalk.
Having ground the chalk together with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and *kuṭhāracchinnā*,
one should form pills the size of a eyeball.
Then, having gone to the abode of Heruka and having cast oneself into the mouth of Heruka, one should recite the mantra until the image offers that pill through its own mouth to the practitioner:
*oṃ vajrakartari hevajrāya hūṃ phaṭ*.
For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while remaining on a single seat; once that accomplishment is attained,
one should draw a line upon the neck of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
If a line is seen upon the neck of the king together with his retinue, and one should break the neck of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), then the enemies shall be deprived of their heads;
thus ends the section on the Vajra-kartari.
Now, the ritual procedure for the Vajra-kuṭhāra is described.
In this regard, one who wishes to shatter the deities of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) should accomplish the *tilaka* of the Vajra-axe.
Having performed the mantra-accomplishment here as before, then, under the Puṣya asterism on the full moon day, one should take a seed of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree—
this is called the *palāśa*.
One should dry that seed during a solar eclipse,
mix it with an equal portion of *kuṭhāracchinnā*, and grind it with *Akṣobhya*.
Having ground it, one should have an axe made;
treading upon it with the foot, one should recite the mantra:
*oṃ vajrakuṭhāra pāṭaya hā hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this [mantra] ten million times as before, one should then, during a solar eclipse, perform the rite for a day and night; having ground that [substance], one should apply it as a *tilaka*.
With that applied, whichever deity the practitioner bows to, he shatters her. This is the procedure for the shattering of deities (*devatāsphāṭana-vidhi*).
Now, the method for producing a fever by burning is explained.
Having first accomplished the mantra as before, one who wishes to cause a fever by burning should write the name of the enemy on an Arka leaf with *viparājikā* mixed with a painter’s ink:
*oṃ hevajra jvara jvara śatrūn bhuṃ hūṃ (3) phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, one should bury it eight finger-breadths deep in the ground;
having placed fire upon it, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Thereupon, fever shall arise in the person targeted for subjugation.
Liberation [from fever] occurs by washing with clarified butter and cow’s milk;
this is the procedure for fever caused by heat.
Now, the method for inducing vomiting of wine is described.

Having accomplished the mantra for vomiting wine as before, one who then desires to make the subject vomit wine should visualize at the subject's navel a wind mandala transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*; above that, one should visualize a belly of wine transformed from the syllable *maṃ*, with disheveled hair and vomiting wine; thus the subject vomits the wine.
"Oṃ vajramudriraṃ maṃ hūṃ (3) phaṭ svāhā"— one should recite this one hundred and eight times; this is the procedure for swallowing my mantra.
Now, the method of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is explained.

Having first accomplished the *Kurukullā* mantra according to the previously described procedure through recitation (*jāpa*) numbering ten million (*koṭi*) and so forth, one who desires to subjugate a woman should go beneath an *aśoka* tree on the eighth day of the fortnight of the *aśoka*, put on red garments, eat *madanaphala* fruit,
apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with the juice of *kāmācikā*, and recite the mantra.
Oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ, may [Name] be brought under my control, svāhā!
She comes within ten thousand recitations;
this is the procedure for subjugation.
Now, the procedure for the retention of the moon and sun is explained:
first, having recited the mantra seven million times, the practitioner of mantra should accomplish the rite;

thereafter, one who desires to retain the moon and sun should recite the mantra, fashion an image of either the moon or the sun out of rice-flour, cook it with steam-sweat, and place vajra-water into a four-finger-deep shallow bowl.
Oṃ vajrārka, do not move! Stay! Stay! Svāhā to Hevajra!
For the stabilization of the sun and the stabilization of the moon, [recite] "Oṃ vajracandra," and so forth.
If one recites [the mantra] ten thousand times, the moon or the sun remains [suspended];
liberation occurs through holding [the breath] with urine.
This is the procedure for the retention of the moon and the sun.
Now, the introduction of the questions regarding Vajrajyotiṣa is explained.
Having first accomplished the mantra through one million recitations (*japa*) and one hundred thousand burnt offerings (*homa*) of red lotuses, the mantra there is:
*oṃ nagrā kumārike divyalocane svāhā*.
With this mantra, at the time of twilight, one should consecrate the eyes of a young girl one hundred and eight times with the five offerings, such as flowers and incense, and then invite her.

On either the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day, at dawn, having established a water-pot (kalaśa) and placed sprouts of a milk-tree upon the pot, one should place oil in a copper vessel and lac-dye in another vessel. Having consecrated these with the aforementioned mantra one hundred and eight times, one should smear the thumb of the left hand with the lac-dye and bathe [the girl] with sesame oil.
The practitioner should recite the mantra;
if another person asks, "Tell me, by whom has my wealth been stolen? or asks about another matter, he sees what it is like.

Thus, having seen [the mark] there along with the thumb, one says: "The property has been stolen by so-and-so; such-and-such an event will occur. This is the procedure for the introduction of questions in the *Vajrajyotiṣa*.
Now, the mantra for warding off cattle is taught:
having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, the words of the mantra in the middle,
and *hevajrāya svāhā* at the end.
Having accomplished this with one million repetitions for each of the ten [mantras], one should then employ them against wild animals:
when "veḍuryā" is uttered, the elephant flees;
when "marmā" is uttered, the tiger flees.
When "tailliyā" is uttered twice, Gaṇḍa flees;
when "ili mili phūḥ phūḥ" is uttered, the serpent flees;
Oṃ śvā tiṣṭha tiṣṭha Hevajrāya svāhā.
Thus is the procedure for warding off animals.

In this same way, having inserted the name of each [creature], such as a deer (*ṛṣabha*) and so forth, in the middle— preceded by the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and followed by "to Hevajra, svāhā" at the end—
the mantras become accomplished through recitation and become effective through fire-offerings (*homa*).
"It is not by mere recitation from a book"—this is the rule of the Blessed One. Now, in the Root Tantra, the deity yoga for the rites of immobilization and so forth is taught.
Here, Vajrā is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); by means of her, immobilization is achieved.
Gaurī is the aggregate of sensation; by her, subjugation is achieved. Vāriyoginī is the aggregate of perception; by her, attraction is achieved.
Vajraḍākinī is the aggregate of mental formations; by her, expulsion is achieved.
The aggregate of consciousness is Nairātmā; by her comes the riddling [vidveṣaṇa].
Bhūcarī is Sparśavajrā; by her comes the summoning [ākarṣaṇa]. Khecarī is Dharmadhātuvajrā; by her comes the slaying [māraṇa].
In this way, there is the immobilization of a Pukkasi; with a Śavarī who has the color of a moonstone, there is pacification; and with a Caṇḍālī, there is subjugation.
The expulsion by means of Ḍombī, the inciting of hatred by means of Vajradhātvīśvarī,
and the killing by means of Jñānadhātu are accomplished.

Thus, all [the rites] in the external and internal [realms] should be known by yogins. Stambhana and the other [rites] are to be accomplished through the yoga of the deity, by means of mantra recitation, fire offerings (*homa*), and the performance of ritual oblations (*bali*), according to their yellow, white, black, dark, and blue colors. This is the rule of the Blessed One in the *Mūlatantra*. Thus ends the seventh chapter, the second section, the instruction on the accomplishment of the expansion of activities (*karmaprasara-sādhanopadeśa*), in the *Hevajra-ṭīkā* in six thousand [stanzas].
Those who behold the Lord of Jinas—whether as fierce, passionate, or of supremely peaceful form—indeed see their own mind as being exactly like that; that mind of aspiration manifests in all forms.
That single mind is the mind of application; it is no-mind, yet it is mind, purified by the three liberations.
Having prostrated with my head to that Vajrasattva, the perceiver who pervades all three times,
this commentary on the Chapter on Deities is written by Vajragarbha for the sake of sentient beings attaining the path, based on the understanding of the Root Tantra;
it concerns the single stage of generation through reliance upon the nature of sentient beings.
The second, however, is the supportless practice of the generation stage.
Here, in the *Laghutantra*, the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the deities.
First, one should cultivate loving-kindness."
Regarding the initial words of such passages, the initial, middle, and final words are introduced from the *Mūlatantra*.
Here, the Blessed One said: "O Vajragarbha, I shall explain the procedure for the sādhana of the deities."
By which the yogic self, the practitioner of mantra and mudrās, attains accomplishment:
at the time of dawn, having discharged urine and feces, the mantra-practitioner should thereafter perform purification and so forth, and sit upon level ground. ||4-5||
Having fashioned a pill consisting of ten substances, one should place it in one's own mouth;
having prepared a mandala before oneself with cow-dung mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth, to Gaurī and the others in their proper order.
Gaurī is in the east (Indra), Caurī in the south (Yama), and Vetālī is situated in the west (Varuṇa).
The goddess Ḍākinī is in the north (Dhanada), while Bhūcarikā is situated below and Khecarikā above; they are to be worshipped there in their proper order.
In the northeast is the goddess Pukkasī, and likewise Śavarī in the southeast; Caṇḍālī is in the southwestern corner, and Ḍombinī in the northwest in due order.
One should worship Hevajra in the center of the wheel together with Nairātmyā.
Furthermore, one should recollect loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth toward all sentient beings.
Then, having worshipped her, one should place that seed-syllable within one's own body;
that seed-syllable, consisting of the letters of her name, should be endowed with its form and the bindu.
Gaurī has gone to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), while Caurikā is in the realm of sound (śabdadhātu); Vetālī is in the realm of smell (gandhadhātu), and Ghasmarī is in the realm of taste (rasadhātu).
Bhūcarī is in the realm of touch (sparśadhātu), while Khecarī is in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The goddess Pukkasī is in the eyes; Śavarī is considered to be in the ears.
The goddess Caṇḍālinī is in the nose, and Ḍombinī is considered to be in the tongue.
Hevajra is in the faculty of the body, while Nairātmyā resides in the mind.
Thus, in the Root Tantra, is the first limb-assignment (*aṅganyāsa*).
One should assign the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *maṃ*, *khaṃ*, *paṃ*, *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, *taṃ*, *haṃ*, and *naṃ* to the aforementioned elements.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the protection of the locations.
Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a double-pronged vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from *hūṃ* within that sun;
and by means of that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-binding.

In this very Root Tantra, one should first meditate on the protection wheel for the purpose of warding off the wicked; the mantra-practitioner should perform the ritual of staking (kīlana) to destroy obstacles. Subsequently, assuming the form of the King of Wrath, he should accomplish his chosen deity.
This Hevajra Tantra, which consists of wisdom and means, is a Yoga Tantra; subsequently, through the movement of the Yoginīs, it is called a Yoginī Tantra with respect to the practice of Nairātmyā.
Therefore, according to the procedure of the Yoga Tantra, the lords of the wrathful deities (krodhendras) such as Yamāntaka and others are to be visualized within the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*).
The leader of the wheel is Vajrahuṃkāra, who is Heruka with six arms.

First, having meditated on a sun mandala in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one visualizes a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) transformed from the syllable *hūṃ* at its center, which has four faces.

By means of that very Viśvavajra, which has become one with the sun, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a vajra-fence and a vajra-cage in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, a vajra-ground above and below—which is impenetrable by all Māras—and various terrifying weapons outside and above and below the fence.

Beyond this, it is stated from the Root Tantra; therein the Blessed One said: "I shall explain in due order the seats of the Wrathful Kings, as well as their faces, colors, arms, weapons, and their pratyālīḍha stances. (15)
Within the vajra-fence, one should place an eight-spoked wheel produced from the eight forms of the letter Ā; having meditated upon that,
one should then further fashion two spokes, one below and one above the fence.
With eleven *rephas*, one should [place] solar mandalas in due order. With eleven wheels of the sun, those are the steps of the Sun;
one should place the syllable *hūṃ* upon each of those solar mandalas.

One should visualize the Wrathful King arising from the syllable *hūṃ*, seated upon a sun-disc in the center; one should meditate on the Leader Vajra-hūṃkāra, who is blue in color, with three faces and six arms, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture. (19)
The root [face] has a blue face and fangs, and is terrifyingly formidable;
the left and right [faces] are white and red, situated like the three channels (nāḍīs).
In the right hands, there is a vajra-knife and a trident in due order.
In his left hands, he holds a vajra-bell, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga;
he wears a crown of victory marked by a double-vajra and bears the image of Akṣobhya and a crescent moon.
A garland of severed heads rests upon his shoulders, and he is adorned with skulls on his head.
With his waist encircled by a tiger skin and the bones of the five mudrās,
possessing nine eyes and a protruding tongue, and adorned with ornaments of serpents—
one should then meditate upon such a leader, Vajrahūṃkāra.
One should place the fierce Yamāntaka, who is black and arises from the syllable *hūṃ*, upon the eastern sun; he stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
has three faces— black, white, and red— and possesses large bellies and three eyes.
They possess the five mudrās and skull-cups, and wear garlands and tiger-skins at their waists.
The lords of serpents and the universal vajras mark them; the family of the Lord is upon the crown of all of them.
Their colors and weapons are distinct, as are their four legs.

In the right hands, there should be a staff, a wheel, and a vajra in due order; in the heart-hand (the first left), a noose with the threatening gesture, and in the remaining left hands, a bell and an axe. || 28 ||
On the head is the Buddha Vairācana, and another is Vajramauli; both are produced from the white syllable *hūṃ* on a solar maṇḍala to the right.
The white wrathful deity Prajñāntaka has faces that are white, blue, and reddish-brown;
he holds, in his right hands in successive order, a wisdom-staff (prajñā-khaṭvāṅga), a thunderbolt, and a staff.
He should hold a pestle, a vajra, and a sword in his left hands.
In the heart [hand] there is a noose with the index finger raised, and on the left side a bell and an axe.
He is crowned by Amoghasiddhi, who is produced from the blue syllable HŪṂ;
he has faces that are blue, red, and white, and possesses the terrifying appearance of a gaping mouth. || 33 ||
Likewise, the universal vajra, the discus, and the pestle are on the right side;
and the bell, the threatening gesture with a noose, and the axe are on the left. || 34 ||
One should place Vighnāntaka upon the sun in the north; Amṛtakuṇḍalī, produced from the blue syllable HŪṂ, [is placed] in the southeast; and Acala should be placed upon the sun in the south. || 35 ||
He has faces that are blue, red, and white, and bears the crown of Śrī Vairocana;
he holds a sword, a vajra, and a wheel in his right hands. || 36 ||
In his heart [he holds] a noose with the index finger, and to the left a bell and an axe;
he is produced from the blue syllable *hūṃ*, and has faces that are blue, red, and white.
In the southwest is King Ṭarki, who wears a crown of Ratnasaṃbhava and holds the Trailokyavijaya mudrā with both hands.
In his right hands he holds a vajra and a sword, and in his left a noose and a goad;
he is produced from the blue syllable HŪṂ and wears a crown of Amitābha. || 39 ||
One should place the mantra of Nīladaṇḍa in the northwest within the solar mandala;
the root mantra is the left [face], while the Raudra [mantra] consists of blue, red, and white faces.
In the right hands, he holds in order a staff, a sword, and a discus;
in the left, a noose with the index finger extended, a lotus, and an axe.

The practitioner of mantra should place [the deity], who is blue in color, possesses great strength, is produced from the syllable *hūṃ*, and is crowned by Amoghasiddhi, upon the sun in the northeast.
With faces that are black, red, and white, and possessing a large belly and a terrifying appearance, he holds a staff, a sword, and likewise a discus in his right hands in due order. (43)
In his heart is a noose formed by the index finger; from the syllable *hūṃ*, dark blue in color, he arises, adorned with Akṣobhya as his crest-ornament. || 44 ||
One should place the uṣṇīṣa upon the head with the left and right hands.
And with the two right hands, he holds a vajra and a lotus; the other [left hand] holds a raised index finger and a sword. || 45 ||
Having ascended the sun in the sky, one should visualize [the deity] in the station of Brahmā,
crowned by Akṣobhya, produced from the black syllable *HŪṂ*.
Below Sumbharāja is Sūrya, whose faces are black, red, and white; he holds a vajra, a wheel, and a trident in his right hands in due order. (47)
Having thus meditated upon the terrifying array of wrathful deities, [holding] a noose with the index finger, a sword, and an axe in the left hands at the heart; || 48 ||
Then the mantra-practitioner, having brought them forth, should cause them to enter his own body;
he should place Yamāntaka on the left arm and Prajñāntaka on the right.
One should place Padmāntaka in the left hand and Vighnāntaka in the right;
Acala on the left thigh and Ṭakkirāja on the right.
One should place Nīladaṇḍa on the left leg and Mahābala on the right foot;
one should place Mahoṣṇīṣa at the site of the crest-lock (śikhā) and Śumbharāja in the anus;
one should place Vajrahūṃkāra in the heart and the first letter of each deity's own name [in their respective locations]. || 51 ||

Having thus performed the ritual of protection with *yaṃ*, *ghraṃ*, *paṃ*, *raṃ*, *aṃ*, *daṃ*, *naṃ*, *maṃ*, *draṃ*, *saṃ*, and *vaṃ* in due order, the mantra-practitioner should then meditate on himself as Vajra-hūṃkāra in a wrathful form;
thereafter, by the command of Sumbha, he should nail down all obstacles and sins.

Oṃ gha (2) ghātaya all the wicked ones phaṭ! Kīlaya (2)! Oṃ sumbha-nisumbha hūṃ ūṃ! Cause them to be seized (2)! Hūṃ (2)! Bring them here, O Blessed One, King of Vidyās, phaṭ! With this wrathful form, having drawn in the obstructors and Vināyakas, the wise one should pierce them all according to the ritual by means of this yoga. 52.
One should visualize the great wrathful Vighnāntaka, with three eyes and six arms, in the form of a trident at the region of the navel and other parts, and upon his head.
Beholding the hosts of obstructors below, one should recite their mantra;
then, one should firmly drive the vajra-stake into the bodies of the obstructors.

Oṃ ghā ghā ghātaya (2) all malevolent ones phaṭ (2); [strike] all the sins of the kīla phaṭ (2); hūṃ (2). Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: nail down the body, speech, and mind of all obstructors hūṃ (2) phaṭ!
And one should visualize Sumbharāja with a vajra-mallet in his hand.
The knower of mantras should strike the vajra-kila with this mantra. 55.

Having struck with the vajra-hammer, [one should say] "Tisṭha! Tisṭha! Having then impaled the wicked ones upon stakes in the ten directions, one should visualize the vajra-fire flashing forth on all sides. || 56 ||
When the wicked have fled and are being burned here and there by that [fire],

then one should contemplate the three worlds as being without intrinsic nature according to the ultimate truth; for in the absence of existence, cultivation is itself non-existence, and such cultivation is not true cultivation at all.
Thus, existence would not be existence; no mental cultivation is perceived. || 57 ||
First is the awakening to emptiness; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
third is the manifestation of the image; fourth is the placement of the syllables.
Having completed these, one should contemplate the Lord, the Sovereign, together with the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas, according to one's inclination, in the sky.

Then, having visualized those [deities] surrounded by the eight mothers and embraced by their own wisdom-consorts (*prajñā*), they enter his own heart. From the syllable *hūṃ*, he should emanate the eight goddesses for the purpose of making offerings to the Blessed One.
Here too, in reverse order, they radiate forth with a single verse, covering the mandala of the sky with their own bodies;
the yogin should then withdraw them and bring them back into his own heart, becoming the embodiment of Hatred (*dveṣa*).
Having seen the Lord Vajrajaṅgha, the Great Compassionate One, in the sky.
One should worship with the eight goddesses, who wear all ornaments:
Gaurī, who holds the moon; and Caurī, who holds the sun.
Vetālī holds a water-pot; Bhaiṣajyadhātrī holds a medicine box; Ghasmarī is Pukkasī with a vajra in her hand; likewise, Śabarī holds a vessel of flavors.
Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), and Ḍombī attains liberation through passion.
The moon is semen, the sun is the menstrual blood, and water is said to be urine. || 61 ||
Alcohol and meat are the medicine; Vajra is known as Vairocana.
Rasa is celebrated as the six flavors; Gokṣādyam is the drum (ḍamaruka) of strength. || 62 ||
Dancing and the drinking of intoxicants—these eight are known as the *samayas*.
With these, the practitioner of mantra should perform worship and go for refuge to the Three Jewels. (63)
One should perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merits, and the dedication of one's own body, solely by taking recourse to the Path. (64)
Having generated the thought of awakening, one should then leave behind the Buddhas;
for the sake of taking emptiness as an object, one should contemplate the object of the aspirational vow. || 65 ||
