Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty; because it is without cause, it is signless; because it transcends the extremes, it is wishless; thus it is entirely devoid of volitional construction. || 66 ||
Because there is no cessation of arising, aspiration is purposeless;
neither a sentient being nor Buddhahood exists, nor do dharma and adharma exist in reality. (67)
Just as an illusion, so is a dream; just as a city of the Gandharvas, so should Buddhas be viewed by those who cultivate reality through their meditations on suchness.
Just as there is an echo, so too is the Dharma-teaching of the Buddhas;
having reflected thus upon the persistence of existence throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, [one should not be attached]. (69)
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, Bodhisattvas perform even killing, as well as meditative attainments and the removal of the cognitive obscurations. (70)
It has not been utterly consumed by the great afflictions, yet not even a mere fragment is preserved by the Bodhisattvas, those great heroes who are compassionate toward all sentient beings. (71)
Having investigated everything—both the state of Buddhahood and the state of a Bodhisattva—one should take emptiness as one's object of focus and recite this mantra. (72)
Having recited "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of emptiness," one should then contemplate the aspiration.
With that mind of aspiration, one should cultivate the divine pride through one's own mind for the sake of sporting in the three worlds.
Here, having meditated upon the mandala circle to be described, adorned with the eight cremation grounds:
In the center of that is an eight-petaled lotus, and beyond that, a solar mandala.
One should meditate upon the preta as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, with the thirty-two vowels [upon] the moon, for the sake of the causes of the marks of a Buddha. (74)
The eighty secondary marks are the syllable *arke* and the syllable *hūṃ*; these two are said to be *sattva*, whose intrinsic nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). (75)
The mirror-like wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment in sequence, their single unified activity, and the manifestation of the [Buddha] image itself. (76)
This is declared to be the dharmadhātu, the supreme fifth gnosis. Hevajra, awakened through the five aspects, shall be two-armed. (77)
With a complexion of blue and reddish luster, his eyes are like red lotus buds;
Akṣobhya forms his crest with a garland of skulls and severed heads.
The wheel, the earring, the necklace, the bracelet, and the girdle—these five mudrās are proclaimed as the purification of the five Buddhas. (79)
The Extensive Commentary on the Meaning (*Arthavistara-ṭīkā*) of the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*. Homage to the glorious Hevajra!

May the nature of the Victorious One—who has utterly purified worldly existence, who is eternally present and all-pervasive, who is non-dual, free from conceptual elaboration, beyond the senses, and the supreme bliss of the *E-Vam*—be victorious!
The mind is not the mind, yet it is the mind; it is not material, but possesses all the sense faculties.
I prostrate to the Svabhāvakāya of the Buddhas, for the sake of realizing the deathless.
From the complete conquest of the King of Qualities arise the eight faces of the Lord of Purification.
The sixteen emptinesses and the compassions are these skulls; the ten immutable [moments] are expressed as the arrangement of that very [skull-]garland upon the shoulders.
In the Kali age, he possesses the nature of Akṣobhya, the crescent moon, the vajra, and the lion throne.
He dwells and sits with Maitreya and the others, along with the liberations and the excellent feet.
With the *Tattvajñānasaṃgraha*, the application of the "Crawling Serpent" mudrā, and a tiger skin,
he entered.
For the sake of benefiting the minds of those who practice bowing and so forth, he adorned them according to the sequence of the parts.
Having bowed, I shall write this commentary, which explains the secrets of this tantra.

For the sake of yogis attaining the great state, the glorious Vajrasattva— the sovereign of the ten perfections who desires the welfare of all sentient beings— [extracted this] from the great tantra of one million verses.
Even the *Laghu-tantra*,
which was well-composed, has its seven sections divided; it abounds in many vajra words and causes [the mind] to tremble.
Since Hevajra was taught,
the text consists of six thousand verses; it is that which follows the Moon Tantra.
This is for the purpose of explaining the cause;
it teaches the Yogācāra practice, yet does not abide in the authentic path,
and is a brief tantra lacking [proper] connection.
Those who act as teachers with wicked conduct,
desiring the wealth and wives of others,
strive in the Dharma only to go to hell.
The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: "The conceptual treatise acts as a yogic practice through pride; having been seized by the vast empowerment, it is the very nature of Buddha Vajrasattva."
One who holds the vajra of great joy will become like fire to some people;
yet on this earth, he is himself the Vajradhara.
It is said that those who wear white garments are worthy of being approached;
they are the merchants and commoners who serve, as well as those who dwell upon the fields and mountains.
The deluded who sell the sublime Dharma, who take what is not to be taken and are utterly consumed by it— these belong to the class of Māras; abandon them now!
They will become gurus to their own disciples;
under the guise of engaging in yogic debate, they will conceal the faults they themselves have committed.
"One who perceives faults will never become a disciple; one who grasps at faults will find no spiritual accomplishment here."— Master Guṇaprabha.
In this regard, there is no doubt:
"I am devoid of compassion, fierce and cruel;
arrogant, coarse, and unrestrained."
A wise person should not engage in self-praise, thinking, "I am the guru; you are the disciple.
These words should never be spoken to one's disciples.
Those who act with hypocrisy and deceit, who are wrathful and point out others' vital flaws, who revile and harbor hatred toward the community of monks—
One who is stubborn, filled with base pride, acts with great greed, pursues improper aims, and is more intoxicated by liquor than a common drunkard— such a person is unfit.
Speaking such self-praise here, one finds fault with those who possess genuine qualities.
To have received empowerments and attained the "A-tshog" [realization] is the Vajrayāna;
the master is indeed a Tathāgata.

Not understanding the intended meaning of the statement, "Having come from the abodes of the ten directions, they perform the consecration," even though it refers to those who have appeared throughout the three times;
Those who are deluded by mere names will, having reviled the Sovereign of Victors, now go to the Raurava hell.

From the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: "The Vajrācārya who has cleansed the mind of the vajra, who has attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, and who has received the supreme empowerment— he is a Tathāgata."

The stages of the Bodhisattvas who dwell in all directions are the world-systems that serve as the support for their bodies. Then, having fully emerged through the five aggregates, they prostrate; thereafter, there are various precious substances and diverse entities within the world-systems.
Having prostrated to the Buddha residing in the East,
that is the yoga master (yogācārya) Vajra. Regarding whatever is explained through symbols, it is likewise the urine and feces.
Akṣobhya and Amitābha,
as well as the Master Vajradhara;
excrement, urine, and semen [the mudrās]— just like the Master, they are like a treasure.
Thus, the Vajra Holder spoke: "The siddhis of body, speech, and mind,
through both the relative and the ultimate."
Among the students who are yogis, regarding the mandala at the foot of the Bodhi tree: as before and after, there are those four;
namely, the intentional (*saṃdhāya*) and the non-intentional (*asaṃdhāya*).
Just as there is neither hair nor lack of hair,
so too are the definitive meaning and the provisional meaning;
the tantra itself resides upon the great earth of the six parameters.
Whatever qualities the master possesses here,
those very qualities by which he has died are the characteristics of Vajrasattva’s qualities, such as the six superknowledges and so forth.
Stable, disciplined, and possessed of the proper gait; patient, free from deceit and hypocrisy, and thoroughly proficient in mantra and tantra.
One who is compassionate and learned in the treatises,
whose nature is pure and whose senses are subdued,
is a master who explains the Secret Mantra.
One who possesses these explained qualities becomes a bhikṣu-vajradhara.
For śrāmaṇeras and lay practitioners, these same [qualities] apply; they are not harmed by diseases in this world, and they possess the ten bases for protection.
It is explained that possessing the bases of training and reaching the ultimate limit of the bases of training are not equal;
thus it was taught in the Root Tantra: "The stage of a Bhikṣu-Vajradhara..."
Just as Nairātmyā requested from the Vajra-holder regarding those few [points] that were difficult for her, he spoke these words concerning the training rules: "The eye is this."
First, one should perfectly possess the five bases of training,
such as the proper conduct of eating and so forth,
and completely abandon the ten non-virtuous actions.

Having approached, one should become a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*). Then, having bestowed the [refuge] precepts, one should become a great virtuous one (*mahāśrāvaka*). Thereafter, the bases of training (*śikṣāpada*) are to be explained.
From *vinna*, one should practice the ascetic discipline (*śramaṇa-vrata*);
then, having understood each individually as superior,
one subsequently attains the specific state of healing.
Having understood that through *maji-di*,
from the consciousness of one's own nature,
there then arises the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One should understand the intent as the Middle Way;
likewise, in other tantras,
it is known as Hevajra.
From the *Niḥsaraṇa* of the *Hūsushaśrī*: "The single vehicle abides as the fruit;
[it includes] the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas here."
This is the third Mahāyāna;
it is not the intention of the Snowy Land Buddhists or the Five Treatises of Maitreya.
Emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects is the initial cause; aspiration is the subsequent compassion; and acting for the benefit of transmigrating beings is like the result of activity.

One who accomplishes the welfare of others after first accomplishing their own welfare is indeed wise; for what kind of person could be considered poor if they were satisfied with their own well-being?
How could one bestow that upon others?
Through compassion for the welfare of sentient beings, strive to provide them with the assembly of bliss, power, and prosperity.
Since cause and effect are the treasury of meaning,
as long as the cause has not been manifested,
for that long there is initially no cause.
From which result will it arise?
These two vehicles other than the Mahāyāna that are described here consist of the paths of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth.
For the sake of providing rest,
I have explained that very emptiness— the differentiation of all phenomena— which acts as their occasional emergence.
From the cause that brings about definitive emergence,
and then from the power of compassion itself,
the fruit— the nature of great compassion— arises.
It arises without an object of observation;
it is without sentient beings, phenomena, or objects of observation.
This compassion is explained as being threefold.
Regarding the winds that perform limited functions,
those who focus on sentient beings as their object are the accomplished bodhisattvas.
For those who abide on the stages,
the two causes of conceptualization have ceased; for those whose nature abides on all stages, there is no objective referent for the Sugatas.
I shall explain the various ways of benefiting beings extensively.
Whatever the cause may be and however it appears, such and such will be the resulting manifestation.
Even if some [grains] were to arise from a field of rice, they would not arise as rice itself; likewise for seeds and likewise for trees.
Just as a tree and its fruit,
and like lightning from beginning to end,
the word of the Sage is virtuous throughout.
First, regarding "from the net of conceptualization":
since results arise accompanied by conceptualization,
this applies to all Buddhists.
The Madhyamaka and Prāsaṅgika do not [assert] emptiness as a mere nothingness.
First, for the purpose of purifying the fields,
one sows the seeds of merit.
Just as one sows seeds upon a field that has been cultivated from the outside,
so too are human beings born upon the field of karma.
It is taught that the impure is not the ultimate expanse;
it is the birth within the six classes of beings,
which is described as the fruit of virtuous and non-virtuous actions.
In a pure realm where beings are not born, when the seed of non-referential compassion is sown,
from that very ground the wish-fulfilling tree of emptiness arises.
When one contemplates emptiness,
from the source of non-referential compassion, there is no doubt that all things arise as the display of the dharmakāya.
Regarding these profound and vast phenomena:
To those such as myself who lack the fortunate destiny,
the mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth—
whatever is pleasing— are not taught.
Through the mandalas, mantras, and so forth of the Svayambhū [tradition],
they will teach Buddha Vajrasattva; these future masters shall be like the sun to the maras and demons.
This certainty is for the sake of establishing that other [reality], namely this very illness; it is the measure for curing that illness.

Regarding the meaning of accomplishment and so forth, these four are based on the words and syllables, and not otherwise. As stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: "Whatever [beings] below—the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others—possess their respective languages, and even those of others..."
The Blessed One, who brought forth the essential points of all phenomena and who is wondrous even by worldly standards,
has uttered this very melody of speech, which possesses the nature of the Great Vedic Grammar (*Mahāvyākaraṇa*). Why, then, would wise people not marvel at this scripture?
The supreme Vairocana, the miraculous Oṃ-kāra, and the illusory Ḍākinīs—
through these,
the wise have definitively established the body of the Bhagavān as being adorned with the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor signs.
The aggregates, elements, faculties, and objects reside within the maṇḍala.
Fools always maintain that dependent origination arises and emerges through cognition;
however, destruction, birth, lunar dates, planetary movements, and so forth are taught in other tantras.
Just as a foolish child who has never tasted milk has no expectation of yogurt, so too,
for one who is utterly devoid of realization, what is the use of mere words?
One should understand the supreme lotus wheel and the seat by means of the vajra.
This short ritual cycle of Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara is to be understood through the *Catuḥpīṭha*;
the definitive meaning is to be understood through the words and supreme symbols of the *Paramādibuddha*.
These and other such tantras...
Other tantras should always be understood through their stable structure and detailed explanations by those who desire to enter the stages.
Thus concludes the first section, which is the praise of the *Yalam* and the introduction to the tantra, from the six-thousand-verse commentary on the *Hevajra*.

Now, at the time of explaining the teaching of the Tantra, first, having clearly perceived the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expressive words (*abhidhāna*), the connection (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*), [the author] says: "For the sake of those people who are devoid of certainty, with the intention of my own mind, I shall liberate them into Buddhahood in this very life. Seated upon the syllable *E-Vaṃ*, surrounded by the network of Ḍākinīs, having entered the heart of Hevajra, requested by Vajragarbha and also questioned by Nairātmyā—from the five-hundred-thousand-verse Hevajra, this concise tantra consisting of seven hundred and fifty verses was taught by the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva. Here, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the Blessed Lord Hevajra together with his consort. The expressive words (*abhidhāna*) are the king of tantras, the collection of chapters that bring about the realization of this. The connection (*sambandha*) is the mutual relationship between the subject matter and the expressive words. The purpose (*prayojana*) is the bestowing of empowerments, such as entering the maṇḍala and so forth. The ultimate purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*) is the clarification of reality (*tattva*) through the empowerment. Having clearly perceived these, for those people who are devoid of certainty—meaning those of the Śrāvaka discipline—with their own mental disposition, he says: "In this very life, I shall thoroughly [attain] Buddhahood. "Thoroughly" means in this very birth; it does not refer to future births, nor to those such as Yakṣas and the like.

Regarding the phrase "completely surrounded by a lattice," this refers to that which is characterized by the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*). When Vajragarbha, having entered into meditative equipoise on the *Hevajra-samādhi*, made a request, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was thoroughly requested. From the thirty-second great chapter of the five-hundred-thousand-verse *Kṛtya-tantra* of the *Hevajra*, the condensed *Laghu-tantra*—which consists of two chapters concerning the nature of the lattice of the miraculous manifestations of complete awakening—is taught by the Blessed One Vajrasattva. For the sake of mundane and supramundane accomplishments through the mundane and supramundane truths, it is taught by means of the generation stage (*utpatti-krama*) and completion stage (*niṣpanna-krama*), the meditation on the maṇḍala circle, and the meditation on suchness (*tattva*). Here, that which is to be expressed is the *Hevajra*, and the *Hevajra-tantra* is that which expresses it. That which is to be expressed also exists by way of the essential nature of the expresser: first, it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on the Vajra Family; then, it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Mantras; then, it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Deities; likewise, it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Empowerment; it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Suchness; it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Offerings; it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on Symbols and the Determination of the Abodes; and it exists by way of the essential nature of the Chapter on the Assembly of the Yoga Circle.

It abides as the essential nature of the chapter on Abiding and Purification; it abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the Bestowal of Empowerment; and it abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the King of Permanence, the Manifestly Perfect Enlightenment.
This concludes the analysis of the first section, the Investigation of the Net of Sound. Next follows the Investigation of the Net of Sound.
"Ḍākinī" refers to the *ḍākinīs*;
"net" (*jāla*) means a gathering;
"assembly" (*saṃvara*) means a congregation; and "together with Heruka" is the definitive meaning.
This very [tantra] exists by way of the essential nature of the chapter on the initial consecration, fire offerings, hearths, and the infinite methods for accomplishing the aims;

then it exists by way of the essential nature of the chapter on the descent of the actual siddhis; and likewise, it exists by way of the essential nature of the chapters on the introductory nidāna of all tantras and the intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
It abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the meaning of the mudrās of all tantras;
it abides as the essential nature of the chapter on the emergence of the vajra seed-syllables;
and [it abides as] the complete purity of the mudrās.
Abiding by way of the essential nature of the fixed proportions for the *vṛsa* and the *pustaka*;
abiding by way of the essential nature of the chapter on the ritual of eating; and the characteristics of the *padmavatī*.

The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* (Tibetan Translation): The nature of the chapter on "Disciplining the Disciples" as it exists, and the nature of the chapters on "The Purification of the Deities" and "The Bestowal of Mantras" as they exist.

The mantra recitation chapter abides by way of its own essential nature; the application and authorization through the meaning of the coemergent abide by way of the essential nature of the introductory narrative;
and thus, those very chapters abide by way of their own essential nature. Then, the Bhagavān Hevajra became the vajra, which is the supreme essence.

Then the Blessed One spoke: “The essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), which is bliss itself. This is the most secret of secrets from the venerable Secret [Tantra]; it must not be spoken of at all to those who delight in the proliferation of conceptual thought.
O Vajragarbha of great compassion, excellent, excellent!”

"Listen, O Vajrasattva, Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, and Lord of the Samayasattva, known as Hevajra!"— having spoken thus at the conclusion of the location, the Blessed One shall now describe the location where he previously entered.

Then, having been exhorted by the speech and vajra-arms of the Blessed One, [the compiler] spoke these words: "Thus have I heard at one time; the Blessed One was dwelling in the embrace of the Vajrayoginī, the body, speech, and mind-vajra of all the Tathāgatas. These are the words concerning his dwelling.
Now, as for the phrase "Thus have I heard at one time," does it refer to the Teacher, the Omniscient One, or rather to the requester who makes the petition?
If one were to interpret this according to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), there would be a fault. Here,
if that which was heard in the past were kept secret, then at that time, primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) would not exist in the future, because it would have been fully known through anger toward others.

If it were not the case that [the Buddha] was the one who performed the cutting, then such expressions as "the gnosis" and so forth would be meaningless; this is because Vajrasattva has stated that it is for that reason.
Therefore, this should be understood as the definitive meaning through another intentional language (*saṃdhāyabhāṣā*).
This very point of definitive meaning is expressed by: "The syllable E, which is of excellent form..."
In the center, adorned with the syllable ŚAM,
it is the abode of all bliss;
it is the Buddha known as Ratnaketu, the Great Bliss Vajrasattva.
"I am the one who has subdued this; I am the Great Bliss. Thus it is said. "Having heard" means having understood. "By me" means by myself.
The time is when one attains manifest, complete enlightenment in a single instant.
The Bhagavān is Great Bliss.
All Tathāgatas are the five aggregates.

Regarding those [deities], their bodies, speech, and minds are the Vajra Lords. The "Vajra Lords of Body, Speech, and Mind" (kāya-vāk-citta-vajra-adhipatis) are the objective phenomena, namely the elements such as space and so forth;
they are the downward-moving [energies] and—

Through the distinctions of the [bodhicitta’s] arrival, by way of the distinctions of one, two, three, four, and five qualities, [the bodhicitta] abides in the upper parts of the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), the forehead, the throat, the heart, and the navel lotuses;

and through the division of the three qualities, it abides at the navel, the secret place, and the vajra-jewel. Thus it is said that the bodhicittas abide in those locations according to the divisions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth.
By reversing this, the reversal of the stages and the exhaustion of the qualities occurs at the vajra-jewel and the secret place.
Through the exhaustion of objects, [the winds] enter the palate, the upper opening, the throat, the pure [place], and the uṣṇīṣa;
this is described as "by the differentiation of the mountains such as the *Himavat*.
Thus, the elements, aggregates, and so forth, are said to be perfected through their very state of being free from obscuration; this is the stage of great bliss.
The syllable E is Locanā;
the syllable VA is Māmakī;
the syllable MA is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; and the syllable LĀ is Tārā.
The syllable Śrī is Vajradhātvīśvarī;
the syllable Taṃ is Prajñāpāramitā.
Then, regarding the aggregates: the syllable E is Vajrasattva.
The letter Ka is Akṣobhya;
the letter Ma is Amoghasiddhi;
the letter Sa is Mahārāja Ratneśvara.
The syllable YA signifies the immeasurable below. The syllable E signifies Vairocana; the syllable MA signifies the vajra earth.
The syllable GA signifies the vajra water.
The syllable VĀṂ is the earth vajra of form;
the syllable NĀṂ is the water vajra of smell;
the syllable BAṂ is the fire vajra of taste; and the syllable ĀḤ is the wind vajra of sound.
The letter *Ta* is the vajra of the dharmadhātu, the ground.
*Śrī* is that which completely clears away all obscurations of splendor.
*Gami* is the lord who destroys the foundation of the world.
Ta-mig is Kṣitigarbha;
Sa-mig is Ākāśagarbha;
Sa-mig is Vajrapāṇi.
Śākya is Samantabhadra;
thus are the twelve sense bases (āyatana).
Śākya is Jaṅgulī.
The letter *ta* is Nairṛtī; the letter *va* is Mālinī;
the letter *ja* is Atibalā.
The syllable Oṃ is extremely blue.
The syllable Śita is white.
The syllable Ga is Ratnapāṇi (Ratnapāṇi).
*Ge* is the *uṣṇīṣa*;
*tsig* is Vighnantakṛt; the syllable *ai* is Prajñāntakṛt.
The syllable JA is Yamāntaka; the syllable HĀ is Yamāri;
and the syllable DHA is the thirty-seventh Samādhi, the principal Vajrasattva, whose nature is the union of wisdom and method.
Thus, there are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
the six perfections,
and the various auxiliary practices.
The six sense faculties, the six activities governed by karma,
and the six faculties of action.
This refers to the "Great Treatise," which was composed by [the author] Vimalamitra. Therefore,
these applications of mindfulness,
the correct exertions, and the bases of miraculous power...
The four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties,
and the five powers.
These are the eight branches of the noble path and the seven factors of enlightenment.
Thus, from the very nature of present great bliss, there is the dharmakāya.
From the exhaustion of sleep comes the exhaustion of dreams;
from the exhaustion of dreams comes the exhaustion of pleasure.
From the exhaustion of these, the innate body (sahaja-kāya),
the dharma-body (dharma-kāya), the enjoyment-body (saṃbhoga-kāya), and the emanation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya) will arise respectively, in their proper order.
Primordial wisdom, mind, speech, and body will become unimpeded.
Therefore, from every side— hands, feet, and so forth, as well as everywhere— the head and face [are present].
In this world,
she remains entirely covered by a veil;
her light pervades everywhere.
It is the subtle, uncontaminated seed; it is without dullness, free from dust, and stainless; it is clear, awakened, and faultless.
The great, powerful, and awakened self, the sublime one who knows all things in their totality; this is the dharmatā of consciousness,
the glorious holder of non-duality.
Thus, the Blessed One Hevajra—who is liberated from all subtle [conceptualizations] and possesses the nature of the four kāyas—is the teacher.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, the lord of the ten bhūmis, is the requester.
This is as taught in the *Vajra Commentary in One Thousand Verses* (*Vajramālā*) regarding the teacher and the requester, as well as the expressive words and the subject matter to be expressed.
This is the second [section], concerning the connection and the definitive determination of the place where [the teaching] resides.
Now, regarding the method for clarifying the speech of the Blessed One, the Great Vajra Essence, Vajragarbha made this request, beginning with the words "By what... and so forth.
Through this, one becomes Vajrasattva. Why do I become a Bodhisattva?
For what reason am I called a Mahāsattva? These are the words concerning the mind that transcends.

Having heard this supplication of Vajragarbha, the Blessed One said: "He is called 'Indestructible Vajra. Because he is the single identity of the three types of beings and through this reasoning of wisdom, he is explained as 'Vajrasattva.
That being who abides in enlightenment is to be called 'Bodhisattva.'"
"Filled with the flavor of great primordial wisdom, he is called the Great Heroic Being (Sattvavīra). Always abiding in the state of reality, he is explicitly designated as the Samayasattva.
This brief summary is explained in detail in the fifth chapter; therefore, one should engage with that very [text].
The Blessed One said:
"That which is indivisible vajra-awareness is expressed by the syllable *ba*.
The body, speech, and mind are indivisible; they are explicitly denoted by the syllable *ba*."
The Bodhisattva, the single identity of the three realms, is expressed by the syllable *E*.

Together with the syllable *E* as wisdom (*prajñā*), the syllable *Vaṃ* is the nature of the immutable (*akṣara*). The Hero residing in the center of the navel, the secret stamen, is the subject endowed with its own innate primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); he is proclaimed as Vajrasattva.
The two ultimates are explained as Heruka; that itself is the "Mover of the Three Worlds.
That very essence is described as such. It is the bliss of the Buddhas;
that itself becomes the Wisdom Vajra. That itself is the innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
That very meeting with the seal is called the "single-pointed vajra.
Having slain the state of the [ordinary] body, it does not become something other than the ritual of purification.
That which abides in the center of the ancient lotus—
The syllable HŪṂ alone is explained as the Sattva; Akṣobhya is that very one. That itself is described as the Vajra of the Heart; he himself is Viṣṇu with four arms.
That itself is Jvala-jvala; that itself is explained as the Dharmakāya.
The Dharma-wheel abode of the Vajra-holder, who possesses the grove of special joy, is also explained as the "Thoroughly Purifying" (*Vaimalya*); it brings an end to sleep and vomiting.
Filled with the flavor of great primordial wisdom, he is called the Great Being (*Mahāsattva*).
At the throat, the center of the enjoyment wheel, Amitābha is to be expressed as the unceasing sound;
he is described as the vajra of speech that brings about birth. Through both the relative and the ultimate, the state of dreaming is likewise exhausted.
That becomes the Saṃbhogakāya; it performs the teaching of the Dharma for the Buddhas.
That very essence is described as the "Bringer of Bliss" (Śaṃkara). With six faces, feet, and arms, Kiṭikiṭa is the Vajra; Heruka himself becomes the third.
One should always abide by the samaya; whatever remains there is what is to be expressed.
The "hare-holder" (candramas) of the samaya is the seminal essence that abides as the separation from great bliss.
It is well-situated within the "da" of Māra, and is explained as the syllable Oṃ.
Now, the manifestation of light is described: it is the suchness of the Vajra Body.
Brahmā is the holder of the Vajra Body; that shall be fully explained. Joy is the essence of Brahmā; it is described as the Form Body (Rūpakāya).
This very state is explained as the wheel within the cave; it possesses the characteristics of the emanation-body of the deceased.
By reversing [the process], it is again stainless; that itself is the exhaustion of awakening.
That itself becomes the Śrīphala fruit; the eight measures are called Heruka.
The Great Hero possesses four faces and is perfectly endowed with sixteen arms; according to the current classification, Heruka is explained as being fourfold.
From the nature itself (svabhāva) arises the Dharma body (dharmakāya), and from the Dharma body arises the Sambhogakāya.
From that, the transformation into Śalya occurs; in that regard, there are not four swift ones.
Brahmā is the holder of the Body-Vajra; Īśvara is the Lord of Speech-Vajra; Viṣṇu is the holder of the Mind-Vajra;
and Vajrasattva is the holder of the Wisdom-Vajra. Thus it is said: "Vajrasattva is the one who possesses effort."

The detailed explanation regarding the decline of the [Buddha] lineage shall be set forth in three parts. That which possesses the very excellence of reasoning is explained as "the lineage" (*rigs pa*).
Through the classification of the four deeds, this is the presentation of the lineages.

"Buddha" refers to the aspiration (*mānīṣita*). "The yogi should know" means this. Regarding the syllables *e-vam*: *ga* is Vajrasattva; *kha* is Vajraratna (the eye); *ra* is Vajravāk (speech); *oṃ* is Vajrakāya (the body). Through these individual names—*me*, *ba*, *ri*, *phu*, *aḥ*, and *ca*—one should grasp the meaning as it is realized; it is not by means of the letters or names themselves.

Here, the entity of the name does not exist as a real thing; for if it did exist, it would at that time have to be apprehended by the mind and the eye, yet it is not so apprehended. Therefore, while it is to be grasped by the ear, the object to be realized by this [name] is what is to be apprehended by the mind and the eye.

Objects such as vases and woolen cloth are established by means of spinning wheels, looms, staffs, shuttles, threads, frames, bases, yarns, and so forth; they are not produced by the mere power of names. It is not the case that the mere sound of their names acts as the cause for qualities such as color and so on, as if they were like a seed.

Thus spoke the Blessed One’s own words. Now, from the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*, regarding the request made by Vajragarbha and the Blessed One’s response: Vajragarbha asked: "O Hevajra, what is this concise summary? Please explain it clearly. What, moreover, is to be expressed by 'Vajra'?"
The Blessed One said: "The syllable *Ra* represents compassion; *Vajra* is said to be wisdom. Listen as I explain this tantra, which is the very nature of wisdom and method.
This brief summary is explained in detail in the Root Tantra; one should engage with that very text.

Now the Bhagavan spoke these words: "Sentient beings, phenomena, and the absence of focal objects—this compassion is explained as being threefold. Regarding the sound 'Ma' (M), there is no focal object; the syllable 'Ha' (H) should be expressed as wisdom.
Through the union of body, speech, and mind, that very essence is the syllable 'Vaṃ'."
The emptiness of all aspects of objects; that which enters into these [aspects] is what is expressed by the term "yoga. A tantra whose nature is the generation stage is to be called a "yoga tantra."
Through the term "yoga" (*yoga*), *oṃ* [wisdom] does not undergo change;
this is called "Yoga Tantra. Hevajra is non-dual.
All [tantras], such as the Guhyasamāja and others, are essentially the nature of wisdom and method.
All are indeed Yoga Tantras; however, by means of the names "Wisdom" and "Method," those that are well-arranged and in which all yoginīs are gathered,
I have taught to the immature as the *Saṃvṛti-yoginī-tantra*.
The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: That which radiates the melody of the voice, arising from wisdom and bliss—this very tantra of the method, I shall now explain according to the conventional truth.
Just as it is, so too are the meditations on the mudrās and maṇḍalas; however they are analyzed, [so they appear].
Having analyzed it in that way, those things characterized by arising and ceasing are [realized as] the indivisible nature of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is the union of wisdom and method.
When knowledge and the object of knowledge are one, it is the non-duality of the City of Light and Compassion.
Emptiness is without expansion; likewise, it is without clothing.
Compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and equanimity—these are the four Brahma-abodes. From the non-conceptualization of all phenomena, these arise.
Through the dharma that is without wisdom, non-duality is imputed;
wisdom and method are likewise so;
the vajra bodies are non-dual.
The aggregates, the elements likewise, The objects and the sense faculties, And the faculties of action— Thus they abide in non-duality.
The vow of all the Buddhas Abides perfectly within the syllable HŪṂ; Through the division of the three families, it is externally conceived.
"From the *Vibhaṅga-tantra*: 'The classification of the six families, and likewise their detailed divisions—the tantra whose nature is wisdom and method, I shall teach; listen!
This is the definitive teaching of the Blessed One’s reply, and thus it is the certainty established for the Yoga Tantra."

Now, the cause of the birth and abiding of the yoginīs shall be explained. In this tantra, the yoginīs—Gaurī and the others—are the five aggregates, the four elements, and the six [objects], categorized according to the fifteen divisions of the lunar phases.
The cause of their birth and abiding is the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the second *Vajrapañjara*.
Therefore, from that, the meaning of the equality of the wisdoms and consciousnesses arises as it truly is.
Likewise: "Summoning, attracting, and piercing; the various types of subduing; paralyzing, causing flight, and causing the earth to tremble;
as well as the manifest [killing] and so forth—these others shall also be explained. O Hevajra, you who are the essence, listen! This is the certainty regarding the causes of birth and abiding.
Now, the causes for generating that [mandala] shall be explained.
First, regarding the knowledge of how *e-vam* arises: the syllable *eṃ* is the cause of the faculty of *hūṃ-ryaka*.
The syllable *hūṃ* is the cause for generating the second. This is the certainty.
When things arise, they do so through the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender;
by means of the conjunction of objects and the sense faculties, the various consciousnesses [arise] individually.
One becomes bound by the fetters of substantial entities.
That bond of entities binds the consciousnesses, the eyes, and so forth.
Through thorough knowledge of that, one is liberated.
By ceasing the objects and the sense faculties, there is knowledge through the thorough knowledge of that.
Therefore, liberation is brought about by the very nature of things.
For those who possess the divine eye, they see objects of the past and future; thus, the six consciousnesses are liberated. This is because the Blessed One said, "That is other than consciousness.
Likewise, that [consciousness] is other than form and so forth; therefore—
With all his limbs, hands, feet, and so forth, with his head and face in every direction,

the Omniscient One, possessing supreme intelligence, entered the world after pervading it entirely. Now, one should explain the meditation on the ultimate truth through the very means of wisdom and method previously described.

To meditate on an entity within space while trembling is like a dream; it transcends the nature of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). To thoroughly understand that, one should meditate on the absence of entities, seeing appearances with a mind free from conceptual construction. This should be called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) that is free from conceptualization and non-erroneous.

Now, there are four types [of direct perception]: sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*), mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), yogic direct perception (*yogi-pratyakṣa*), and self-reflexive direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). These cognitions function by way of indicating their objects, engaging with them, attaining them, and having the characteristic of experiencing them.

That very appearance is established by means of examples, as follows: a mirage, a magically conjured city, a reflection, a dream, a phantom army, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, the moon in water, and space.
Thus, it becomes the letter E of wisdom. Likewise, [it is] called "the essence."
The meditation on the absence of intrinsic nature is the primordial wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*). *Heruka* is great bliss; just as insight is, so too is everything else.
By meditating on the thorough knowledge of that [bliss] as being without substantiality, it becomes method (*upāya*).
Likewise, from the word *tathatā* (suchness), it is said: "The fruit is like the lord of the land.
The syllables *e-vam*, which possess the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), abide as the bathing place—that is, they abide in the east.
Furthermore, the bathing place of great primordial wisdom (*mahājñāna*) accomplishes the total abandonment of all conceptual constructions.

It is certain that [this] is free from conceptualization regarding the maṇḍala circle, the *samaya-mudrā*, and the *jñāna-mudrā*; it is the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā* that is free from the power of conceptualization.

This very [wisdom] is the body of Vajrasattva, the one who moves throughout the three worlds, the *vaidūrya* jewel. [It is] difficult to overcome, difficult to conquer, and difficult to withstand. It consists of the six aggregates, the six elements, the six consciousnesses, the six faculties, the six objects, the six action faculties, and the six activities of the action faculties.

Although these entities are pervaded by the play of the wisdom body (*jñānakāya*), they are not born from [the union of] the mouth [and] the source, because there are no entities subject to destruction.

Here, in the second chapter of the *Hevajra Tantra* which establishes the spiritual attainments (*siddhi*), Vajragarbha makes a request, and the Blessed One provides the response. For the sake of the understanding of ordinary beings in terms of relative truth, he teaches the bliss of the two organs through the generation stage.

For instance, Vajragarbha asked: "Through the yoga of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), one meditates on the supreme bliss of the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) which is without meditation; what need is there for the generation [stage]? Here, the so-called "completion stage" refers to the union of conceptual thought and the two organs, which bestows the state of Buddhahood itself. Therefore, what purpose is served by generating mandalas through conceptual thought or by means of mudrās?
Having heard these words, the Blessed One Hevajra spoke:

"That great bodhisattva is exhausted by the force of lack of faith. This is from the perspective of relative truth; for in that way, although it resides in the flower, one does not realize fire from the non-existence of the flower.
"Likewise, because forms and so forth lack intrinsic reality, the perception of bliss itself would not occur"—this is from the perspective of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Regarding the negation of even that [bliss] in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it says:

"Neither entity nor non-entity. This refers to the cognition of all aspects. "I am a Buddha because I have realized entities"—this means that by knowing entities as they truly are, one acts for the benefit of others.

The deluded do not understand this. Even those who have conquered laziness regarding what has been taught are those whose [defilements] have been thoroughly overcome by the power of the two faculties, and so forth; thus, the provisional and definitive meanings of the former and the latter have been explained extensively in that very [text].

Now, this shall be explained as it was taught in the chapter on the *gotra*: Here, because it pervades the three realms—including the past, the future, and the present—the Buddha’s primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) would have to arise within the body if it were dependent upon it through the relationship of support and supported, like the scent in a flower. Just as there is no fragrance when there is no color, so too, if that [color] were absent, the scent would not exist; therefore, it is not so.
Therefore, because it pervades both the external and the body, it is described as "abiding in the latter" and "abiding in the earth.
Since it does not cease when the body is absent, it is certain that it is not "born of the body."
As it has been said:
"Just as no one, however old they may become, can climb up to the sky,
so too, even though this body perishes,"
"Primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) is indestructible. Thus it is said.
In the six-thousand-verse commentary on the *Hevajra*, primordial wisdom is defined as the certainty of the non-duality of wisdom and method.
Now, the "tastes" (*rasa*) within the body of Hevajra shall be described.

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* Here, the Vajragarbha requested: "Those which flow through the thirty-two channels are destroyed in the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Here, it should be explained as "great bliss": [it refers to] the thirty-two consonants beginning with *ka*, which are the nature of the three wheels of the secret [center], together with the thirty vowels; these possess the nature of the great house of the non-dual.
Regarding that, it is said: "By means of the seal of the syllables *e* and *vaṃ*, which are the essences of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
It is as follows:

concerning the statement "kā kh g gh ṅa" and so forth, the space elements—namely *ha*, *ka*, *ha*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*)—are produced from the throat; this is known by the eye [of the practitioner].
That which arises within it is established by the thorough investigation [of the statement]: "It should be grasped as being possessed by madness.
As for the "element," it refers to the element of space.

Likewise, regarding *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṅa*: because they arise from the palate, they are known through the wind element, which is the letter *i* (*ali*). Likewise, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*, and *ṇa*: because they arise from the teeth, they are known through the fire element, which is the letter *ṛ*. Likewise, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, and *na*: because they arise from the lips, they are known through the earth element, which is the letter *lṛ*. Likewise, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*, and *ṃ*: because they arise from the nose, they are known through the water element, which is the letter *u*. Likewise, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*: because they arise from the throat, they are known through the space element, which is the letter *a*. Thus, the five groups of consonants are produced from the five locations, and their respective elements are made known by the five vowels.

These are the fivefold nature of earth, water, fire, wind, and space; they are the six constituents consisting of the channels (*nāḍī*), vital essence (*bindu*), wind (*vāyu*), and the element of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

The syllables *E* and *HŪṂ* are the two unchanging [principles]. As for the syllables *E-VAṂ* and so forth, since primordial wisdom draws forth the bodhicitta, they are taught as the means for drawing forth the bodhicitta.
Regarding the phrase "dripping into the abode of great bliss," this refers to the three aspects of dripping, flowing, and not dripping.
Among these, the three principal ones are at the center;
below them are the channels that cause the destruction of feces, urine, and semen, which are located beneath the navel.
Above the navel are the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *avadhūtī*.
Here, by the nature of wisdom alone,
one abides in purity through the method of the corpse-stage.
In the central direction of Abhyantā, there is the very state where subject and object have been purified.
In this context, "moon" refers to the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, the nature of the lunar digits is the downward flow of the vital breath. The word "foot" (*pada*) signifies the sun, and its essential nature is the upward flow of the vital breath through the right nostril. By that nature, it abides in the flavor (*rasa*).
Thus it was said:
"The Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, is renowned as day;
wisdom is renowned as night."
As it is said: "Just as Raima spoke,
so does Candrasena speak now."
The mandalas of consciousness, mental formations, feeling, perception, and form abide in their respective positions according to the sequence of their emergence.
The five mandalas of earth, water, fire, wind, and space abide in their respective positions according to the sequence of their dissolution.
By completely revolving the two *lagna*s (ascendants), the *lagna* of equal knowledge (*samatājñāna*) extensively expands, whereby thirty mandalas are released from the *iḍā* and *rasanā*.
The mandalas of the *avadhūtī* and so forth, such as the *ṭa-śa-ga-rā*, appear in the *rasanā* according to their respective order.
Then, by reversing the sequence, the letters *ṭu-du-ṇa* are joined in the right [channel] through the process of union, while [the others] are in the left.
These are the present *piṇḍavāsaumārās*.

Likewise, there are those such as *khyam-su-aṅ-phyugs* and those such as *sa*, which are the relationship between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) through the divisions of body and intention.
Similarly, it is according to the sequence of the *jñāna* [wisdom] of *śarabaraṇāṃ māṃ jñā*.

Then, when Aries (Meṣa) arises, it is "jaṅ ka ru" through the sequence of joining with the left [nostril]. Likewise, when Taurus (Vṛṣabha) arises, it is "dhu. Similarly, when Gemini (Mithuna) arises, it is "ne. Then, when Cancer (Karkaṭa) arises, it is "ne pā pā pū ba mā."
Likewise, "māna" refers to the rising of the sign Aries (*meṣa*).
Then, "kanyā" refers to the rising of the ascendant of Sagittarius (*dhanu*). "Tulā" refers to Libra (*tula*).
Regarding *nada*, *datha*, and *śeṣa*, they are the eastern streets (*śarāṇa*).
*Śeṣa*, *śvaka*, and *daśi* are the fierce mandalas (*maṇḍala-dhura*) by virtue of their characteristics.
Likewise, the *nākīra* roots are the causes of the mandalas; those which bring about cognition from among these should be explained as the joints of the hands and feet.

Regarding the right hand and arm, this is the *lagna* (ascendant) of Cancer; its mandala consists of the elements such as earth and so forth. On the lower joints of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger, they are respectively [earth, water, fire, air, and space], as stated.

Then, during the birth-lagna, the mandalas of space and so forth are located on the joints of the elbow and the upper arm, respectively, according to their sequence: on the lower joints of the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger, and thumb.
Likewise, during the Capricorn lagna, the mandalas are on the joints of the right upper arm and forearm, at the boundaries of the second set of joints starting from the elbow.

Likewise, at the junction of the left upper arm and the forearm is the ascendant (lagna); at the joints of the two rows of finger-joints and so forth are the mandalas. Then, at the junction of the right hand and the forearm is the cold ascendant (śiśira-lagna).

At the joints of the three rows of phalanges beginning with the thumb, the mandalas are situated as before on the left hand; at the joint of the little finger and so forth, during the time of the fixed *lagna*, the mandalas are at the joints of the three rows of phalanges. Such is the certainty regarding the northern course.
Now, for the southern course, it is as follows:
The right waist corresponds to the *karkaṭa* lagna;
at the joints of the first row of phalanges of the right foot, beginning with the big toe, the mandalas of earth and so forth are situated respectively.

Then, the left waist corresponds to the *siṃha* lagna; at the joints of the first row of phalanges of the left foot, beginning with the little toe, the mandalas of space and so forth are situated respectively. Thus it is said.
Likewise, at the junction of the left knee and the thigh is the ascendant of Gemini; at the junction of the two feet, starting from the big toes and so forth, are the mandalas.
Similarly, at the junction of the right knee and the thigh is the ascendant of Libra.

The mandalas are at the joints of the second series of phalanges, beginning with the little finger. Now, the ascendant of Scorpio (Vṛścika) is at the joint between the right foot and the knee; the mandalas are at the joints of the third series of phalanges, beginning with the ankle.

Likewise, at the junction of the left foot and the knee is the period of the bow (dhanus). At the junctions of the third series of the collection of groups, such as the thumbs and so forth, the mandalas are arranged in their respective order.
Thus, there are sixty mandalas; these constitute the fifty-five spokes of the wheel, while the four thousand empty positions are of the nature of the syllables *e* and *ai*. This is the explanation.
Therefore, on the circle of the [sweat-]drops is a lotus with thirty-four petals.
By the word "petals," the mandala—
It is said that the channels through which sixty breaths flow are the "clay-pots" (rdza),
while those four through which empty [breaths] flow are the "vessels" (mo).
Thus, among the channels situated within each respective *lagna* (ascendant), there are those through which the empty [breath] flows.
In the west, the wind flows;
in the south, the fire flows;
in the north, the water flows.
In the center is Aṅghata, where the maṇḍala of primordial wisdom flows;
as it is said:
"The hero dwells in the center of bliss."

Regarding the sphere of activity for filling the grains: thus, the sixty-four divisions of the flow of the sixty mandalas of the *uṣman* (aspirated) letters are those that cause the empty [mandala] to flow.
Just as the sixteenth part of the moon is a mere instant (*kṣaṇa*), one should understand that at this time, the complete mandala also flows; this refers to the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
The *iḍā*, which is of the nature of the moon, is the uneven junction.
The equal time-conduct is the *rasanā*, which has the nature of the sun.
*Yavadatta* refers to the cessation of subject and object within the central direction;
it should be understood as the mandala of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus it is said.
In the present [wheel], the spokes of the wheel of the *kāpa* (mouth) are forty-four;
four of these are empty.
Next, in the wheel of phenomena (*dharmacakra*), there is an eight-petaled lotus; on those eight petals, according to the divisions of the time-measures, are the eight transits (*saṃkrānti*).
The consciousness of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, which consists of the forty-five-fold temporal movements (*kālacakra*).
Then, there are the thirty-two [petals] at the throat.
Regarding the complete enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) [chakra], it has thirty-two lotus petals; this is according to the oral instructions (*upadeśa*) of the Guru.
In the tantra, it is taught by way of reverse order.
Regarding that, there are sixteen divisions of moments [of transition] at the two junctions. At the forehead is a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Through the division of their corresponding durations, there are sixteen transits.
At the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) is a four-petaled lotus;
therein are the transits in the shape of the junctions of the lunar phases.

Regarding the external movement here: at the time when the slow breath is exhaled, the mandala of space flows into the nostril. When the mandala of space flows through either the left or the right nostril—at the beginning or the end [of the cycle]—it flows externally during that measure. When the mandala of wind flows, it touches the upper part of the nostril.
When the fire mandala flows, at that time one should know it as being felt on the right side of the nostril.
When the water mandala flows, at that time one should know it as being felt on the left.
Whether on the left or on the right, when the practitioner faces directly toward the east, one should know that the earth mandala is circulating.
Now, the yogi should understand the five locations within the nostrils:
on the left and on the right, according to the divisions of the expiring and inhaling *lagnas* (ascendants).

Herein, regarding that which was explained extensively in the five-hundred-thousand-verse *Hevajra*, the Blessed One’s certainty is this: because it is so voluminous, those who have little need for it might become terrified by such a vast explanation.

The wheel consisting of the twelve *lagna* (ascendants), such as Capricorn and so forth, should be understood here according to the *Catuḥpīṭha*; for it is said that "the characteristics of the [signs] are also to be understood through other tantras.
Furthermore, the statement that "the Rohiṇī, Darśa, Mohita, and so forth are the channels through which the uneven and even *lagna* flow" is spoken in another intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*);
it teaches the rejection of the good and bad [results] of those channels, as well as their birth and death.
For that reason, the lalanā carries the flow of Akṣobhya,
while the rasanā intensely carries blood;
the prajñā is explained as the flow of the moon.
It is taught that "Abdhātā is renowned as that.
This refers to the water element; when the water element expands, it is the left channel, Lalanā. Blood is the fire element.

The effort of the fire element on the left is *rasanā*. When that arises, there is a lotus born from water on the left, and a jewel born from fire on the right. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the *avadhūtī*; the moon is the channel of the seminal drop (*bindu*), and that itself acts as the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) which possesses the nature of bliss. Thus, it is said that one should bind the emptiness and place the vajra mountain in the center as the supreme deity.
It is well known as Avadhūti.

Likewise, Candra (Moon), Soma (Moon), Rāhu, Vāmā (Left), Rasānā (Taste), and Agni (Fire) are the channels of the present sequence, which is the view regarding the pervasive movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Furthermore, Śukra (Semen), Lalanā (L), and Kuhu (K) are below the navel.
The wheel, the rīkha-gre, and the single-pointed vajra.
The upper gates and the lower gates—those with lower openings—will now be explained. Here, the fifteen vowels belong to the white side, while the sixteenth is the *bindu*.
These channels also reside by encircling the *avadhūti*.
It is as follows:
A, Ā, I, Ī, U, Ū, Ṛ, Ṝ, Ḷ, Ḹ, E, Ai, O, Au, Aṃ, Aḥ. These are the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth [vowels] according to their sequence.
Likewise, the qualities (guṇas) are:
A-ra, E, A-ra, O, A-la.

This refers to the *ṭāla* and so forth, according to their respective sequences. Regarding that, the "protections" (*antratu-saṃvara*) are those such as *ha ara ltu ba*, which are the eleven [syllables] and so forth, according to their respective sequences.
The sixteenth [vowel] is suspended in the center of the *śṛṅgāṭaka*. At present, it places the nectar of immortality upon the palate at the forehead by its very nature;
externally it is "cooling," and internally it is called "Kāya."
Likewise, regarding the thirty-two channels: "Oṃ, namely Abhedyā, Sūkṣmarūpā, Varā, Śreṣṭhā, and Gayatrī are the winds of the left;
these are the deities of the first day and so forth. Thus it is said.
Then, Rāvaśā is the gate of birth;
Kṣamāvatī is the gate of death. Umā is the giver of coolness; Uṣmā and Lalana are [the gates of] heat.
These refer to the eleventh [tithi] and so forth; this is the sequence for the ascending order (*udaya-krama*).
The fifteen [tithis] of the waxing moon belong to the *lalanā*, while the *avadhūtī* belongs to the sixteenth.

Then, from the first tithi of the dark fortnight onwards, they reside in the *rasanā*; these fifteen tithis of the waning moon follow the sequence of the descending order (*apāya-krama*) through the nature of the long vowels.
It is as follows:
*lā vā rā ā hā* refers to the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth [days] of the lunar fortnight, respectively.
Then, according to the classification of the increase of qualities, one should apply these words to the continuum of the [practitioner]:
"Thus the Blessed One spoke: 'The secret even more secret than secrets...'"

The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* states: "Regarding the definitive explanation of the *Vajragarbha*: that which was spoken by Vajrasattva is the non-conceptual gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of twelve [aspects]."
The Lord in the middle of the three is situated within the secret life-force;
he has reached below and above it.
Possessing a brilliance like a flash of lightning,
consciousness and the sensory elements, abiding within karma, cause all things to manifest.
The sovereign power of the earth, Mado,
resides as the central queen at the navel;
[she is] in the secret place.
Even the very peak of the upper [realm] is like lightning as it falls;
this is said to be wisdom that accords with itself.
This is here declared to be Caṇḍālī;
it consists of three channels at the base,
and likewise three ascending [channels].
The peak of delusion resides in the center; at the time of entry, the peak is on the left,
and at the time of exit, the peak is on the right.
Water, fire, and space flow;
the lalanā is perfectly situated on the left, while the rasanā is said to be on the right.
That avadhūtī within the central channel is described as Gaṅgā;
having made three paths from the forehead to the center of the earth, one proceeds from there.
At the center of the heart, having traversed the three paths, one returns once more.

At the centers of the forehead and throat, having traversed the three paths, one proceeds once more. At the centers of the forehead and the crown of the head, having traversed the single path, one proceeds once more.
Having sent one [the breath] into the ear, it returns once again after perceiving its activity.
In the left nostril, the syllable *hūṃ* is perfectly situated at a distance;
on the right is the channel *mā*. In the center is the *nābhi*; at the navel and so forth, they are like wheels.
These are themselves the three and five paths;
from the navel, they proceed and return through the center of the *avadhūti*.
From petal to petal, the *lalanā* and *rasanā* are explained.
From that central channel (avadhūtī), which is marked by moon upon moon,
it penetrates through and reaches the uṣṇīṣa.
At that time, when a person performs the desired [practice], the rkyang ma and ro ma [channels]—

From the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: "By means of the application of their union, the fierce fire blazes intensely; it blazes within the center of the navel and certainly emerges from the mouth of the central channel. Having pierced the mark of Rāhu and the moon, it touches the face of the syllable HŪṂ."

Through contact with the letter *ḍa*, there is the letter *ha*. Then, white nectar dissolves into *ra*. While performing the activities of the maṇḍala, when the sense faculties are obstructed and joy and so forth arise, the drop (*bindu*) perishes from the moon. Once the letter *śa* has been purified into *bi*, [it becomes] *pa*.
The moon at the forehead and the sun at the throat, then entering Rāhu;
when the *caṇḍālī* enters the navel and ascends, it proceeds to the secret wheel.
This is the best [practice] regarding the secret wheel.
This is explained extensively by the power of the *Rada*.
Below, the three *Ḍākinīs* clearly demonstrate where accomplishment is attained.
The very state of homage to the seven births is the siddhi of the conduct of the *māra*.
This year, the four seasons will pass; the senses and the continuum of the country will follow.
Through subsequent inference, one awakens from sleep and so forth; this is the virtuous activity of the Buddha in the land of sorrow.
Just as mercury is bound externally, so too is this essence of primordial wisdom.
It destroys all mantras and sorcery and bestows vast siddhis. Likewise, for one who enters through delusion and falls into the secret wheel,
as long as they remain there for seven days, it will grant them great liberation.
Above, Rāhu is said to be the sacrificial animal; the great boar of the Moon, having become the *laṅgala* of Brahmā, bestows the fruits of death and liberation.
Likewise, one should fill [the channels] with blood, sinews, and marrow flowing down.
These [seven] births are called "vomit"; they are not other than the external cattle.
The seven births of the *hva-ga* are the supreme lords in every respect. Just as there is birth and death for the body, so too is the meaning of *daśa-dha-śrī-hoṇ*.
The flavors of food and drink, the six types of cooked and heaped [dishes], through the act of giving, become milk; this is the first stage of its development.
Thereafter, it turns into blood itself; this is clearly the second stage.
Third, it becomes the skin; fourth, it becomes the blood;
fifth, it becomes the flesh; sixth, it becomes the fat;
seventh, it becomes the marrow; this [series] continues up to the seventh.
Based on that very [reality], the six yogatantras are described as being of the "families" (*gotra*).
"Family" is explained as the body; that which arises from the family is called semen, and its capacity is called menses.
The body is said to be the cause that produces [the result].
The pervasive consciousness of awareness abides in the center of those very [elements]. Relying upon the lunar seat, he is Heruka, the nature of the three worlds.
The heroes dwelling above and below are the lords of the ḍākinī wheel. It should be described that the crown wheel is established by means of the four types of *hrīḥ*.
At the forehead, there are six petals; at the throat, thirty-two;
by means of eight wheels, four spokes [are formed]. These are perfectly established in the navel wheel. At the secret place, there are thirty-two;
these are described as the spokes of the wheel, or alternatively, as the petals of a lotus.

By the nature of being bestowed and empowered, consciousness is thoroughly stimulated; it possesses the [sites] such as the *sthāna* and *upasthāna*. Those are the petals of the lotus of the channels;
at the crown of the four goddesses is the letter *Ḍā*. This is to be called the "Great Ocean."
The first maṇḍala of the wheel of the vajra arises here. The first maṇḍala of the wheel of the vajra arises here.
It becomes endowed with the eight bindus of the vajra at the tip of the nose.
The two eyes, as well as the ears, nose, tongue, and the hanging [genitals],
are Gaurī and the others. Form and the other [sensory objects], as well as earth and the other [elements],
are divided into lunar phases and are proclaimed in that very context as Nairātmyā.
Three faces and six arms, located at the throat; she is indeed [accompanied] by thirty-two [deities].
In the heart as well, the eight goddesses and this four-armed one truly reside.
She is the great Vajra of Mind, born from the family of Akṣobhya.

The "Shaking the Three Worlds" chapter consists of six [sections]. Through the very nature of these six, the assembly, the attachment, and so forth, are the *bhaṇḍa* of the secret wheel. Furthermore, the three upper and lower seals (*mudrā*) are the heroes who arrest the six wheels.
The channels of the navel are firm; from them, the feet and so forth arise. Those [channels] number seventy-two thousand, and within that many parts of the body reside the goddesses.
At the forehead, the mandala of the moon perfectly resides.
In the region of the throat, one should visualize the fire mandala of Vāgvajra.
Abiding in the center of the Rāhu mandala is the consciousness of all embodied beings.
At the tip of the terrifying [serpent], the jewel is well-situated and unadorned.
Upon the maṇḍala of Amoghasiddhi, resting atop a crossed vajra (viśvavajra), there is a surrounding circle of five:
a lotus, a vajra, a jewel, a sword, and a fifth, the "born-vajra" jewel; these are explained as the six faces of the Buddha.
In that regard, these families of all the Buddhas are of great power:
scent is produced from earth; taste arises from fire;
musk and so forth arise from water; and this tangible quality arises from wind.
From the *prāṇa* [wind] comes the transformation of sound; from *sthūla* [the short vowel] comes the *dharmadhātu*. It is the faculty of the mind (*manas*), which is known by all embodied beings.
It is generated by the bone of the "End-maker" (Yama); from the blood comes Prajñāntaka.
From Padmāntakṛt and the others, Vighnāntaka is explained as the one who causes obstacles to arise;
from the feet, he is called Āvarta. From the slaughter of the king Śrī, he becomes the Blue Staff (Nīladaṇḍa); from sound, he is the Great Powerful One (Mahābalā) from the nails.
The clusters of hands and feet are the houses; the divisions of the three qualities (guṇas) are explained as the twelve signs. The collections of fingers are the sixty-day periods of time.

The upper and lower breaths of those who possess ritual purity abide like the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). The sweat that reaches the mouth is the smoke; the sweat that reaches below the navel is the fire.
Just as it is externally, so too within the hollow [of the body], one will certainly arise upon meeting [the deity].
The twelvefold meaning of the subject matter is Hevajra with twelve arms, because he obstructs the twelve links [of dependent origination]. This is the fourfold measurement according to the stages.
The sixteen hands represent the phases of the moon;
they signify the knowledge of the sixteen realities.
The eight faces are the cessation [of the eight consciousnesses].
The supreme lord has eight faces;
he whose feet bring to an end the moon, the sun, darkness, and fire.
Having blocked and dispatched the half-months,
from the mouths of the twenty-four arms and the four faces, Kālacakra duly emerged just as before.
By negating the consonants beginning with *ka*, and by means of the speech of the twenty-four *samdhā-bhāṣā* roots, the six vowels are also negated.
This explains the six legs.
By means of cessation, the nine faces [constitute] the ninefold [mandala] of Vajrabhairava.
Regarding such tantras as these,
because they bring about the cessation of karma and the mental states [of those] who have made their commitments, [they are taught].
Thus it was said by the Sovereign of the Land of China.
Furthermore, extensive teachings were spoken in the Tantra of Ṇava;
these were explained solely for the sake of being understood by the immature.

"The fundamental conduct of this very *kulagau* should be understood from the commentary on the summarized meaning of the thirty-two verses [contained] in the *Cakrasaṃvara-tantra*. This is the excellence of the Tathāgata; its extent should be known from the *tantra* itself.
Furthermore, the Blessed One taught the certainty of the *Hevajra-tantra* in thirty verses within the chapter on the *Kula* of the *Hevajra*."

Thus ends the fifth chapter on the family, which summarizes the yoga of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa from the sixfold commentary on the *Hevajra Tantra*, and which constitutes the section on the generation stage within the [tantra].
The chapter on the family is complete.
It has taught the meaning of various sounds.
Regarding the explanation of this meaning through the symbolic classes and so forth, up to the Sambhogakāya:
these are the symbolic mantras of the Buddhas.
In the tantra, these two are clearly explained.
Now, the symbolic convention of suchness; this is the second, the thorough expression of conventional terminology.
Regarding what is called the "symbolic convention of suchness":
Possessing the speech that is the language of all sentient beings,
he is the drum of Dharma endowed with a great sound;
he is the great resonance of the Dharma drum.
The one who abides in non-abiding nirvāṇa is described as the speech that pervades all.
It is the mantra that perfectly expresses the terminology of clarity; it is that which opens the forest of the symbolic ground and its meaning.
Regarding the recitation that follows the ultimate meaning:
through the beauty of the lack of intrinsic nature,
the mantra is free from the analysis of its constituent parts.
Abiding in the state of the mother-field, one recites;
the life-force will flow without interruption. Abiding in the state of the father, one recites twenty-one thousand times.
Six hundred [breaths] constitute a day and night;
five such days and nights constitute one hundred thousand [breaths], and eight thousand [such units] constitute one *gapa*.
Starting from the first day of the dark fortnight, until three full moons have occurred; starting from the first day of the light fortnight, until the end.
Recite during the interval of the three completions;
at the time when the dawn breaks,
on the full moon day, I shall be accomplished.
Having prostrated to Vajrasattva,
one thoroughly turns the wheel of Dharma;
[this is accomplished by] eight thousand recitations.
Four hundred thousand and likewise one hundred thousand with force;
by these, accomplishment is achieved.
It is said that it is not by means of a rosary.
Through the fire offering (homa) and mantra worship,

by making [the ritual] timely and performing the ritual procedures, other obstacles and hindrances are utterly destroyed; by that which has been consumed, all [negativities] are rendered non-existent.
Those scholars who possess learned intellects should clearly explain and proclaim those [teachings] by means of their mouths and rosaries.
For those who desire external enjoyments,
the mantrin should employ the hammer of merit;
this is the great *tīna* [seal] that destroys the head.
By entering, it seizes the internal [elements]. When the life-force of the lunar days is destroyed, this brings about the state of a sky-farer (*khecarī*).
When the life-force of one month is slain, it abides in the heart; for yogins, the deathless arises.
If one burns the syllable *la*, all these will become omniscience itself;
[visualize] the wheels of the forehead,
throat, heart, and navel in their proper sequence.
Bound by the [vowels] *va* and *jra*, and likewise burned by *da*, it is so. By arresting the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one desires the state free from passion.
Through both awakening and burning, the mantrin becomes a Buddha.
When prāṇa and vyāna are exhausted here,
the two branches become internal;
this occurs through the cessation of cause and effect.
One will not deviate from the state of Buddhahood. As long as the life-force of living beings continues to circulate, so long does existence persist.
When the circulation of the life-force is completely severed, there is no death and no further rebirth.
Thus, this is the contemplation of the neuter mantra;
it should be understood through the symbols of suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke these words:
Now, from this point forward, the chapter on mantra shall be explained.
It is as follows:
the mantra for the bali offering to all bhūtas.
All those who arise from the elements consume all beings; this occurs according to the number of mantras.
*Oṃ yākāro mūlasarvadharmānām ādir anutpannaḥ*.
Here, by the sound of the letter *ma*, the indestructible sound is indicated.
The letter A is the essence of all letters; it is the supreme, great, and unchanging.
The Great Life-force is unborn.
By the passage beginning with "That which is called the grove is tasted," one recognizes the *Māyājāla* (Net of Magical Illusion).
All of that is omniscience.
The omniscient, spontaneously aware, and sublime one; he who knows himself and knows others, possessing all means of knowledge;
the supreme individual who benefits all.
"Beyond worldly examples,
the supreme master of knowledge and the knowable"—
such passages refer to the speech of the omniscient one, which is the language of all mantras and the mind of awakening; thus, it is of indeterminate meaning.
The elements such as earth that have arisen from the [five] constituents are the "elements," which are the phenomena characterized by the nature of the sense faculties.

Their "mantras" are the five syllables that constitute the nature of the five aggregates; specifically, by the syllable Oṃ, the aggregate of form is the Vajra Body (Kāyavajra). By the syllable Āḥ, the aggregate of perception is the Vajra Speech (Vāgvajra).
The syllable *ya* represents the aggregate of consciousness, which is Body-Vajra.
The syllable *kṣā* represents the aggregate of feeling.
The syllable *ha* represents the aggregate of formations.
Regarding the offering of the torma to those [deities]: finally, it is said that one should cause it to burst forth with the syllable *HŪṂ* and scatter it with two *PHAṬ* syllables.
Thus, what has arisen from the syllable *OṂ* is expanded by the syllable *ĀḤ*, and it is intensified by the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The syllable Āḥ transforms [it] into nectar;
the syllable Hūṃ causes it to be purified;
by the three syllables, [it is] offered.

By means of two *phaṭ* syllables, [the obstacles] are expelled. By covering [them], they are liberated; this is performed with the garuḍa mudrā. With the mudrā of total victory over the three realms, they are summoned.
This means that one should request the [deities] to depart by forming the vajra-mudrā with the hands and snapping the fingers. These mudrās should be understood according to other tantras.
Likewise, the seed syllables of the Tathāgatas correspond to their respective accomplishments as follows: the syllable *HŪṂ* is for Vairocana; the syllable *A* is for Ratnasambhava.
The syllable *Aṃ* is Amitābha, located at the forehead.
The syllable *Ṣa*: having placed the symbolic body of longevity, one recognizes the Vajra-Ḍākinī; it is Amoghasiddhi, located at the secret place.
The syllable *Hūṃ* is Akṣobhya, located at the crown of the head.

Now, following that, the mantra of the Six-Armed One is: *oṃ devī-trāṃ vajra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Here, the definitive meaning is as follows: just as the syllable *oṃ* and the others serve as the seats for the deities, so too are the syllables of the mantra established with certainty. As for the remaining [syllables], they are the arrangement of the limbs; *si* and so forth are arranged in successive order, while *ba* and so forth are arranged according to their respective sequence.

The three *Hā* syllables summon the wisdom beings (*jñānasattva*); the syllable *Phaṭ* causes them to enter; the syllable *Ga* brings about delight; and the syllable *Hā* provides satisfaction. This is the essence of Hevajra.
Thus, it is certain that all mantras are preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, have *Aḥ* and *Svāhā* at their end, and have *Namaḥ* and *Phaṭ* in the middle.
In this way, as before—
"Ṭīra Phaṭ" is for the Six-Armed One. Likewise, for the Four-Armed One, it is "Rūpa Rūpa" (or "Guru Sāda"). Similarly, for the Two-Armed One, it is "Oṃ Devatā-janma.
These mantra-extractions should be understood from the oral instructions regarding the syllables *Hūṃ* and *Phaṭ*. *Ga-saḥ*.
The mantra for blessing the body, speech, and mind is as follows: the syllable OṂ blesses the body, which is Vairocana upon a moon mandala;
the syllable ĀḤ blesses the speech, which is Amitābha upon a lotus.
