The wave of the *tsa*-script emanations is the central mandala of the [five] families;
it is Akṣobhya.
This should be understood as the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), stated for the purpose of extracting the vowels such as Āmoghā and the others for the mantra.
On the earth [plane], one should grasp the vowels *ī*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ* through the definitive meaning by means of the individual grouping (*pratyāhāra*) recitation:
*i-ru-la*.
The syllables "WÀ ĀR ṆṆA SA YA RA BA LA Ṭ SO" belong to the lunar phases of the white fortnight.
According to the method of recitation and for the sake of clarity, it is certain in the Root Tantra that these were not spoken by the Blessed One.
Likewise, there is the mantra for generating the city.
Oṃ a ṭa ṭha ṣa ha.
This is by way of the meaning of "slow" (dala) and "to cut" (a).
By way of the definitive meaning, the letters a, ka, and ha become the objects to be severed.
The *i* and *āśa* sounds are produced from the palate.
The *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* sounds are produced from the tip of the tongue.
The *u*, *ūpa*, and those possessing *mu* are produced from the lips.
The syllables Ṛ, TŪ, LA, and SA become *so*.
OṂ AMRAHAGAṄVAṢA MANANA SVĀGHA.
This is the mantra for summoning the city.

The chapter on the extraction of mantras should be learned from the oral instructions of the Guru. In the Root Tantra, the pith instructions of definitive meaning state that the vowels (*āli*) are the examples for the moon, and the consonants (*kāli*) are the examples for the sun. On each respective day, one should perform the recitation by means of the sixty consonants, which are the examples for the sun.
By means of the sounds *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*, the definitive meaning of *āli* and *kāli* is expressed.
If one performs one hundred thousand recitations of the *āli* and *kāli* mantra, and thereby causes those three to move, it is said that "even a single city will go mad.
This refers to the expression of *āvi* and *kāli*.
*Adgasye*: A Ā Ai Ī Ṛ Ī Ā Ū LṚ E Ai Ar Ār O—these are the inhalations.
The exhalations are the *kāli* [consonants].
Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa; Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña; Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa; Ta Tha Da Dha Na; Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma; Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa.
First, the syllable AṂ is moved to the left.
For summoning, add *oṣṭha* at the end;
this is the mantra for shaking the city.
Furthermore, by means of single-pointed meditative concentration and the recitation over red flowers, and—
Regarding the statement "by means of *sindūra*," it refers to what will be explained later.
By means of the immeasurable, one should recite the mantra of Kurukullā, the Buddha-like one;
here, the support of the syllable *Oṃ* is accomplished.
The syllable *gra* completes the speech of *la-au*.
For the class of wind, it is sealed with *ka-ru-ku-lha-’od*.
At the forehead is *ma-e*, and on the tongue is *hā-ro*.
Kuḥ,
hūṃ kararu,
śalaku.
Regarding "the secret goat's milk," this refers to the white subsidiary [limb].
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while inhaling;
at the time of exhaling, one must not move the rosary. This is the Karakṛt mantra.
Now, the meaning of the mantra for protecting the cow shall be explained:
the syllable *Oṃ* denotes a soft seat;
the syllable *Jaḥ* denotes a moon-like [seat] arising from fragrant earth in a place without fixed location; and by the syllable *Ra*, there is a sun mandala with seven flames.
The letter *ka* represents the crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*).
Having constructed a ten-spoked wheel below, above, and in all directions, one then places the horse-headed King of Wrath (*Hayagrīva*) in the center from the syllable *hūṃ*.
On the eastern spoke is Yamāntaka.
On the spoke of the [eastern] wheel is Yamāntaka;
on the spoke of the western wheel is Padmāntaka; and on the spoke of the northern wheel is Vighnāntaka.
In the southeast is Acala;
on the summit of the southwest is Yama-rāja;
in the northwest is Nīladaṇḍa.
In the northeast direction is Mahābala;
on the upper spoke is Uṣṇīṣa;
and below is Sumbharāja.
Then, by uttering the second [syllable], there is the solar mandala;
by the letter *ya*, there is the crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*).
Through their merging into one, the threefold vajra enclosure is formed.
6. With the three syllables, [one visualizes] the vajra ground, the tiered palace, and the vajra-lotus seat.
With the syllable *yaṃ*, [one visualizes] the umbrella.
The syllable *pa* is for striking with the ritual dagger (*kīla*).
The syllable *sa* is for secretly inviting the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

By means of the syllable *ha*, all [practices] such as making offerings and so forth, as well as the confession of misdeeds and so forth, will be proclaimed; thus it becomes mantra, and the words of the mantra should be recited.
In this *Laghu-tantra*, all matters consistent with the tradition have been implicitly completed; thus, they are concealed from those wicked masters who lack full understanding.
One should learn [this] through the stages of the lineage of the sublime gurus and so forth, for it is not something to be found by merely poring over books.
Otherwise, even the Blessed One—who has perfectly realized the many tantras joined together according to whatever is appropriate in other tantras—would be one who possesses only a mere duality.
It is not by means of the faith of a fool alone. As the Blessed One has said:
"My speech is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle," and so forth.
It is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and exclusively virtuous in the end;
it is not the case that it is virtuous at first and non-virtuous at the end, nor is it [virtuous] at the beginning and...
In the middle, it is non-virtuous; at the end, it is virtuous.
This is the conceptual construction of those who have described births: first, the meditation on discursive thought (*vikalpa*);
in the middle, the meditation on the bliss of the two organs; and [at the end,]...

Finally, regarding the statement that "one meditates on great bliss by donning emptiness upon forms and conceptualizations," this is seen as the result of all such improper words. As it says in the *Sālikā*:
"The grain of the śāli does not arise from [other] seeds."
The fruit arising from conceptual thought as its cause will be non-conceptual;
that which is born from non-conceptuality—
The result is non-conceptualization; for that reason,
the cause is virtue in this life and virtue in the future.
O Brahmin, it is virtuous. As is the seed, so is the sprout;
as is the tree, so is the fruit.
This entire world is seen as dependent origination;
it is not some mantra of another lineage.
That is the means for accomplishing other activities;
in this world,
there is nothing whatsoever that is more efficacious than it.
Just as it was clearly explained to me in the *Hevajra Root Tantra*,
that very same [point] is also [taught] in this tantra.
I shall now explain the expansion [of the ritual].
The seed syllable of the earth, ŚYĪ, performs the rite of paralysis; likewise, it performs the rites of delusion and destruction.
The seed-syllable of the earth element of water always pacifies;
likewise, it enriches and neutralizes poison.
The seed-syllable of the fire element summons liquor.
Exhalation and movement are constant;
likewise, when one is provoked by anger, the winds cause the poison to increase.
The six seed-syllables of emptiness perform the severance.
Likewise, there is killing and dying;
they are established by the seeds of primordial wisdom.
Clothing, begging bowls, and joy—
The very state of being mute, deaf,
and mentally impaired is also [attained] through the seeds of the mind, speech, and body of primordial wisdom.
The mantrin performs [the ritual] in that very sequence:
from the union of the mandalas of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and primordial wisdom.
One will suffer from boils,
skin diseases,
leprosy, deafness, blindness, and a blocked nose.
Splitting,
deafness, and illness are produced by the karmic residues of previous lives.
*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: On mountain peaks, in forest retreats, On the shores of great oceans,
And in those primordially established *dūrvā* grass meadows.
In these locations, one should perform great activities: reciting mantras, likewise meditating,
performing fire offerings, and constructing mandalas, each in accordance with its respective capacity.
Otherwise, accomplishments will not arise. When practicing mantras and deities elsewhere than in the pure abodes of noble beings,
one must thoroughly invoke them with mantras.
The mouth performs all actions;
therefore, the wise should recite the names and mantras with the mouth.
The root mantra becomes the body;
that which is called the essence (hṛdaya) is the speech endowed with harmony; and the essence of the one who is thus is as follows:
It shall be expressed as the mantra of the mind;
that which is known as the seed-syllable of primordial wisdom shall be expressed as the mantra of primordial wisdom.
The essence for purchasing the ritual substances, the essence mantra, the root mantra,
the wisdom mantra, and the mantras of speech and body.
One should perform the appointed recitations according to the sequence;
until the siddhi arises, one should invoke, recite, and make offerings.
Otherwise, the ritual will be impaired.
The accomplishments of mantra are not subject to change;
by grasping this through faith,
one’s mouth is filled with nothing but afflictions.
The syllables *a*, *ra*, and *la* arise from fire, earth, and water; *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* likewise.
*Śa*, *ḍha*, *na*, and *ña* should be assigned to the eastern direction, while *ra* and *ṇa* belong to the northern realm.
From the sequence of Fire, Air, Wind, and Ishāna,
the syllables Kaṃ, Ha, and Sviṇa are placed respectively above and below.
In the center, one should make offerings to Āḥ.
In the presence of the Buddhas, the Gurus, and those who recite the sublime Dharma,
one should not disparage others; rather, one should regard them as the Victorious Ones themselves.
By means of the wind mandala of phenomena, it is completely elevated; by means of the essence of the mind-mandala of *au*, it is the supreme.
Jambudvīpa is the third [continent], triangular;
Aparagoyānī in the west is square;
and Pūrvavideha has the appearance of a half-moon.

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* (Tibetan Translation): By the one whose nature is the water mandala, [which is] half-way toward the north and devoid of *svāmi*; by the moon, whose essence is emptiness, the mandala itself is fully expanded; below the Brahma-egg, by means of the essence of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
The mandala of the fire-mother [is formed].
In the center is the bindu, pure in every aspect;
it becomes the nature of the deities above and below.
Having bound [the horse] to the hitching post,
on that morning one should recite the mantras and so forth; other than that,
[one should prepare] a maṇḍala upon the ground.
One should act as with a colored-powder maṇḍala;
one should worship the thirty-six [elements], such as the six aggregates, the six constituents, and form and so forth.
Earth, water, fire, and wind—
The emission of semen is likewise;
what is explained as the "six elements" is the aggregate of form for embodied beings.
The palatal, the retroflex,
the dental, the labial, the nasal,
and the semivowels— these are taught as the six classes of phonemes.
It clarifies the meaning of entities and non-entities:
words, actions, the nose, life-force, the body, and likewise the faculty of the mind.
The aggregate of consciousness consists of six types, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth; likewise, there are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and—
In order to purify tangible objects and the dharmadhātu, the flesh of sensation is divided into four;
likewise, through the doors of the six sense faculties, it is so arranged.
The consciousnesses thoroughly engage, causing the objects and the sense faculties to engage; the six types of formations are fully explained,
as are the life-force and the downward-clearing winds that are ever-present.
The three upper and lower paths are understood;
flowing through the six parts,
even the aggregate of primordial wisdom is sixfold.

The thirty-seventh is the Great Mind. Through the thirty-six sublime [elements] such as earth and so forth, and the letters ka and so forth, there are seventy-two constituents (dhātus) by their very nature.
The six vowels beginning with *a* and so forth, through their classification as short and long, are explained here as being sixteen in number. These vowels are precisely sixteen.
Possessing the correct transmission of the syllables "Ma" and so forth, the hundred-syllable mantra should be recited eight hundred times;
this is described as the yogi’s mantra recitation.
With half of one hundred and eight hands,
the rosary is said to be held there;
by means of the divisions of the lunar mansions and the feet.
In the third [chapter], it shall be fully explained:
it is endowed with clarity, purity, and the melodic tones.
Hūṃ! Regarding the time of the stars: why is that very fourth [moment] so?
It is because it arises from the birth of awareness, like the tip of a blade of grass.
I shall now explain the characteristics of mantra:
whatever arises from the syllable *aṃ*,
consisting of vowels, consonants, and nasals.
They arise perfectly from the element of space;
those [consonants] are known through the letter *ha*.
The syllables *oṃ*, *i*, *ya*, and *śa* arise from the palate.
The vowels and the characteristics of the consonants arise perfectly from the wind element; know that these originate from the letter *ya*.
From *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *ra*, and *ṣa*, the retroflexes (*ūṣman*) arise.
The vowels and consonants arise perfectly from the fire element;
the letter *ra* is that which makes them known.
Whatever becomes the *ūpamaṇḍala*, the vowels,
consonants, and the great elements themselves,
have truly arisen from the water element.
Now, by means of the letter *sarva*, which makes [the meaning] known,
whatever *kṛt* suffixes are produced from *sa*, the characteristics of vowels and consonants arise perfectly from the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
These are known from their respective labels; although they include the anusvāra and visarga,
they are devoid of vowels and consonants.
Perfectly arisen from the element of primordial wisdom,
it belongs to the family of the six elements:
earth, water, fire, wind, phlegm, and sweat.
In this world of the six elements, he is the great primordial man (puruṣa), the Great Taintless One; he is the Lord, the self of earth and so forth, and of *ka* and so forth.
The mantra of the aggregates and elements indicates the individual withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*);
it is taught for the purpose of accomplishing the *prāṇa*,
and the accomplishment of the mantra is likewise that very reality.
The mantra of the Omniscient One is likewise not produced by the sequential stages of a child’s reading; rather,
it consists of the consonants and vowels that arise from the throat, the palate, the throat-lips, and their combinations.
As for the other places,
those [consonants] are produced from a single nature; in a single place such as the throat or the mouth, and so forth.
The melody born from natural purity is the constant utterance of mantras; it is not expressed by two [separate] sounds.
That which is perfectly endowed with the vowel *a* does not desire its own abode.
Now, regarding natural purity:
when those who perform the ritual of piercing [the vital points] have been uprooted,
it is endowed with the vowels such as the letter E and so forth.
Regarding the second point, that which enters:
it is not that which is born from a pure nature;
it becomes the transformation of the manifesting essence.
Upon the yellow mandala of the Great Powerful One (Mahendra),
the syllable LA arises from the syllable HŪṂ.
The white mandala is that of TASTE (rasa).
The syllable *ja* gives rise to [the fire mandala];
the red mandala of fire arises from the syllable *ra*.
The black mandala of wind [arises from the syllable *ya*].
The syllable Ya arises from the letter Sa. The green mandala of space arises from the letter Ra. The visarga arises from the bindu.

Regarding the mantra for causing rain to fall: first, one hundred thousand recitations of this mantra must be performed; by reciting it ten million times, the mantra is accomplished. When one has performed one million fire offerings (*homa*), at that time the practitioner causes the *nāgas* to bring down rain by means of the offered *bali* cakes. For this, there is no need for the ritual of a mandala.

Regarding the mandala ritual, it is certain in the Vāyutantrodaya that one must first perform one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) and ten thousand fire offerings (*homa*); otherwise, the *vidyās* will not cause rain to fall. Now, the procedure for *sinadralava* will be explained:

here, whenever there is an excessive amount of rain, at that time, one should place a clay bowl filled with charnel ground cloth. The mantra practitioner, sitting upon a spread of charnel ground cloth, should recite this mantra.

OṂ ĀRYA ŚAMAŚĀNA Ā Ā HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. Regarding this [mantra] for splitting the earth as well, one should perform the approach (*sevā*), fire offering (*homa*), and recitation (*japa*) as before. At the time of splitting the earth, the ritual manual for Vajraśṛṅkhalā should be explained; here, for the sake of subduing sentient beings who are difficult to tame, one should accomplish it by reciting the Vajraśṛṅkhalā mantra ten million times, or even one hundred thousand times. Then follows the accomplishment of the wrathful Lokeśvara.
Grind *tholokor* (cinnabar), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and *lañci* together with *kamyur ba da* (quickly falling water) into pills the size of eyeballs; these are called "eye-pills.
Then, having gone to the house of Heruka and positioned oneself before the face of Heruka, one should recite this mantra until the face of the image sprinkles those pills upon the practitioner.
*Oṃ vajrakartari vajra jvala hūṃ phaṭ*. For the sake of attaining siddhi, one should perform the recitation while remaining on a single seat.
Then, it will be accomplished.
To achieve this, one should draw the image of a face on the neck of the pill.
When the king and his retinue see the image upon the neck of the pill, if the neck of the pill is then severed, at that moment the enemies will become headless.
The Vajra Kīṭikā is complete.
Now, the narrative of the purification of the vajra shall be told:
here, those who desire to destroy the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) should accomplish the vajra battle-axe (*vajraparaśu*).

Here, too, the establishment of renown should be performed as previously described. Then, the constellation Puṣya took the seeds from the Brahma-tree; that Brahma-tree is to be called the Nāpalaśa. Its seeds are the great Kuṭhāra.
Mix them together and strike with the vajra of Akṣobhya.
Having seized the fish-eater, one should press down on her feet while reciting the mantra:
OṂ VAJRAKŪṬĀRA PĀṬAYA HŪṂ.

PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Having recited this, on the day the sun is seized—the great day of accomplishment—one should apply a drop (*bindu*) in the form of an enemy. By doing so, that which was to be accomplished will be clearly realized.

Thus, the ritual for subduing deities—the method for accomplishing the fever of the *Raudra* [deity]—shall now be described. Having accomplished the mantra as before, one who desires the power of the fever-rite should take mustard seeds, *kṛtaka* (mustard), and the ash of a funeral pyre; these should be applied to the leaf of an *arka* tree, inscribing the name of the enemy upon it.
Then, on the full moon of the month of Vaiśākha, one should bury it at a depth of eight finger-widths. Having established a fire of chaff, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times:
OṂ HEVAJRA JVARAṆA KṢE HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
From now on, the disease will gradually infect the patient.
If one washes the leaf with cow’s milk after it has been removed, the patient is liberated;
this is the ritual for severe infectious fevers.
Now, the ritual procedure for vomiting wine will be explained.

Having accomplished the mantra for vomiting as before, one who desires to induce the vomiting of wine should visualize at the navel of the object of practice a *raṃ* syllable, from which a rapidly moving wind maṇḍala arises. Above that, one should meditate on a woman with loose hair, intensely agitated by liquor, who is vomiting wine. Then, recite the mantra: *śraṃ*.
Wait for the completion of the practice. One should recite the mantra "Oṃ haba £ ma du mū takiṅga amhaṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" more than one hundred and eight times.
This is the sādhana for subduing through fear.
Now, the method of bringing [others] under one's power will be explained.
As previously stated, it involves the mantra of the *kudukūlī*—the "horse-like" [deity]—and so forth, in tens of millions.
Regarding the accomplishment of the assembly of the Deceiver:

thereafter, one who desires to distinguish the thoroughly purified [state] should go beneath the *aśoka* tree, don yellow garments, and deliberate. Eating rice, one should anoint the body with the juice of *kāñcika* and recite the mantra completely.
Oṃ kūrūkullā hūṃ amukam vaśīkuru svāhā.
It is said that by reciting this ten thousand times, she will come; thus, one brings her under control. Now, the seizing of the moon and sun shall be explained:
having first recited [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times, one should then recite the mantra over blood.
Then, for one who desires to seize the moon and the sun, having fashioned a moon or a sun from what has emerged from [the substance] bound to the nose, one should cook it with cow-vapor.
Having placed it inside a vessel one *śarī* in size using a vajra-rod, one recites the mantra: *oṃ bandha rakṣa mā melā tiṣṭha vega jaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is for the complete seizing of the sun.
Regarding the "Seizing of the Moon," it is as follows: *Oṃ vajra carje*, and so forth.
If one eats the *kheśa* food, one will abide in the profound state.
If extracted from the urine, it is the *gro kha ba lo*.
Thus concludes the ritual for seizing the moon and the sun. Now, the procedure for causing the vajra-star to descend to the earth shall be explained.
Having accomplished the mantra by reciting it one million times as before, and performing one hundred thousand fire offerings with white lotuses.
Regarding that, the mantra is: *Oṃ nagrā kumāri hūṃ dīva caloṭṭa svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra one hundred and eight times over the right breast of the clay [image], one should worship it with the five sensory offerings, such as flowers, incense, and so forth, and then request the deity to attend.
On the fourteenth or eighth day, at the time of dawn, having placed the vase, upon it—

One should place the sap of milky trees into a copper vessel containing sesame oil. Having recited this mantra one hundred and eight times over it, one should smear lac upon the thumb of the left hand and anoint the tip of a palm leaf with it.
Then, having shown [the object] to the young woman, the mantrika recited the mantra and asked, "Who has taken the substance of the śarapuṣpī?
What other visions did you see?
Thereupon, she saw Śeṣamati approaching.
One should say, "So-and-so is taking the substance;
it will become a fault for the purpose.
For the sake of severing the vajra-heel, one enters into the *pāda* [of the deity]. To avert its force, one should recite the mantra of the essence of the *gaṇa*.
First, place the letter *m* and in the center write the mantra words along with "guru-deśa" [repeated] one hundred thousand times; then, when applied to cattle, they will flee. Thus it is said.
If one recites this, the elephants will run away.
If one says "Nya ya ṣa," the tiger will flee.
If one says "Ū le ai li mū," the snake will flee.
By the mudrā of the hand that subdues Vaiśravaṇa, the fleeing thief will be captured.
*Oṃ śāta he vajrāya śvāṭha*. This is the ritual for averting animals.
Thus, having placed in the center the name of whichever deity [is being practiced],
one should recite the mantra beginning with *oṃ*, followed by the name, and ending with *cchejaya svāhā*.

The Blessed One has definitively stated in the Root Tantra that accomplishments are attained through the performance of the fire-offering ritual (*homa*), and not merely by reading the volumes of scripture.
Regarding *ha*, the deity yoga for the activities such as *rañjana* (delighting) and so forth shall now be explained by means of the passage beginning with "Vajrā and...
Here, "Vajrā" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

That is the mountain-dweller. Gaurī is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); she is the one who experiences [it]. Vajradākinī is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); she is the one who discerns [it].
Vajraḍākinī is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); she is the one who impels [them].
Gaurī is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which causes one to fall;
she is that by which one is weighed.
Caurī is the object of cognition (*vedya*), the vajra *A*; she is that by which one is agitated.
The Dharmadhātu of Khecarī is Sāmānyavajrā, who performs the activity of slaying.
Likewise, the yellow Pukkasī performs the activity of paralyzing.
And by means of the light of the moon-like conch-shell, Māmakī performs the activity of pacifying.
By means of the pestle-mudrā, one brings [the object] under control; by means of the mortar-mudrā, one expels [the object].
By means of the [pestle-mudrā], [one performs the action].
Now, the yogi must understand all of this: yellow, white, and so forth. Through Vajradhātvīśvarī, one performs the rite of wrath;

through Jñānadākinī, the accomplishment of killing. By means of yellow, black, red, and blue colors, one performs the rites of delusion and so on. Through the yoga of the deity, one should accomplish the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and the assembly of torma offerings. This is the certainty of the Blessed One in the *Ḍamaruka-tantra*.

Whatever the Victorious Lord meditates upon, by that very act he perceives his own mind;
for all these forms are the mind that displays them. The engaging mind is also that single mind;
its non-conceptual power consists of the three doors of liberation.
Having realized the awareness that has existed throughout the three times, Vajrasattva gathered [the teachings] from the heart; through realization from the Oral Lineage (Śrutatantra),...
This is the commentary on the chapter beginning with "Ga.
In order that sentient beings may attain the path, Vajragarbha shall now explain this. One is the stage of generation, which consists of focusing upon sentient beings and phenomena.
Second, the objectless [meditation] is that which accomplishes the completion stage. Here, in the *Laghu-tantra*, the Blessed One gave this instruction:

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* Next, from this [text], the chapter on the deities shall be explained. Regarding the words "First, one should generate loving-kindness" and so forth, the initial sections are introduced according to the Root Tantra; as for the intermediate sections...
It is said that even at the final moment [this occurs].
Therein, the Blessed One declared: "By means of which mantra and mudrā, when distinguished, the yogi himself attains accomplishment."
The ritual for the accomplishment of the deity Līlāvajra shall be explained by Vajragarbha.
At the clarity of dawn, the mantrin—
After voiding urine and excrement and having purified myself with water,
I sit down comfortably on a soft seat.
Having fashioned a small vessel from the nature of the ten types of clay,
place it in your own mouth; then,
the five-headed demon will emerge.
Having performed the five direct perceptions, one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth,
in succession to Gaurī and the others.
In the east is Śvetadūti, the Dharma-thief Yamāntaka;
in the north is Vetālī;
in the west is Yakṣiṇī, the Ḍākinī.
Below, Bhūcarī resides; above, she is explained as being in the sky.
One should measure her according to the proportions of the ground-plan: in the northeast is Pukkasī, and likewise in the southeast is Śavarī.
At the crown of the head is Tumburu;
in the wind [channel] is Ḍombī; in the sequence of the earth [element], Keṅkaḍa Vajra is at the center of the wheel.
Offer together with Nairātmyā. Then, for the sake of all sentient beings, cultivate love, compassion, and so forth.
Having made those offerings, place them upon one's own body.
The seed-syllable of the name is the letter *A*; together with the syllables *kaṅ-bi-g* and *ra-wa-na*,
it is the *khams-kha-ron-ma*.
RĪ is for the element of taste;
Carcikā is from the element of the tangible; Dharmadhātveśvarī is for the element of phenomena. Herein, this chapter on the Father shall be explained.

Regarding the phrase "First, one should generate loving-kindness" and so forth, these words introduce the initial sections of the Root Tantra; they consist of the preliminary rites and the concluding rites.
The Blessed One then spoke: "By means of which mudrās and mantras, yogins shall distinguish their own nature. I, Vajragarbha, shall explain the ritual for the accomplishment of the deity."
After voiding urine and excrement and sitting upon a clean seat,
one should fashion a khaṭvāṅga consisting of ten parts and insert it into one's own mouth.
When the five Māras have arisen, having confronted them directly, one should offer flowers and so forth, as well as meat and the like, according to their respective types.
To Yama, the Lord of Death, one offers white food; to Dharmarāja, one offers meat; to the Vetālas, one offers blood from the direction of the water.
The yakṣī, the goddess, and the ḍākinī dwell below as the Earth-Walkers (khecara); above, they are explained as the Sky-Walkers (khecarī). One should worship them in that order.
In the northeast is Saurāṣṭra; in the southeast is likewise Giriṣa.
The boundary of the donor is Caṇḍālī; from the sequence of the wind and the *guhyamudrā*, one should worship Hevajra together with Nairātmyā at the center of the wheel.
Subsequently, one should recollect love, compassion, and so forth for the sake of sentient beings.
Having made offerings to those [deities], one should place them upon one's own body according to their respective locations.
As for the seed-syllables of the names: from the letter *ma* [the earth element] and the bindu, there is the *rasa* (taste) element; in the *rasa* element is *ghasrī*.
You are superior to the element of the knowable.
[From the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: The goddess Pūṣṇī is in the eyes; in the ears is Rūpavajrā;
the goddess Ghoṣā is in the nose; and in the tongue, Gandhavajrā is asserted to reside.
The body faculty is Hevajra, residing in the mind of Nairātmyā.

This is the initial placement of the syllables upon the continuum of consciousness. One should place the seed-syllables *ga*, *rba*, *gha*, *kha*, *pa*, *śa*, *ṭa*, and *naṃ* upon the explained elements. Then, one should contemplate the arising from the locations as follows:
Having meditated on the sevenfold respectful seats upon the mountain,
from the syllable HŪṂ arises a sun disk and a crossed vajra;
from that very vajra, there is a fence and—
This is also what is called "the visualization of the tent-like enclosure.

Regarding this very [practice], first of all, the mantra practitioner should perform the repelling of malevolent beings through the wheel of protection, and the driving away and pinning down of obstructors and those who lead one astray by means of the body of the King of Wrathful Deities; thereafter, one accomplishes the desired deity.

Through wisdom and skillful means, this *Hevajra Tantra*—which is a Yoga Tantra—is subsequently to be explained as a Yoginī Tantra by way of the conduct of the yoginīs, in the essence of the *Nairātmyā-sādhana*.
Therefore, according to the ritual of the Yoga Tantra, one should visualize the protective wheel (*rakṣācakra*) of the sovereign lords of the [Yamāri] family, such as Yamāntaka and others.
The principal deity of that wheel is Vajrahūṃkāra, who is none other than Hevajra.
First, with hope, he visualizes the mandala of the sun in front of him; in its center is a four-faced crossed vajra, which has arisen from the complete transformation of the syllable HŪṂ.

The Viśvavajra itself must merge with the sun into one. Then, the mantra practitioner should meditate upon vajra-fences, vajra-canopies, and vajra-foundations throughout all directions, above, and below—indestructible by anything—and outside the fence, as well as below and above, various terrifying weapons. Beyond that, one should proceed to the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*), where the Blessed One spoke these words regarding the seats of the wrathful kings:
"The seats of the wrathful kings shall be explained in sequence."

The faces, colors, hands, and implements, the left leg extended and the right drawn in—these are the feet. Regarding the sequence of the *Guhyasamāja* (Vajrapañjara): one should compose it according to the *Cakrasaṃvara* tantra. Both the lower part of the dance and the arrangement of the seats should also be performed.
By means of these eleven corpses, the solar mandala is established in its proper order.
The eleven solar paces are those very suns themselves.
Having discarded them, one should arrange the syllables *Soḥ* and *Hūṃ* upon the solar mandalas;
from the syllable *Hūṃ*, they arise and abide within the sun.
One should meditate on the kings of the wrathful deities.

Upon the central sun seat, one should visualize the Invoker Vajra-Hūṃkara. He is blue, with three faces and fierce eyes, standing with his left leg extended in a posture of defiance. His face is like the moon; he bares his fangs and is terrifyingly fierce. His left and right faces are white and red, respectively, just as they appear in the three primary [mandalas].
The vajra, the curved knife, and the trident are in the right hands in successive order;
the vajra, the small drum, and the skull-cup are likewise in the left hands.
He has a variegated vajra, a topknot, and fangs; he possesses Akṣobhya and a crescent moon.
From a garland of skulls upon his shoulders, there is a crown upon his head itself. He is endowed with bone ornaments and mudrās, and his waist is wrapped in a tiger skin.
With pure generosity, his tongue quivering, adorned with a continuous stream of snakes—
such as this Vajra Hūṃkāra, one should cause the hungry spirits to thirst.

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* Oṃ gagagagatāya sarvadūṣṭān phaṭ māraya phaṭ sarvapāpa phaṭ | Kīla āḥ vajradharā ājāpa ati sarva biganānāṃ śāyathā kacittaṃ kaila ya | Oṃ dāgar ā koṭaya ā keṭ | There is no meditation on entities, nor is there meditation itself. Thus, entities do not become real; meditation is non-existent. *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* One should summon Hevajra; the yogi himself becomes the embodiment of wrath. With the vajra-born compassion, one gazes upon the Lord in the sky.
The eight goddesses, adorned with all manner of ornaments, present offerings: Gaurī holds a great deer; Caurī holds a vessel that has triumphed over the Māras;
Vetālī holds a water-pot; and Ghasmarī holds medicine.
Pukkasī holds a vajra in her hand; Śavarī holds a corpse;
Caṇḍālī beats a hand-drum; Ḍombī is filled with passion.
Moon is described as *rajas* (menstrual blood); sun is urine. Water is semen.
*Svān* refers to marrow and flesh; it is explained as the vajra form of the Wrathful One.
*Rasa* is said to be the six tastes; *gokū* and so forth are the powers. *Tandu* is the offering of liquor; these are known as the eight commitments (*samaya*).
By means of these, the yogi should worship Hevajra, the principal deity, together with his retinue. Then, the practitioner of mantra should take refuge in the Three Jewels,
confess all misdeeds, and rejoice in merit.
One’s own body itself is like snow, and it too depends upon the path.

Having thoroughly generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should pray for the Buddhas to depart. While acting for the benefit of others within emptiness, one should analyze even the act of begging in this way:
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty; it is without cause, without effect, and without conditions.
Since it is eternally non-existent, there is no engagement with it, and it is devoid of volitional formation. Because it is without arising and ceasing, it is without increase or decrease.

There is no Buddha and no sentient being; there is no phenomenon and no substratum of phenomena. Just as with a mirage, a dream, snow, or a city of gandharvas, so too should Buddhas and sentient beings be viewed through the meditation on suchness.

Just as a reflection appears upon a mountain, so too do the Buddhas hear the Dharma. Having analyzed it in such a manner, until the end of existence, for the sake of becoming a cause for the excellence of sentient beings, the Bodhisattvas—though remaining in the lotus-like state—do not waver from the afflictions, the maras, the entrance into the [three] realms, or the obscurations of the knowable. *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* Having thus analyzed in detail, until the end of cyclic existence, for the sake of the excellence of sentient beings, the Bodhisattvas remain; though they do not waver from the afflictions, the maras, the entrance into the [three] realms, or the obscurations of the knowable.
Even though the Great Wrathful One has certainly incinerated it, he protects even a mere fraction of it;
[this is] the great heroic Bodhisattva.
Those who have compassion for all sentient beings, having thoroughly investigated all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves, [should practice].
Within the expanse of emptiness, one should recite this secret mantra:
*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Having recited that, one should then bring to mind the *dharmadhātu*.
With that mind of aspiration and the pride of being a mantra practitioner,

one should perform the circumambulation for the purpose of sporting [in the mandala]. Here, one should visualize the wheel of the mandala to be explained, adorned with eight petals, and in its center, an eight-petaled lotus.
One should meditate upon the mandala of the [deity] and then, by way of the nature of the dharmadhātu, upon the seat of the corpse.
From the causes of the Buddhas' names, there are the thirty-two vowels of the moon and the eighty consonants of the sun.
In the center of faith is the syllable HŪṂ; that itself is called the "aspect of the sattva. It is the nature of the innate joy of the deity, the mirror-like wisdom, and the wisdom of equality.
From the stages of conceptualization without [inherent] existence,
those [deities] accomplish the single activity;
this occurs through the complete perfection of the form.
This is the explanation of the dharmadhātu;
it is the supreme fifth, the indeterminate.
It is the manifest awakening of the various deities.
He is the two-armed Hevajra,
with a complexion like the dawn, the stars, or Brahmā;
he possesses the splendor and majesty of a red lotus.
Wearing a garland of skulls upon his head,
with Akṣobhya as his crest-jewel, he possesses a wheel and earrings.
The crown, earrings, bracelets, necklace,
and belt are renowned as the five mudrās, being the complete purity of the five Buddhas.

(74) Regarding the *Guhyasamāja-tantra* treatises and the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: by means of the rites of fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and other acts of worship, from the perspective of the *prakṛti* (nature); by means of the chapter on the certainty of accomplishment (*siddhiniścaya*), from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; and by means of the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) as found in the *tantra* and other sources. By means of the chapter on the festival of Hevajra (*hevajrotsava*), from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the purification of the *mudrā* and the ritual for drawing the *paṭa*, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the book of Hevajra, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the purification of food, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the characteristics of the *padminī* woman and the chapter on the characteristics of the disciple, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the purification of the image and the chapter on the grasping of mantras, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; by means of the chapter on the recitation of mantras, from the perspective of the *prakṛti*; and by means of the chapter on the authorization for the yoga of the innate meaning (*sahajārtha*). This very *tantra* consists of twenty-two chapters on the nature of reality (*svābhāvika*). The Blessed Lord Hevajra spoke to Vajragarbha: "At that time, this essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas is the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*). It is the venerable lord, more secret than the secret, and the most secret of all secrets. O Vajragarbha, listen well, listen well! You who are fully satisfied with the desire for duality—listen to the essence of Vajrasattva; listen to Samayasattva, Mahāsattva, Mahābodhisattva, and Hevajra. [The text ends with] "He dwelt there," according to the words of the Blessed One. Therefore, the phrase "dwelt there" is the beginning of the words of the Blessed One. Consequently, having previously spoken, the Blessed One describes his place of residence. These words—"Thus have I heard at one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in the *bhagas* of the Vajra-women of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas"—are uttered by the Blessed One in response to the request of Vajragarbha. Are these words "Thus have I heard at one time" spoken by the omniscient Guru? Or are they a summary of the treatise (*śāstra*) intended for worldly purposes? Both positions are flawed. If it were a report of what was heard in the past, there would be no knowledge of the future based on another's scripture. Furthermore, such introductory phrases used by compilers of treatises are meaningless, as they were not spoken by Vajrasattva himself. Therefore, these words are to be understood as having a specific purpose and relying upon intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*). Their meaning is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This Buddha-casket, the locus of great bliss, has the form of a high letter *ya*, the most excellent shape adorned with a lotus-stalk;
it is the Great Bliss of Vajrasattva, the very self of the Guru. This Great Bliss was heard and known by me personally at one time, from a single moment of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

The Blessed One is great bliss; all Buddhas are the intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) for the five aggregates taken together; body, speech, and mind are the Vajras; the left [side] refers to physical, vocal, and mental activities; the Vajra Consorts are the sense faculties, objects, and so forth; the Vajra Elements are space and the rest; "upward and upward" refers to the cutting of the skull-torch; the distinction of coming and going pertains to the five locations of the throat, heart, and navel;
the threefold division within the *bhagas* is the division of the navel, the secret place, and the form-vajra jewel.
The distinctions of bliss and so forth, the dwelling in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*),
the inversion, and the loss of qualities [occur] in the secret place, the jewel, the navel, and the crown; specifically, for the sake of the exhaustion of the aggregates,
they dwell in the divisions of the heart, throat, forehead, and skull by way of the distinctions of the outflow (*nisyanda*) fruit and so forth.
From the passage beginning with "the aggregates and so forth," which illuminates the prostration of great bliss,
the letter *ya* represents Locanā and the letter *va* represents Māmakī.
The syllable MA is Pāṇḍarā,
the syllable YĀ is Tāriṇī, and the syllable ŚRŪ is Vajradhātveśvarī.
The letter *ta* is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
while the aggregates (*skandhas*) are again the letter *ya*, which is the beginning of Vajrasattva and the others.
The letter *ka* is Akṣobhya and so forth; the letter *si* is Amoghasiddhi and so forth;
the letter *sa* is Ratnasaṃbhava and so forth.
The syllable MA represents Amitābha and others; the syllable YA represents Vairocana and others;
the syllable BHA represents Gandhavajrā and others.

Ānanda, the wheel of the form-body is awakened through the purity of its characteristics.

Picūvajra (? Heruka, the principal [deity] with sixteen feet, is the Heruka of the *svābhāvika-dharmakāya*. [This is according to] the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*: the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*.

Compassion: *Vajraprajñāṣaṭsāhasrikāhevajraṭīkā*, [referring to] compassion that is without support for sentient beings (*sattva-nirālambā*) and without support for phenomena (*dharma-nirālambā*).
*He* and *Vaṃ* are speech.

O Vajra! The *Yogatantra* of the nature of emptiness consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Through the yoga of means and through wisdom as well, Hevajra is the *Yogatantra* free from duality. Indeed, the *Samāja* is the union of wisdom and means; thus, by the names of wisdom and means, the means exist on the left, while it is explained to me that wisdom proceeds from the right. That which is called the *Upāyatantra* is the practice of the *mudrā-maṇḍala*, characterized by arising and destruction. The yoga of wisdom and means is characterized by the non-duality of the three vajras. It is the unity of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the non-duality of emptiness and compassion. The four liberations (*vimokṣa*) are emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-origination. The sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Because of the perfect awakening to phenomena, they are free from obstacles and devoid of duality. Wisdom and means are also the non-dual vajra-bodies, the six sense bases, the elements, the faculties, and their objects, by which the action and the agent proceed. This is the restraint (*saṃvara*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, established in the syllable *evaṃ*. Listen to the *Tantra* whose nature is wisdom and means. Listen to me regarding the distinctions of number, divided into the three defects, the fifty, and the sixty-fold divisions. The realization of reality (*tattvāvabodha*) is the establishment of the state of the *Yogatantra* by the Blessed One, the cause for the arising of the Yoginīs. Now it shall be told: the five elements, the four worlds, and the six faculties. There is a division into fifteen digits (*kalā*) starting with Nairātmyā. The syllable *HŪṂ* is the cause of those [deities], and Heruka is the light of gnosis (*jñānāloka*). From that, what kind of goddesses arose? O Vajragarbha, listen! Hevajra speaks: the goddess Cākṣuṣī is the speaker, the *mudrā* for paralyzing and expelling, and Mārāṇī for killing—listen, O Vajragarbha! This is the rule for the arising and abiding of the goddesses. Now the cause of their arising shall be told: beginning with the syllable *evaṃ*, the syllable *evaṃ* is the cause of Heruka; the syllable *HŪṂ* is the cause of the second [deity]. By the relationship of object and subject, and by the actual state of things, through the union of the sense faculties and their objects, various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are seen. They are seen bound by the bonds of the five aggregates (*skandha*). Through the awakening to that—the cessation of the activity of the sense faculties and their objects—one is liberated. One sees by means of the faculty of sight; the five conceptualizations are liberated. For the Blessed One, there is no conceptualization; likewise for form and the other [objects]. Therefore, hands and feet are everywhere; faces with eyes are everywhere; ears pervade all, and he exists thus. The supreme meditation (*dhyāna*) of wisdom and means shall now be declared. Meditation and the object of meditation exist by the state of space; meditation is free from atoms and dreams. Having perceived it with gnosis, contemplate it as free from conceptualization. That direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of four kinds: sensory cognition, mental cognition, the yogic, and that which has entered through the knowledge of instruction and scripture. Thus, one is established by nine examples: a reflection, an image, sound, wind, an illusion, a creator, a mirage, a mirror, and a reflection in water. Space is wisdom; the drop (*bindu*) is the form of wisdom. (Prajñāpāramitā; Heruka)
As is Prajñā, so is Upāya. In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* it is said: "Thus, Prajñā and Upāya are the Cakra, the Karmamudrā, and the Jñānamudrā."

Great Bliss. The channels of the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*).
Ka, etc. The unstruck (*anāhata*) sound. *Evaṃ*.
Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ka; Visarga; ha and the *ha*-class consonants;
ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; i; cu; ya, śa; the letter *ya*.

*Tā, thā, dā, dhā, nā*; *ḷ, tu, la, sā, sā, śā, sā, jñā*—thus, thus, *Lalanā* is *Prajñā* and *Rasanā* is *Upāya*.

‘Prajñā’, the practitioner’s ‘Upāya’, the ‘Vajrin’ as ‘Prajñā-Śiva’, the ‘Śakti’ as ‘Lalanā’, the sequence of emanation (*sr̥ṣṭi-krama*), ‘Vijñāna’, ‘Saṃskāra’ (formative actions), ‘Vedanā’, ‘Saṃjñā’, and ‘Rūpa’.

Rasanā is engaged in the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*). Lalanā and Rasanā are the channels (*nāḍī*); Rasanā is the channel of Capricorn (*makara-lagna*), [consisting of] *khā*, *gā*, *ghā*, *ṅā*. Lalanā is the channel of Aquarius (*kumbha-lagna*), [consisting of] *vijñāna* (*ṅā*), *ghā*, *gā*, *khā*, *kā*. And [Lalanā is] the channel of Pisces (*mīna-lagna*), [consisting of] *ca*, *chā*, *jā*, *jhā*, *ñā*. [Rasanā is] the channel of Aries (*meṣa-lagna*), [consisting of] *ñā*, *jhā*, *jā*, *chā*, *ca*. [Lalanā is] the channel of Taurus (*vṛṣa-lagna*), [consisting of] *tā*, *thā*, *dā*, *dhā*, *ṇā*. [Rasanā is] the channel of Gemini (*mithuna-lagna*), [consisting of] *ṇā*, *dhā*, *dā*, *thā*, *tā*. [Lalanā is] the channel of Cancer (*karkaṭa-lagna*), [consisting of] *pā*, *phā*, *bā*, *bhā*, *mā*. [Rasanā is] the channel of Leo (*siṃha-lagna*), [consisting of] *mā*, *bhā*, *bā*, *phā*, *pā*. [Lalanā is] the channel of Virgo (*kanyā-lagna*), [consisting of] *tā*, *thā*, *dā*, *dhā*, *nā*. [Rasanā is] the channel of Libra (*tulā-lagna*), [consisting of] *nā*, *dhā*, *dā*, *thā*, *tā*. [Lalanā is] the channel of Scorpio (*vṛścika-lagna*), [consisting of] *sā*, *śā*, *kṣā*, *jñā*. [Rasanā is] the channel of Sagittarius (*dhanu-lagna*), [consisting of] *kṣā*, *jñā*, *sā*, *śā*, *sā*. The Northern Solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the Southern Solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) are the wheels of emanation (*nirmāṇa-cakra*). The locations of emptiness (*śūnya-sthāna*) are as follows: thus, the channels of the wheel of emanation are empty channels, empty channels, and the central channel (*avadhūtī*). The mandala of gnosis (*jñāna-maṇḍala*) is at the navel; the staffs (*daṇḍa*), the moments (*vikalā*), the channels, and the mandalas are emptiness. The wheel of emanation consists of the odd signs (*viṣama-lagna*); Lalanā is the even signs (*sama-lagna*). The central channel (*avadhūtī*) is the even and odd signs. The mandala of gnosis is the wheel of emanation. The staffs are the transits of the staffs (*daṇḍa-saṃkrāntayaḥ*), which are emptiness. The transits of the wheel of dharma (*dharma-cakra*) are the watches (*prahara*). Lalanā and Rasanā are the signs (*lagna*). The channels of the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhoga-cakra*) are the enjoyments. The guru is the moment (*muhūrta*). The transits are the transits at the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), the twilights (*saṃdhyā*), and the transits. This is the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*. The vital breath (*prāṇa*), the staffs, and the channels are the mandalas of the wheel of emanation—mandala, mandala, mandala, mandala. The verses on the signs are the channels of the four seats (*catuḥpīṭha*): Lalanā and Rasanā are the channels. Rasanā is Akṣobhya; Lalanā is Prajñā.

Rasanā, Avadhūtī, Lalana; Rasanā, Avadhūtī. The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* states: Vajrā, Nāḍī, Indivisible (Abhedyā), Ai, U, R, I, A, E, Ar, O, Al, Ha, Ya, Ra, Va, La; Sūkṣmarūpā, Divyā, Vāmā, Kūrmajā, Bhāvakī, Sekā, Dosā, Vistā, Mātrikā, Śarvarī, Sītadā, Ūṣmā—these are Lalana.

Rasanā: *l*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *ha*; *āl*, *au*, *ār*, *ai*, *ā*; *ḷ*, *ū*, *ᾷ*, *ī*, *ā*. Vajragarbha, listen to this secret beyond secrets, which I have taught as the bestower of liberation upon yogins and the cause of all accomplishments.
Indeed, the Gnosis Body (jñānakāya) has been described by Vajrasattva as the Lord residing at the navel, the secret place, and the center of the three peaks.
Like streaks of lightning, they move up and down above the essence and cause the sense faculties located within the body to burst forth.
That Bhuvaneśvarī resides in the navel, on the southern peak, in the secret place, resembling a flash of lightning.
She is called Caṇḍālī because she is known as self-luminous wisdom. Above there are three peaks, and likewise below.
The peak of Brahmā is in the middle, the peak of Viṣṇu to the left, and the peak of Rudra to the right, by which [the channels carry] feces, urine, and semen.
The peak of Rāhu is said to be in the middle of the Moon (the left), the peak of Sūrya to the right, by which [the elements] water, fire, and space [are conveyed].
They say Lalanā is on the left and Rasanā likewise on the right; Avadhūtī is situated in the middle, and Dombinī is designated as Vāyu (wind).
Having formed three paths from the navel to the middle of the heart, they proceeded; having formed three paths from the heart to the region of the throat, they proceeded;
indeed, having formed three paths from the middle of the forehead to the end of the throat, they proceeded;
having formed three paths from the middle of the forehead to the crown of the head, they proceeded; and having formed three paths from the crown of the head to the tip of the nose, they proceeded.
*Lalana* is the left nostril, *rasanā* is the right nostril, and *avadhūtī* is situated in the middle.

The five wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the navel, the five groups, and the three paths are traversed by the coming and going of *avadhūtī* at the junctions. *Lalana* and *rasanā* indeed proceed from petal to petal; having pierced Rāhu at the navel, they flow as the waves of the sun and moon.
Having pierced the crown, she goes forth; she is called Avadhūtī. In the yoga of the union (*sampuṭayoga*), the Caṇḍālī blazes up from below within the Lalanā and Rasanā.
Having burned [the elements] in the center of the navel, she proceeds by way of the Dombī path; piercing Rāhu and the Moon, she touches the Haṃsa.
Touched by the Haṃsa, she flows as white nectar, burning the five constituent elements while bearing the five mandalas.
When the objects of the senses have been ceased, supreme bliss arises; the drop (*bindu*) flows from the moon, and the *haṃsa* abides in the head.
Rāhu indeed [abides] within the moon, and from the forehead down to the throat, Candālikā proceeds through the center of the navel by means of the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*).
Having proceeded by way of the secret wheel, she is known as the "Great Beast" (*mahāpaśu*); situated below the trident, she is called the "Three-Fold Mouth."

The *paśu* (the bound soul) belongs to the seven classes of beings; it moves within the sphere of the Siddhas and Khecaras. In a state of fainting (*mūrchā*), it destroys all disease; in dissolution (*laya*), it removes the qualities of the elements. When there is an obstruction of the objects of the senses, it indeed bestows sovereignty. Endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā*, it indeed grants the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
It quickly bestows the state of being a Buddha in the activities of waking and so forth, just as mercury, when bound, is bound by the drop of its own knowledge.

When [the vital essence] is wounded by the secret wheel at the end of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Paśu, it bestows longevity; through its powerful upward projection, Rāhu is declared to be above, while the Sun and Moon are called the Great Animals (mahāpaśu). Indeed, falling into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), they grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Blood, sinews, and marrow must be caused to fall with effort; here, these are to be understood as the animals, for no animal exists outside.
Within this body, the Lord is the animal through the practice of seven births; all six types of bodily constituents (dhātu) have been consumed and drunk.
Those who have become sentient beings cook [their own flesh]; that is their first birth. Therefore, they become blood-beings, and this is seen as the second stage.

After that, they become meat-eaters; in the fourth stage, they become skin-makers. In the fifth, the channels are produced, and in the sixth, the bones are manifested. In the seventh, they indeed become marrow-beings, established in seven revolutions. The six sheaths are known as the foundations of the lineages.

They say that the family (*kula*) is the body; from the family the atom (*aṇu*) is produced, and its power (*śakti*) is said to be the impurities (*mala*). That is the cause for the birth of the body.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is well-established there, situated between the two [extremes]. He who is Heruka, the Lord of All, whose nature is the three worlds, joined with the sun and moon, exists both above and below.

There are exactly four channels (nāḍīs), which are proclaimed as the wheel (cakra) at the crown of the head; there are thirty-two channels in the throat-wheel (kaṇṭhacakra); eight channels in the forehead; sixty-four channels in the heart and the navel; and thirty-two channels in that which is called the secret place (guhya). These wheels and channels may also be known as petals or as lotuses (padma). Indeed, the Yoginīs are to be grasped as those who perform manifold ritual actions; they are the objects of the senses and the cognitions of the senses. All the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and secondary seats (apīṭhas) are the channels, the petals, and the lotuses.
Mahāmāyā is situated there at the crown of the head together with the four goddesses.
Its origin is in the center of the navel; first, it is superior to the mandalas on the forehead, where the Picuvajra resides, and there the eight channels have their support.
Likewise, they are located in the pair of eyes, as well as in the ears, nose, and pair of tongues.
Gaurī and other goddesses, such as Rūpā and so forth, are the elements beginning with earth within the sphere.
In the nature of Nairātmyā, the lunar digits (*candrakalā*) have been described.

Picuvajra has three faces and six arms; in the throat are the thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*). Viṣṇu, belonging to the family of Akṣobhya, has four arms and resides in the heart together with the eight goddesses. In the navel of the three worlds, he dwells together with the sixty-four Yoginīs.
The five ḍākas and the five ḍākinīs reside in the five cakras, while the Lord resides in the secret cakra.
He is the Lord of the three worlds, together with the thirty-two ḍākinīs; these sixty-five deities of the six cakras constitute the Kālacakra of the six families.
In the forehead and the head there are twenty channels, as well as nasal obstruction and phlegm; in the throat and the heart there are forty [channels], as well as bile.
There are sixteen channels at the navel and eight channels at the secret place that sustain the winds.
In the secret wheel, ten channels are naturally obstructive.
Three channels, one above and one below, obstruct the six wheels.
Within the body, the channels are empty; there are seventy-two thousand of them, and there are as many goddesses within the body. The number of body hairs is three and a half crores;
the number of body hairs within the body is the same as that which exists externally.

Six breaths constitute one *pāṇīpala*; sixty *pāṇīpalas* constitute one *ghaṭikā*. Two *ghaṭikās* constitute a *muhūrta*; three-quarters of a *ghaṭikā* [is added] to [each] *muhūrta* to form a *prahara*; five *ghaṭikās* constitute a *lagna*. One *lagna* is a single *prahara*; two *praharas* constitute a junction (*saṃdhi*); and at four such junctions, day and night are completed for sentient beings.

The twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*) are the day and night; twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths (*śvāsa*) are the solar *daṇḍas*; twenty-four fortnights (*pakṣa*), twelve months, six seasons (*ṛtu*), and four ages (*yuga*).

There are three times (*kāla*) and two solstices (*ayana*) in the body. A day consists of one hundred and eighty breaths; according to the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*, a fortnight consists of one thousand eight hundred breaths, a month [of thirty-six hundred], a season [of three thousand six hundred], and a *yuga* [of four thousand five hundred].

Time consists of seven hundred and twenty breaths; a solstice (*ayana*) consists of eighteen hundred and ten breaths; two solstices consist of eighteen thousand breaths; and there are twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*). The intermediate breaths (*madhya-śvāsa*) are sixty-seven thousand five hundred and sixty-five, calculated by quarters of fortnights. In the *avadhūtī*, time consists of three fortnights and three years of breaths, which is the death of sentient beings. In the *lalanā*, during day and night, the death of the Moon occurs after three years.

In five nights, there is solar death on the right solar channel; in three years, [death occurs] in the left channel after three days. The zodiacal wheel situated [therein] undergoes a loss of its [full] duration through three years.
In the second [case], confinement necessarily occurs after six months and three days;
thus, three days are added to the three months.
Within three years, the eleventh chapter [of signs] is gradually abandoned.
The left [channel] continuously [abandons its portion] in thirty-three days; with a triple interval by the sun, the breath abandons the *garbhaka* in three days, and death occurs in one night.
By ten nights, the zodiac sign in the southern channel [is abandoned]; in the second chapter, death occurs within two years.
In the third [case], death occurs in fifteen days or in one year;
in the fourth, death occurs in twenty days or in six months;
in the fifth, death occurs in twenty-five days or in three months.
In the sixth [chapter], one lives for two months with twenty-six days;
in the seventh, for one month with twenty-seven days.
Beyond that, one should abandon the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh chapters after thirty-three days, [calculated] by multiplying the number of days, lunar dates, and directions by five.
Having abandoned the right, the breath moves to the left; for one day it remains in the middle.
When the irregularity of the breath arises, one has reached death: the semen flows downward and the menstrual blood (rajas) flows upward.
The mind is bound by the breath through karma; due to the power of karma there is death and rebirth, yet rebirth does not occur in that same way.

Just as knowledge comes from a teacher, as a lamp from a lamp, as a seal from a seal, as a face from a face in a mirror; as sound from an echo, fire from a sun-crystal, and light from the sun; as saliva from eating an *āmlikā* fruit, and as a sprout from another *āmlikā* tree from its seed—without these, there is no nature of cause and effect.

All phenomena arise neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause; such is the case everywhere. *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* Oṃ. The syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are primordially unarisen.

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* **Six-Armed Hevajra:** *Oṃ deva picūvajra hūṃ (3) phaṭ svāhā* **Four-Armed Hevajra:** *Oṃ kiṭi-kiṭi vajra hūṃ (3) phaṭ svāhā* **[General Mantra]:** *Oṃ jvala-jvala-bhyo hūṃ (3) phaṭ svāhā*

*Oṃ āḥ hūṃ tathāgata vairocana amitābha akṣobhya a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ l̥ l̥ e ai o au aṃ etc.* Thus, the *purakṣobhamantra* (mantra for harassing the city): *Oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā*.
The cerebrals are [ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa]; u, pu, va, and upadhmānīya are the labials;
l, tu, la, and sa are the dentals.
Om, a, ā, ha—beginning from this [point] are ṇa, ṇa, ṇa, ma, ṇa, kṣa, svāhā.

The *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* [states]: *Ā*, *ka*, *ca*, *ta*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *sa*; *āli-kāli*: *a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū ḷ e ai ar āl au al aṃ aḥ*; *ha ha ya ya ra rā va vā la lā*; *ka kā kha khā ga gā gha ghā ṅa ṅā*; *ca ca cha chā ja jā jha jhā ña ñā*; *ta ta tha thā da dā dha dhā ṇa ṇā*; *pa pā pha phā ba bā bha bhā ma mā*; *ta tā tha thā da dā dha dhā na nā*; *sa sā ṣa ṣā śa śā kṣa kṣā*. *Oṃ vausat*. Recite: *Oṃ hrīḥ kurukullā oṃ rakṣa vajrahuṃkāra krodharāja yamāntaka prajñāntaka padmāntaka vighnāntaka acala tarkvi nīladaṇḍa mahābala uṣṇīṣa śumbharāja rakṣā huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (29) The practitioner should perform [the rites]. By means of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of mind, speech, and body, in their respective order, the activities such as paralyzing (*stambhana*) and so forth are accomplished. (30) These rites are always accomplished by means of the maṇḍalas consisting of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and gnosis (*jñāna*). (31) Deafness, blindness, delusion, paralysis, and intoxication are likewise accomplished by the aforementioned seed-syllables. (32–34) In a forest, on a mountain, or in a pavilion of trees, on the seashore, in a cremation ground, or at a place of accomplishment (*siddha*), first perform the recitation of mantras and meditation. Having offered the oblation (*homa*), one should draw the maṇḍala with one's own essence; for him, there is never a failure in accomplishment. (33–34) Even in other places, if the mantra of the Goddess is pleased by this, the ritual action is performed by that very means, even by a king or a serpent. (35)
Therefore, the wise one should recite the name; he should always meditate with the body alone.
With the body alone, the mantra comes into being. The heart-mantra consists of speech;
the mental mantra is the *upahṛdaya* (near-heart), which is declared to be the seed-syllable of gnosis (*jñāna-bīja*). His *jñāna-mantra* shall be as follows: (36–37)
The subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) is [worshipped] with the seed-mantras (*bījamantra*), and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).

This sequence of meditation and recitation (*japa*)—pertaining respectively to wisdom, mind, speech, and body—is always performed with diligence through worship, recitation, and so forth; then it shall bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), otherwise it will not grant accomplishment at all. (38–39)
If, through mere faith, there should thus arise bodily affliction, then [the syllables] ya-ra-la-ca-ta are declared to be air, fire, earth, and water.
(40) These should be applied by the wise in order to the directions starting from the east: fire, north-east, south-west, wind, and likewise the north-east. (41)
Having performed the *ha-hā* placement slightly below that, one should likewise worship again;

with *aṃ* and *āḥ*, one should worship the mandala of all Buddhas in the center. The Guru should always draw the mandala according to the previous method. Furthermore, one should draw the mandala of the five Jinas by this very same [method]. The Dharma, recited from the mouth of another, was previously taught in the circular [mandala] of the wind-mandala in Videha. (42–43)
Due to its nature as a circle of fire (*agni-maṇḍala*), Jambudvīpa is triangular; in the western portion lies the square land-mass of Aparagodānīya;

(44) and Uttarakuru has the shape of a half-moon, [arising] from the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*). Indeed, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is of the nature of emptiness (*śūnya*), yet it is again of the nature of Lakṣmī.
(45) Below is the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*), the Sun of Knowledge (*jñānārka*), the emission (*visarga*), and the Bindu situated in the center.
Then, having drawn the deity upon the mountain—both below and above—one should worship it with mantras and so forth.

(46–53) Now, one should draw the mandala as before, a mandala of dust. The six aggregates (*skandhas*), the elements (*dhātus*), the six sense organs (*indriyas*), and their objects (*viṣayas*)—these thirty-six should always be worshipped.

(47) The earth element, water, fire, wind, semen, and blood are the six elements (*dhātus*). Furthermore, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) among living beings is revealed as the six constituents (*ṣaṭkāyas*). (48)

The [consonants] ending in the throat, palate, and head, those of the lips and teeth, and those with the nose—though consisting of six types, cognition arises through the application of existence and non-existence. (49)

44. That is the heart of the mantras and the source of the arising of their reflections.

50. And the bodily signs of an enemy are those of a friend who is not indifferent. 51. (128) The voice of an enemy takes away the life of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt. 52. Indeed, from the characteristics of an enemy's bodily signs, diseases arise.

53. (129) The five gutturals (*kavarga*) are, by their nature as consonants, of one single heap. 54. Their families are to be known according to the sequence of the elements, beginning with earth. 55. 56. Gha, jha, ḍha, bha, and ḍha are enemies born of water. 57. (131) Ga, ja, da, ba, and da are enemies born of earth. Kha, cha, tha, pha, and tha are enemies born of wind.

*Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā* (1): Huṃ Hevajra; *Ananta*, Āḥ Phūḥ Nāga; Aṃ.
The five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are *nāgadamanaka* and elephant ichor (*hastimada*).
(The *saṃpuṭa* and *maṇḍala* [are also included]).
Ananta.
